article_title: GEMS Space Science Sequence
citation: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, What Works Clearinghouse. (2012, June). Science intervention report: Great Explorations in Math and Science® (GEMS®) Space Science Sequence. http://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Reform-based space science unit pattern: models, hands-on investigations, peer discussion, and misconception-targeted activities
description: The GEMS® Space Science Sequence embodies a reform-based instructional pattern in which "The sequence utilizes models, hands-on investigations, peer-to-peer discussions, reflection, and informational student readings." Activities "target core space science concepts and common misconceptions that students might have about them", and students working in small groups "evaluate alternative explanations, use evidence to support them, and critique the merits of an explanation." Each unit builds on knowledge from previous units and can also be used independently.
requirements: Teacher professional development and implementation support as provided in the evaluated study
Small-group work structures for evaluating and critiquing explanations
constraints: In the evaluated trial, teachers in both groups were instructed to refrain from adding any activities to those present in their assigned curriculum
target_learning_goals: Core space science concepts and addressing common student misconceptions
Evaluating alternative explanations and using evidence in science
examples: The trial compared this pattern against a district curriculum centered on a more didactic presentation of space science concepts, including direct instruction, reading of text, and students answering very focused questions
key_sources: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, What Works Clearinghouse. (2012, June). Science intervention report: Great Explorations in Math and Science® (GEMS®) Space Science Sequence. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/612

article_title: Closer to Home
citation: Ehrlich, S.B., Connors, M.C., Stein, A.G., Francis, J., Easton, J.Q., Kabourek, S.E., & Farrar, I.C. (2020). Closer to home: More equitable pre-k access and enrollment in Chicago. Chicago, IL: UChicago Consortium on School Research, NORC at the University of Chicago, and Start Early. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/
title: Use the geographic distribution of school-based pre-k classrooms—particularly full-day classrooms—as a policy lever for equitable access and enrollment
description: The article concludes that where districts place pre-k classrooms, especially full-day ones, shapes which student groups can access and enroll in pre-k, and that deliberately reallocating classrooms toward under-enrolled, high-need neighborhoods can reduce enrollment inequities. As the authors state, "the geographic distribution of school-based pre-k (particularly full-day) may be an important policy lever for addressing inequities in student access and enrollment in Chicago." Chicago reallocated classrooms and converted half-day to full-day classrooms in neighborhoods with high poverty and low pre-k enrollment.
requirements: Districts must be able to reallocate or convert classrooms across neighborhoods and fund full-day options, as Chicago did through strategies including a federal Preschool Development Grant-Expansion.
constraints: The study is descriptive and does not directly test policy effectiveness or identify access as a causal mechanism for enrollment changes; findings are interpreted as observed patterns and initial evidence of potential levers.
target_learners: four-year-old pre-k students, particularly students of color, English Learners, and students from low-income families
target_learning_goals: equitable access to and enrollment in high-quality early childhood education
examples: CPS reallocated pre-k classrooms to neighborhoods with a history of under-enrollment, expanded full-day options in high-need neighborhoods, and centralized the application process with prioritization for high-priority students.
key_sources: Ehrlich, S.B., Connors, M.C., Stein, A.G., Francis, J., Easton, J.Q., Kabourek, S.E., & Farrar, I.C. (2020). Closer to home: More equitable pre-k access and enrollment in Chicago. Chicago, IL: UChicago Consortium on School Research, NORC at the University of Chicago, and Start Early. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/closer-to-home

article_title: High-Quality Early Childhood Assessment: Learning from States' Use of Kindergarten Entry Assessments
citation: Yun, C., Melnick, H., & Wechsler, M. (2021). High-quality early childhood assessment: Learning from states' use of kindergarten entry assessments. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/high-quality-kea
title: Georgia GKIDS Readiness Check: a brief KEA embedded in a yearlong formative assessment system
description: Georgia's Readiness Check, used since 2016, is the first part of the GKIDS assessment system, 'a yearlong suite of kindergarten assessments connected to state content standards that provides teachers with ongoing information needed to guide instruction.' It covers social and emotional learning, English language arts, and mathematics while remaining relatively brief: 10 of 20 items are direct assessment performance tasks such as naming letters and counting aloud, and 10 are observation-based. It aligns with the Work Sampling System used in Georgia's preschool program, and all new kindergarten teachers must complete initial professional development on the GKIDS system.
requirements: All new kindergarten teachers must complete initial professional development on the GKIDS assessment system
target_learners: kindergarten children in Georgia public schools
target_learning_goals: social and emotional learning, English language arts, and mathematics readiness
examples: Figure 5 shows the Readiness Check includes 10 performance tasks
key_sources: Yun, C., Melnick, H., & Wechsler, M. (2021). High-quality early childhood assessment: Learning from states' use of kindergarten entry assessments. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/high-quality-kea

article_title: Community Schools Certification: An Approach for Implementation
citation: Germain, E., Maier, A., Espinoza, D., & Oakes, J. (2025). Community schools certification: An approach for implementation. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/220.412
title: Georgia Department of Education LEAD staged certification and recognition pilot for whole child education model schools
description: From 2021 to 2023, the Georgia Department of Education piloted a certification and recognition process for community schools implementing a whole child education model. The process recognized schools as they progressed through stages characterized by the acronym LEAD (Learning, Emerging, Achieving, Distinguished), each with benchmarks for structures and processes; later stages expected evidence of integration with the schoolwide improvement plan, impact, and outcomes. The finalized standards and coaching were praised by educators, but the pilot faced capacity challenges and was shut down for consolidation and reorganization.
requirements: Sufficient capacity within the certifying agency and completed certification materials, including consensus-defined standards and a rubric, before launch.
constraints: The pilot faced challenges throughout due to capacity issues within the Department of Education and a rush to begin before certification materials were completed.
target_learners: K-12 students in Georgia community schools
target_learning_goals: staged implementation progress
whole child education
examples: Later stages (Achieving and Distinguished) expected evidence of integration with the schoolwide improvement plan, impact, and outcomes.
key_sources: Germain, E., Maier, A., Espinoza, D., & Oakes, J. (2025). Community schools certification: An approach for implementation. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/220.412

article_title: New Mexico Community School Profile: Los Padillas Elementary School
citation: Germain, E. (2024). New Mexico community school profile: Los Padillas Elementary School. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/new-mexico-community-school-los-padillas-brief
title: Genius Hour: student-elected enrichment blocks in the extended day with showcase events
description: Genius Hour is Los Padillas's extended-day enrichment structure in which "Students select an extracurricular activity to focus on daily for 6 weeks," with options ranging "from coding, robotics, and circuits to knitting, soccer, martial arts, and mariachi." All teachers are involved, keeping classes small for individualized attention, and academic skills are woven in informally. Each 6-week cycle ends with a Genius Hour Showcase where parents and caregivers observe what students produced, serving also as family engagement.
requirements: Extended day schedule with time built in for enrichment
All teachers involved so classes stay small
constraints: Devised as part of the school redesign and directly tied to community priorities gathered in visioning sessions
target_learners: Elementary students (PreK–5) in a Title I, predominantly Hispanic dual language school
target_learning_goals: Student choice and voice
Academic enrichment
Relationship-building across grades
Family engagement
examples: A former educator attributed a major reduction in bullying, fights, and disciplinary action to Genius Hour, noting cross-grade relationships and belonging as drivers; more than 70 caregivers attended the Genius Hour showcase.
key_sources: Germain, E. (2024). New Mexico community school profile: Los Padillas Elementary School. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/new-mexico-community-school-los-padillas-brief

article_title: Do Gains from Generative AI-Enabled Adaptive Pretesting Persist? Evidence from a Retention Study
citation: Mahir Akgun and Sacip Toker. (2026). Do Gains from Generative AI–Enabled Adaptive Pretesting Persist? Evidence from a Retention Study. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22328
title: GenAI adaptive AI agent with response-contingent prompting and withheld solutions
description: The study's adaptive AI agent is a generative large language model configured via a structured system prompt defining its instructional role, response scope, and escalation logic. During pretesting it applied "response-contingent prompting": targeted probes for misconceptions, elaboration requests for superficial responses, and advancement for adequate engagement. "Direct solutions and posttest-relevant answers were explicitly excluded from the agent’s allowed outputs during pretesting." In the adaptive retrieval condition it additionally reviewed prior session performance signals to adjust conceptual depth.
requirements: A structured system prompt defining the agent's instructional role, response scope, and escalation logic, with direct solutions excluded from allowed outputs during pretesting
constraints: The study was conducted within a single instructional context; the article states replication across domains and task types is needed to assess generalizability
target_learners: undergraduate students in an upper-division applied statistics course
target_learning_goals: multiple linear regression concepts including predictor selection, multicollinearity detection, model comparison, and interpretation of regression coefficients
examples: In condition G1 the agent reviewed prior session performance signals, increasing conceptual depth for weaker content areas while maintaining challenge in stronger areas
key_sources: Mahir Akgun and Sacip Toker. (2026). Do Gains from Generative AI–Enabled Adaptive Pretesting Persist? Evidence from a Retention Study. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22328

article_title: Designing assessments in the generative AI era: A tailored assessment framework for ICT tertiary education
citation: Ahangama. (2026). Designing assessments in the generative AI era: A tailored assessment framework for ICT tertiary education. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00582-0
title: GENESIS framework: a five-pillar, institution-wide model for GenAI-era assessment reform
description: GENESIS (GenAI-Enabled Strategic and Instructional System for Assessment) is a five-pillar, institution-wide practice framework for assessment design in the GenAI era. The article describes it as "a five-pillar, institution-wide model emphasising shifts in institutional values, governance, and support as prerequisites for sustainable assessment reform". It emerged from thematic analysis of 80 documents and structures reform as a sequential transformation from values through governance and support infrastructure to curriculum, competencies, strategies, and methods.
requirements: Institutional values and dispositions must be established before policy or operational changes
constraints: Developed for ICT tertiary education at AQF levels 7 to 9 in Australia
target_learners: ICT tertiary students at AQF levels 7 to 9
target_learning_goals: Valid measurement of ICT graduate learning outcomes in the GenAI era
examples: The framework was derived from thematic analysis of 80 publicly available web-based documents published between 2023 and 2025
key_sources: Ahangama. (2026). Designing assessments in the generative AI era: A tailored assessment framework for ICT tertiary education. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00582-0

article_title: AI AI Tell Me: A Model Study on the Effect of Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Feedback on Intonation in Violin Education
citation: Yakup Aksoy. (2026). Yapay zekâ, yapay zekâ söyle bana: Keman eğitiminde yapay zekâ destekli geri bildirimin entonasyona etkisine yönelik bir model çalışması. Online Journal of Music Sciences, 11(2). https://doi.org/10.31811/ojomus.1897062
title: Four-dimension taxonomy of generative AI feedback content: explanatory, descriptive, suggestions and conclusion
description: The study's content analysis organizes the feedback that DeepSeek and ChatGPT gave on students' cent-based intonation tables into four dimensions. As the article states, "yapay zekâ destekli sistemlerin (Deepseek ve ChatGPT) sunduğu geri bildirimler; açıklayıcı, tanımlayıcı, öneriler ve sonuç boyutlarında yapılandırılmış olup, öğrenci gelişimini çok yönlü olarak desteklemektedir." Explanatory feedback included theoretical information such as what a cent is; descriptive feedback covered positive/negative deviations and problem regions; suggestions spanned instrument care, technique, aural development and self-regulation; and conclusions included general evaluation and future expectations.
requirements: Feedback must be based on students' cent-level intonation deviation data supplied to the AI systems
constraints: The taxonomy was derived from feedback on a single intonation étude measured in cents, without visual or postural analysis
target_learners: violin students in higher education music teacher education
target_learning_goals: intonation skill development
technical and musical self-regulation of practice
examples: The article cites feedback such as "Bb4: -50 → +11 (Aşırı düzelme, ancak bu sefer tiz)" showing micro-level descriptive analysis, and "15 gün sonra ±50 cent’ler ±20’ye düşecek…" as a future projection

article_title: AI-Generated Slides: Are They Good? Can Students Tell?
citation: Juho Leinonen, Lisa Zhang, and Arto Hellas. 2026. AI-Generated Slides: Are They Good? Can Students Tell?. In Proceedings of Western Canada Conference on Computing Education 2026 (WCCCE 2026). ACM, New York, NY, USA. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.13532
title: Five-tool GenAI slide generation evaluation (NotebookLM, M365 Copilot, Claude, Cursor, Claude Code)
description: The article evaluates five accessible GenAI tools for transforming online textbook chapters into lecture slides for a 5 ECTS Web Software Development course: NotebookLM, M365 Copilot, Claude (Sonnet 4.5), Cursor, and Claude Code. The tools "represent different points on the spectrum from automated to instructor-in-the-loop workflows". Each was prompted with the same textbook-derived prompt requesting a 15-minute lecture segment with peer-instruction exercises, and assessed for factual accuracy, completeness, and pedagogical soundness.
requirements: Accessible tools (free, under USD$30 per month, or institutionally licensed) and instructor-authored source materials
constraints: NotebookLM had no out-of-the-box slide generation at the time; styling rules in the initial prompt degraded content quality, so styling was separated as post-processing
target_learning_goals: lecture slides covering HTML, Svelte, shared state, CRUD, and the Fetch API
examples: Slides were generated for four first-two-weeks topics chosen to represent varied content types: code-heavy, diagram-heavy, and conceptual material

article_title: AI-Generated Traces for Novice Programmers: Learning Effects and Learner Differences in a Multi-Institutional Study
citation: Yuri Noviello, Naaz Sibia, Anastasiia Birillo, Thomas Overklift Vaupel Klein, Michael Liut, and Gosia Migut. 2026. AI-Generated Traces for Novice Programmers: Learning Effects and Learner Differences in a Multi-Institutional Study. Proceedings of the 31st ACM Conference on Innovation and Technology in Computer Science Education V. 1 (ITiCSE 2026). https://doi.org/10.1145/3803400.3809346
title: Generated Animated Traces (GATs): AI-generated, analogy-based, narrated animations synchronizing code, execution state, and conceptual analogy
description: GATs are AI-generated instructional videos for CS1 that synchronize a Source Code View with the currently executed line highlighted and a Conceptual Analogy View, e.g., "searching for abunnyin physical boxes to illustrate awhileloop". They were produced through a human-in-the-loop pipeline in which an AI-driven system generates scripts, traces, manim-based animations, subtitles, and voiceover, with light human editing for pedagogical clarity. The study compared GATs to textual explanations matched in learning objectives, conceptual scope, and line-by-line execution order.
requirements: Underlying code snippets and instructional logic consistent across presentation modalities
Human-in-the-loop editing to refine timing, correct layout issues, and ensure pedagogical clarity
constraints: Effectiveness was context-dependent and short-term in the reported studies
Benefits did not transfer to long-term exam performance
target_learners: Novice programmers in introductory CS1 courses
target_learning_goals: Understanding program execution, including variable state, control flow, and memory operations
examples: Five intervention topics: while-loop, arraylist, hashmap, file reading, and file writing, deployed in Java at TU Delft and a three-topic subset in Python at UofT

title: GenAI-integrated professional development program embedding ethical reasoning for EAP educators
description: A field-tested professional development program for higher education EAP educators that integrates generative AI training with ethical reasoning. The article states the study "designed, implemented, and evaluated a GenAI-integrated Professional Development program that embeds ethical reasoning within a multicultural Global South institution," engaging 97 educators in quantitative testing and 15 in qualitative interviews. The authors state the model "can be adapted for use in other contexts."

citation: Crompton, H., Burke, D., Nickel, C., Bozkurt, A., Miao, F., Sharples, M., Greene, J. A., Parsons, D., Gill-Simmen, L., Edmett, A., Pegrum, M., de Waard, I., Bonk, C. J., Garcia, M. title: Eight core thematic areas for GenAI policies and guidelines in higher education
description: A consensus-driven framework of eight interconnected thematic areas that should form the content of GenAI policies and guidelines in higher education: "academic integrity, ethical use and responsible use, privacy and protection, equitable access, GenAI literacy, integration strategy, human oversight and accountability, and institutional support and infrastructure." The framework was derived from grounded coding of open-ended Delphi panel responses, and the article stresses that the areas are highly interconnected rather than independent, with academic integrity operating as a central regulatory anchor and GenAI literacy as a cross-cutting capability. The order of the eight areas does not connote importance or sequence.
requirements: Guidance structures must address all eight interconnected thematic areas as an integrated ecosystem rather than a collection of independent policy areas
constraints: The order of the eight areas does not connote a level of importance or order

title: Treat GenAI literacy as a foundational enabler of effective GenAI governance and a potential graduation outcome
description: The expert panel widely agreed that GenAI literacy — understanding how generative AI works, its appropriate uses, and its limitations — should be treated as a core future learning skill set, with many advocating that it become a required learning outcome for graduates. As one panelist argued, "GenAI literacy, as one panelist argued, is the foundation of any effective GenAI policy because it empowers students to use these technologies critically and responsibly rather than naively." The article recommends institutions establish expectations for GenAI competency, require literacy training programs, and help students gain skills to evaluate outputs, cite or acknowledge GenAI assistance, protect their data, and integrate GenAI into problem-solving.
requirements: Training must address not only prompting and tool use but also implications for epistemic development, autonomy, agency, identity, and moral and social development
constraints: The article notes high usage does not ensure understanding: in a 2025 global student survey, 80% of undergraduates reported using GenAI yet many expressed concerns about accuracy and proper use
target_learning_goals: critical GenAI literacy

examples: Panelists advocated treating GenAI competencies as a core future learning skill set and making GenAI literacy a required learning outcome for graduates

title: Six-process framework for keeping GenAI policies and guidelines current and relevant
description: A framework of six standalone, non-sequenced processes identified through grounded coding of Delphi responses to ensure GenAI policies and guidelines remain current: creating a dedicated GenAI Committee, conducting regularly scheduled policy reviews, providing ongoing professional development and support, communicating with all stakeholders, evaluating the effectiveness and impact of GenAI, and monitoring external developments. As the article states, the panel coding "identified six key processes to ensure that GenAI policies and guidelines remain current and relevant in HE settings." The six are standalone processes rather than a sequence of action, and Table 2 operationalizes each with concrete actions such as investing in research partnerships and monitoring changes in laws, data privacy standards, and industry standards.
requirements: An ongoing institutional mechanism with clear ownership, such as a multidisciplinary committee with faculty, administrators, and students
constraints: The order of the six processes does not connote a sequence of action or importance; each is a standalone process

title: Design GenAI policies for equitable access to prevent exacerbating digital divides
description: The panel voiced concern that without deliberate action GenAI could exacerbate digital divides or create new inequities. As one panelist warned, "the digital divide remains a problematic issue and GenAI policies that do not explicitly address access risk furthering the divide along class and other socio-economic lines." The principle calls for institutions to provide access to approved GenAI platforms through campus licenses or shared platforms, avoid assignments requiring paid tools, accommodate students lacking off-campus connectivity, and conduct equity audits of GenAI technologies before adoption to evaluate fairness and accessibility.

constraints: Panelists noted that access without the knowledge and skills to use GenAI can negatively impact students as much as not having the technologies

target_learning_goals: equitable participation in GenAI-enhanced learning

title: Use GenAI to support, not replace, human learning and critical thinking through proactive integration strategy
description: The panel strongly advocated proactive strategic integration of GenAI into teaching and learning, guided by the central principle that "GenAI should be used to "support, not replace" human learning and critical thinking." This means designing curricula and assessments that leverage GenAI to enhance learning while assessing higher-order skills so that simply copying GenAI's answer would not fulfill the task. Panelists advocated in-class, oral, or application-based assessments and process-focused assignments requiring students to document their thinking and GenAI use, while keeping curricula aligned with GenAI-adoption realities in workplaces.
requirements: Curricula and assignments redesigned to test deeper learning and critical thinking, reducing over-reliance on GenAI-generated responses
constraints: Panelists warned against outright bans, favoring proactive integration over prohibition
target_learning_goals: critical thinking
preparation for a GenAI-enriched workforce
examples: Panelists recommended guidelines that educate students on using GenAI as a support tool for critical thinking and creativity rather than as a shortcut to completing work

article_title: How motivation and roles influence metacognitive engagement in student-GenAI interaction
citation: Cui, Y., Yan, W., Chiu, T. K. F., & Nakajima, T. (2026). How motivation and roles influence metacognitive engagement in student-GenAI interaction. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education, 23(34). https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00610-z
title: Four-role taxonomy of GenAI roles: instructor, enhancement tool, replacement tool, collaborator
description: The article develops a four-category taxonomy of the functional roles students assign to GenAI in authentic interaction. It extends the tripartite Instructor–Collaborator–Tool taxonomy of Ouyang and Jiao (2021) by splitting the Tool category using Fügener et al.'s augmentation–automation distinction. As the article states, "When GenAI was used to reduce cognitive load, extend the student's capabilities, or assist with tasks the student could not accomplish independently, the role was coded as Enhancement Tool", whereas a Replacement Tool substitutes for the student's own thinking. Roles were coded per interaction log from log content plus retrospective accounts.
requirements: Coding requires access to the stated purpose of each interaction, combining log text with the learner's retrospective account, since roles "could not be reliably inferred from surface text"
constraints: Applied to learning-related undergraduate GenAI use in authentic, self-initiated dialogues; motivation coded as a binary intrinsic-versus-extrinsic contrast rather than finer SDT subtypes
target_learners: Undergraduate students using GenAI for learning
target_learning_goals: Metacognitive regulation of student-GenAI dialogue
Self-directed learning with generative AI
examples: Roles were observed in 120 authentic interaction logs: Instructor 25.0%, Replacement Tool 45.8%, Enhancement Tool 21.7%, Collaborator 7.5% (Table 2)

article_title: GenAI as a Frenemy in Teaching: Perceived Autonomy and Risks
citation: Dai, H. M., Ni, K., Meng, H., Ju, B., Crawford, J., & Teo, T. (2026). GenAI as a frenemy in teaching: Perceived autonomy and risks. Australasian Journal of Educational Technology, 42(3), 157–179. https://doi.org/10.14742/ajet.11301
title: Develop clear guidelines and risk management strategies addressing integrity and student misuse of GenAI
description: Because teachers' risk aversion significantly shapes adoption decisions and their concerns centre on students' GenAI use, the article recommends that policymakers establish clear guidelines and risk management strategies. It states "Policymakers should develop clear guidelines and risk management strategies to address integrity and student misuse." Clear policy is positioned as a condition for thoughtful GenAI integration rather than as a substitute for teacher judgement.
requirements: Policy-level authorship of clear GenAI guidelines and risk management strategies
constraints: Adoption requires careful consideration of context and human-AI interaction, per the article's overall conclusion
target_learning_goals: Academic integrity in GenAI use
Prevention of student misuse of GenAI
examples: The article's implications for practice or policy direct policymakers to develop clear guidelines and risk management strategies addressing integrity and student misuse.

article_title: Educating minds with generative AI
citation: Laura Desiree Di Paolo, Andy Clark & Thomas Wachter. (2026). Educating minds with generative AI. Communications Psychology 4:128. https://doi.org/10.1038/s44271-026-00522-8
title: GenAI as epistemic infrastructure that organises how knowledge is produced, circulated and legitimised
description: The article conceptualises GenAI as epistemic infrastructure: systems that 'do more than provide access to knowledge: they organise how knowledge is produced, circulated, evaluated, and legitimised'. When institutionalised in education, GenAI may assume this infrastructural role, as with AI-powered teaching management systems that consolidate curriculum planning, instructional support, assessment and progress reporting in one algorithmically mediated environment, imposing participation structures on teachers, administrators and parents and reshaping what counts as legitimate participation in the educational system.
requirements: Sustained and explicit reflection on pedagogical infrastructures and methodologies when GenAI is introduced
constraints: The authors warn that without such reflection, GenAI is likely to amplify values already dominant, such as performance, standardisation, optimisation, and error avoidance
target_learning_goals: epistemic practices and norms of knowledge production and evaluation

article_title: Reimagining Success and Failure: Equitable Assessment Practices in an Age of Artificial Intelligence
citation: Dollinger, M., & Nieminen, J. (2026). Reimagining success and failure: equitable assessment practices in an age of AI. Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice, 23(1). https://doi.org/10.53761/20z06b11
title: Two-dimension framing of equitable assessment reimagining: distribution of knowledge and agentic assessment
description: The paper organises its argument for equitable assessment in the age of generative AI around two key dimensions along which entrenched notions of student success can be challenged: "distribution of knowledge and agentic assessment". Distribution of knowledge concerns who gets recognised as knowing, moving beyond individual performance toward "diverse ways of knowing"; agentic assessment concerns valuing "collaboration and student agency over individual performance and predetermined standards". The framework is used to reposition GenAI from an integrity threat to a lever for redesigning assessment.
requirements: Applies to higher-education assessment contexts where generative AI is available to students
constraints: Proposed as a conceptual argument in a conceptual paper, not an empirically tested framework
target_learning_goals: equitable recognition of diverse ways of knowing; student agency in assessment
examples: The paper's abstract proposes exploring how GenAI may challenge entrenched and exclusionary notions of student success across these two dimensions.
key_sources: Dollinger, M., & Nieminen, J. (2026). Reimagining success and failure: equitable assessment practices in an age of AI. Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice, 23(1). https://doi.org/10.53761/20z06b11

article_title: Reimagining Success and Failure: Equitable Assessment Practices in an Age of Artificial Intelligence
citation: Dollinger, M., & Nieminen, J. (2026). Reimagining success and failure: equitable assessment practices in an age of AI. Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice, 23(1). https://doi.org/10.53761/20z06b11
title: Design assessment to value collaboration and student agency over individual performance and predetermined standards
description: This principle holds that in the age of generative AI, assessment should be designed as "a catalyst for more equitable assessment that values collaboration and student agency over individual performance and predetermined standards". Rather than treating GenAI use as an integrity violation to be policed, educators treat it as an occasion to redesign assessment so that success is not defined by individual performance against predetermined standards. The paper advances this as a design orientation for higher education.
requirements: Educators willing to reconsider entrenched definitions of student success and failure in assessment design
constraints: Advanced as a conceptual proposal; the supplied text reports no empirical evaluation of the redesign approach
target_learning_goals: equitable assessment; student agency; collaboration
examples: The paper proposes GenAI as an opportunity to move away from assessment practices that sort and rank students toward approaches that recognise diverse ways of knowing.

article_title: 'AI Should Help Them Learn, Not Learn for Them': University Staff Perspectives on the Role of Generative AI in Education
citation: Enright, H., Horvath, D., Petrovic, K., & Šarkić, B. (2026). “AI Should Help them Learn, Not Learn for Them”: University Staff Perspectives on the Role of Generative AI in Education. Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice. https://doi.org/10.53761/d5n2yh02
title: GenAI in education should support student learning rather than replace it — helping students learn, not learning for them.
description: The article's framing principle, drawn from its title, is that generative AI in education should serve student learning rather than substitute for it: "AI Should Help them Learn, Not Learn for Them." This principle captures staff views that GenAI risks eroding essential academic skills such as critical thinking and creativity, while its productive use lies in enhancing teaching practices and student-centred learning activities.

constraints: Staff reported potential erosion of essential academic skills such as critical thinking and creativity when GenAI is used inappropriately.

Creativity
Academic skill development
examples: Staff survey respondents at an Australian university articulated this framing in their perspectives on the role of GenAI in learning and teaching.

article_title: Research on the optimization of the training system of university faculty development centers in the context of GenAI: a comparative analysis based on Chinese and Kazakhstani universities
citation: Bi T, Araily S, Lyu A and Xiu S (2026) Research on the optimization of the training system of university faculty development centers in the context of GenAI: a comparative analysis based on Chinese and Kazakhstani universities. Front. Psychol. 17:1890508. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1890508
title: GenAI pedagogical readiness: a seven-dimension faculty competence construct
description: The article defines GenAI pedagogical readiness as "university faculty members' capacity to use, evaluate, and regulate GenAI in course practice". The construct comprises seven dimensions — basic GenAI understanding, prompt design, AI-supported instructional design, AI-supported assessment, critical judgement, educational ethics, and disciplinary transfer — each measured by four items on a 1–5 agreement scale. It builds on TPACK, DigCompEdu, and AI literacy frameworks but focuses specifically on whether faculty can judge, revise, assess, and regulate generated materials in course practice. The framework connects baseline readiness, training design, and prompt-level evidence through situated professional learning, technology-integrated pedagogical judgement, and institutional mediation.
requirements: Measured through a seven-dimension scale with four items per dimension on a 1–5 agreement scale, translated into Chinese, English, Kazakh, and Russian with back-translation and reconciliation
constraints: Primarily self-report; the authors note concept interpretation and response styles across language backgrounds may still have affected part of the evidence
target_learners: University faculty with current higher education teaching responsibility
target_learning_goals: Using, evaluating, and regulating GenAI in course practice, including prompt design, assessment redesign, and responsible-use explanation
examples: The scale showed total-sample Cronbach's alpha ranging from 0.822 to 0.889 and McDonald's omega from 0.825 to 0.891, with partial scalar measurement invariance supported across the Chinese and Kazakhstani samples

article_title: Fear and Awe: Making Sense of Generative AI Through Metaphor
citation: Carmen Vallis, Stephanie Wilson, Alison Casey. (2025). Fear and Awe: Making Sense of Generative AI Through Metaphor. Journal of Interactive Media Education. https://doi.org/10.5334/jime.972
title: Four-category taxonomy of GenAI metaphors in higher education: Functions, Roles, Qualities, Agency
description: The article proposes a four-category taxonomy of metaphors used to conceptualise generative AI in educational contexts, derived from thematic analysis of workshop artefacts. Functions metaphors "conceptualise GenAI in terms of its tasks and practical capabilities as tools or materials"; Roles position GenAI in human-like relationships; Qualities describe its "unknowable, unreliable, or magical nature"; and Agency attribute volition or autonomous action, often expressing concerns about control and power. Unlike prior AI metaphor studies, the authors argue their categories capture how metaphors emerge through collaborative social meaning-making linked to pedagogical concerns and lived experience.
requirements: Derived from collaborative workshop elicitation with multidisciplinary participant groups rather than individual elicitation
constraints: The authors acknowledge categories might reflect aspects of the workshop design in addition to participants' authentic conceptualisations
target_learning_goals: critical AI literacy
sensemaking about emerging technologies
examples: Sample metaphors include Swiss army knife (Functions), frenemy (Roles), black box (Qualities), and sinister robot (Agency).

article_title: Development and validation of the generative AI assessment literacy scale for higher education students
citation: Nie J, Zhang Z, Lu X, Zhang Y and Zhang M (2026) Development and validation of the generative AI assessment literacy scale for higher education students: psychometric evidence and associations with feedback engagement and academic integrity. Front. Educ. 11:1934632. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1934632
title: Generative AI assessment literacy as an assessment-specific integrative construct with five dimensions
description: The article defines generative AI assessment literacy as "students’ assessment-specific capacity to understand assessment criteria, judge the appropriateness of GenAI use, verify AI-generated content or feedback, disclose AI use ethically, and use AI-supported feedback for responsible revision in assessment-related learning tasks." It is positioned as an integrative construct, not a replacement for general AI literacy, assessment literacy, feedback literacy, or academic integrity literacy, becoming salient when GenAI is used within assessed work. The five GAA-LS dimensions represent a sequence of situated judgments moving from criteria and task boundaries to verification, disclosure, and feedback-based revision.
requirements: The construct applies when GenAI is used within assessed work, where students must make situated judgments about criteria, task boundaries, evidence quality, disclosure, and revision.
constraints: The article states it is not proposed as a replacement for general AI literacy, assessment literacy, feedback literacy, or academic integrity literacy.
target_learning_goals: responsible GenAI use in assessment-related tasks, including criteria interpretation, verification, disclosure, and feedback-based revision
examples: The GAA-LS operationalizes the construct as 18 items across five dimensions: assessment criteria awareness, AI-task appropriateness judgment, verification and evidence checking, ethical attribution and academic integrity, and feedback uptake and revision literacy.

article_title: Generative AI-supported instruction as a cognitive scaffold: effects on senior high school students' geometric reasoning and proof construction
citation: Davor I (2026) Generative AI-supported instruction as a cognitive scaffold: effects on senior high school students' geometric reasoning and proof construction. Front. Educ. 11:1869961. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1869961
title: Generative AI as a cognitive scaffold bridging Van Hiele level transitions and reducing extraneous cognitive load in geometry proof
description: The study grounds its intervention in Van Hiele's model of geometric thinking and Cognitive Load Theory. In this framework, "generative AI-assisted instruction is viewed as a scaffold that assists students in progressing from one level to another within the Van Hiele levels", supporting the transition from informal visual intuition to formal deduction. From the Cognitive Load perspective, AI-generated representations and prompts reduce extraneous load from diagram construction, freeing resources for selecting theorems, justifying choices, and ordering logical steps. The AI is positioned as a mediator of reasoning, not a provider of complete proofs.
requirements: The AI must provide vivid imagery, require justifications for what is observed, and assist in arranging deductive steps, without giving complete proofs or final answers.
constraints: The article states the cognitive mechanisms underlying the observed improvements were not directly measured, so the theoretical account remains an interpretation.
target_learners: senior high school students in geometry courses
target_learning_goals: geometric reasoning
proof construction
transition from visual intuition to deductive reasoning
examples: The intervention had the AI develop dynamic visual representations and provide guided prompts with which students justified relationships, identified relevant theorems, and arranged logical statements.

article_title: Generative AI as a Didactic-Pedagogical Mediator: Rethinking Human Roles and Pedagogical Design in Higher Education
citation: Moganadas SR, Marín-González F, Nun SH and Gan CL (2026) Generative AI as a didactic-pedagogical mediator: rethinking human roles and pedagogical design in higher education. Front. Educ. 11:1856839. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1856839
title: GenAI as a bounded didactic-pedagogical mediator, distinct from tool, tutor, assistant, scaffold, or co-educator
description: The article's central conceptual contribution is defining GenAI as a bounded didactic-pedagogical mediator: a non-human technological artifact that can support explanation, feedback, scaffolding, and knowledge representation while remaining dependent on human judgment, disciplinary validation, and institutional governance. The authors argue this role is conceptually distinct from adjacent interpretations "such as tool, tutor, assistant, scaffold, or co-educator." GenAI's pedagogical significance depends on how its outputs are framed, interpreted, questioned, verified, revised, and integrated by human actors within disciplinary and institutional contexts.
requirements: Outputs must be treated as provisional and evaluated through source verification, comparison with disciplinary evidence, and human pedagogical judgment
constraints: GenAI's fluency should not be presumed as sufficient grounds for assigning it epistemic authority or independent pedagogical responsibility
LLM outputs may contain fabricated claims, reproduce biases, or vary in quality across prompts and contexts
target_learning_goals: critical evaluation of AI-generated content
disciplinary reasoning
epistemic judgment
examples: The article contrasts this mediator role with AIEd frameworks that classify AI through functional roles such as tutoring, assessment, and analytics

article_title: Generative AI technologies and educational outcomes: a comprehensive meta-analysis comparing traditional and AI-driven approaches
citation: Ying Dong. (2026). Generative AI technologies and educational outcomes: a comprehensive meta-analysis comparing traditional and AI-driven approaches. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications. https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-026-06903-y
title: GenAI educational-effect framework: personalized learning, feedback, gamification, and contextual adaptation
description: The article proposes a framework in which GenAI improves educational outcomes through several mechanisms: it "may offer personalized learning experiences" and effective feedback, process and analyze large amounts of data to "provide timely and contextual feedback", integrate gaming factors to enhance real-time student interaction, and help teachers adjust teaching styles and modify content for diverse student needs. The framework organizes the meta-analysis's moderator structure (feedback, game assistance, country, educational level) and grounds each intervention type in a theory: constructivism for GenAI technologies, metacognition theory for GenAI feedback, and Self-Determination Theory for game-assisted GenAI.
requirements: GenAI interventions must be classified by type (GenAI technologies, GenAI feedback, game-assisted GenAI) for the framework's mechanisms to be tested separately
constraints: The article states over-reliance on GenAI as a replacement for human teachers negatively influences outcomes; GenAI should complement human instruction
target_learning_goals: academic achievement
higher-order thinking
writing skills
learning motivation
examples: The meta-analysis operationalized the framework's outcomes as academic achievements, higher-order thinking abilities, and writing skills, and its moderators as feedback type, game assistance, country, and educational level

citation: Ying Dong. (2026). Generative AI technologies and educational outcomes: a comprehensive meta-analysis comparing traditional and AI-driven approaches. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications. https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-026-06903-y
title: 53-study PRISMA-screened evidence corpus on GenAI and educational outcomes
description: A corpus of 53 included studies assembled through a PRISMA-based screening process from an initial 1096 records across Web of Science, Scopus, Springer, ScienceDirect, and Wiley, with gray literature searched to minimize publication bias. The screening removed duplicates, ineligible records, and studies with unreliable designs or missing key data (mean, standard deviation, or sample size). Quality was rated on AERA reporting standards (6–18 points), yielding 28 high-quality (52.8%), 19 medium-quality (35.8%), and 6 low-quality (11.4%) studies, with inter-rater reliability Cohen's kappa = 0.82.
requirements: Included studies must report quantitative or qualitative data on the hypothesized outcomes and have a control group and reliable intervention
constraints: Studies lacking key data (mean, standard deviation, or sample size) were excluded; unpublished, retracted, or overlapped publications were excluded
target_learners: students across university and secondary levels
target_learning_goals: academic achievement
higher-order thinking
writing skills

article_title: Human-centered GenAI feedback design in higher education: a multisite experiment on direct, reflective, and hybrid approaches to scientific argumentation
citation: Ates, H. (2026). Human-centered GenAI feedback design in higher education: a multisite experiment on direct, reflective, and hybrid approaches to scientific argumentation. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00614-9
title: Process model of GenAI-supported feedback: designs distribute evaluative work and act directly and indirectly through uptake and self-regulated learning
description: The article proposes a process model in which feedback design affects argument-quality gain, conceptual learning, and delayed AI-free transfer both directly and indirectly. As the model figure states, "feedback design affects four-dimension argument-quality gain, conceptual learning, and delayed AI-free transfer both directly and indirectly through feedback uptake and self-regulated learning during revision." The core theoretical claim is that alternative designs "distribute evaluative work differently across learners, peers, and AI-supported tools," so designs requiring comparison, selection, and justification of revision decisions better preserve evaluative judgment and epistemic agency.
requirements: Feedback designs must be understood as process configurations involving source, sequencing, and structured evaluative activity, not feedback-source exposure alone
constraints: Mediation models test statistical association between condition differences in outcomes and revision processes, not a strict within-cycle temporal causal sequence
target_learning_goals: scientific argumentation
evaluative judgment
self-regulated learning during revision

title: Gen-AI-tecture: a bespoke, locally run ComfyUI generative-AI image creation and editing workflow for architectural education
description: A bespoke generative-AI image workflow implemented as a localised ComfyUI environment in which students upload or select images, describe changes in natural language, and receive multiple visual alternatives. article_title: Structuring Transparency: Developing Domain-Specific Generative AI Declaration Frameworks in Higher Education
citation: Nicholas Micallef, Olga Petrovska. (2026). Structuring Transparency: Developing Domain-Specific Generative AI Declaration Frameworks in Higher Education. International Symposium on Artificial Intelligence and the Transformation of Higher Education Symposium (AITHE). https://www.swansea.ac.uk/staff/nicholas.micallef
title: Frame GenAI declarations as reflective instruments rather than compliance artefacts, using granularity, task specificity, intensity, prompt transparency, and reflection over punishment
description: The framework is guided by five principles that "collectively shift declarations from compliance artefacts to reflective instruments": granularity over a binary yes/no; task specificity; intensity as well as presence (Minor, Moderate, Extensive); prompt-level transparency via brief explanations and example prompts; and reflection over punishment, framing the declaration "as a description of process, not an admission of guilt". Reducing perceived stigma of disclosure

citation: Dumlao, J. M. Z., Wang, M., Xie, Z., Hu, J., Bar, I., Chaney, G., III, Gold, H., & Teplitskiy, M. (2026). Generative AI Availability, Grades, and Student Satisfaction at a Large University. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21534
title: The GenAI substitution hypothesis: assessment susceptibility to GenAI automation conditions whether AI availability inflates grades without learning
description: The GenAI substitution hypothesis holds that students may substitute GenAI capabilities for their own mastery on assessments that can be completed outside instructor observation, earning satisfactory grades without the cognitive effort that promotes learning. The article defines "GenAI susceptible assessments as those where GenAI tools may directly substitute for student ability, like take-home exams, problem sets, and essays", contrasting them with in-person closed-book exams, presentations, and live demonstrations where full automation is precluded. If true, grades should rise disproportionately in susceptible courses and lose signaling value.
requirements: An assessment structure weighting susceptible (unproctored, take-home, or open) assessments heavily enough that GenAI could substitute for student effort
constraints: Substitution need not be strategic; instructors perceive an 'illusion of competence' when students complete assessments with GenAI, per work the article cites
target_learning_goals: validity of grades as signals of mastery; student learning and satisfaction under GenAI availability
examples: The study operationalizes the hypothesis as a prediction that grades rise disproportionately in high-susceptibility courses after ChatGPT's release, and finds no such differential effect

citation: Rana Abou Khamis, Hala Assal, and Ashraf Matrawy. (2026). Unanticipated Effects of Generative AI on Expertise Pathways and Performance Perception in System Administration. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28650
title: Two-shift account of GenAI's unanticipated socio-technical effects on technical work
description: The article proposes that GenAI's effects on technical professions extend beyond accelerated workflows through two connected shifts. The first is compression of expertise pathways, where "GenAI allows users to skip many foundational, hands-on tasks that once served as the training ground for technical judgment." The second is a performance perception shift, where fast output becomes the expected norm while human validation effort stays invisible. The account is grounded in reflexive thematic analysis of interviews with 14 sysadmins and IT professionals with 2 to 15 years of experience.
requirements: Applies to technical professionals who use GenAI in daily work, as the interviewed sysadmins did
constraints: Findings are within the context of system administration workflows; the authors expect but do not demonstrate the effects in other technical fields
target_learners: Novice and early-career technical staff including interns
target_learning_goals: Development of technical intuition, diagnostic judgment, and the expertise needed to validate AI-generated output
examples: The article's interview study with 14 sysadmins identified the two shifts through Braun and Clarke's reflexive thematic analysis

title: Use GenAI image generation as an early-stage visual scaffold for ideation, not as a replacement for hands-on making or instructor judgement
description: The principle holds that image-generation tools should support early exploration, comparison, and critique before students commit time and materials to physical sampling, while final outcomes continue to rely on instructor feedback, material testing, and hands-on studio work. In this course, "GenAI was used to support ideation, not to produce final assessed artifacts", and students were instructed to treat outputs as early-stage prompts requiring interpretation and later hands-on testing. The article notes current text-to-image models have limited understanding of yarn behaviour, stitch formation, and workshop feasibility, so technical judgement must remain grounded in studio practice.

Prompt scaffolding should use domain-relevant design parameters rather than generic image-generation keywords

Lower student ratings for time saving and direct incorporation into final outcomes show clear limits

description: The article's practical implication is that GenAI literacy development for special education undergraduates should not stop at operational skills. constraints: The supporting evidence is cross-sectional and limited to special education undergraduates in four Chinese provinces, so causal interpretation and generalizability are limited.

citation: Yan Z, Fang Z and Zou W (2026). The association between generative AI use and university students' critical thinking: a moderated mediation model of GenAI feedback literacy and reflective thinking. Front. Psychol. 17:1939286. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1939286
title: Dual-route pattern: direct association at low reflectivity, feedback-mediated association at high reflectivity
description: The article proposes a dual-route account integrating the extended-mind framework, cognitive load theory and feedback-literacy theory. GenAI can act as a complementary cognitive partner or a substitute depending on use; feedback literacy is the channel converting AI exposure into critical thinking; reflective thinking determines which route dominates. The article states: "We refer to this contrast between a predominantly direct association at low reflectivity and a predominantly feedback-mediated association at high reflectivity as a dual-route pattern." constraints: All variables were measured concurrently by self-report in a cross-sectional design, so the account describes associations, not demonstrated mechanisms

reflective thinking
examples: The PLS-SEM model with 421 Chinese undergraduates estimated both interaction terms with opposite signs, consistent with the dual-route reasoning.

title: Generate-Then-Validate: a Phi-2-based question generation pipeline with expansive generation and selective validation
description: A question generation pipeline that uses the 2.7B-parameter SLM Phi-2 as both generator and validator, requiring no fine-tuning. Its two stages are expansive generation, which builds MCQs through a five-step incremental prompt (seed, stem, choices, answer, explanation), and selective validation via syntactic filtering, answer confidence evaluation, and an LO alignment check based on log-probability relevance. The authors state that "our pipeline first performs expansive generation to create an abundance of candidate questions and refine them through selective validation based on novel probabilistic reasoning". Applied to 41 AP Environmental Science LOs, it produced a final pool of 3,205 MCQs from 8,200 candidates.

citation: Shan Li, Juan Zheng. (2026). Generativism: Toward a Learning Theory for the Age of Generative Artificial Intelligence. https://orcid/org/0000-0001-6001-1586
title: Generativism: a learning theory framing learning as iterative co-construction of knowledge between human learners and generative AI systems
description: Generativism is a proposed learning theory for the generative AI age, organized around four constructs — epistemic partnership, distributed agency, generative literacy, and adaptive metacognition — and four principles specifying their relations. The article defines learning as "the deliberate co-construction of knowledge through iterative human-AI interaction", positioning learning as neither purely human nor AI-driven but emergent at the intersection. It reframes AI from "tool" to "cognitive partner" and offers a foundation for rethinking instructional design, learning, assessment, and expertise development.
requirements: Learners must retain responsibility for interpretation and judgment when working with AI, and the four constructs are interdependent: partnership requires agency decisions, agency requires literacy, and literacy requires metacognitive regulation.
constraints: The framework is a theoretical proposal; the article reports that no new data were generated or analyzed in this study.

target_learning_goals: durable understanding and expertise development through human-AI knowledge co-construction

article_title: Generativism: Toward a Learning Theory for the Age of Generative Artificial Intelligence
citation: Shan Li, Juan Zheng. (2026). Generativism: Toward a Learning Theory for the Age of Generative Artificial Intelligence. https://orcid/org/0000-0001-6001-1586
title: Generative literacy: a critical literacy comprising prompt competence, evaluative judgment, epistemic vigilance, and integrative synthesis
description: Generativism defines generative literacy as "a form of critical literacy oriented toward prompting, evaluating, refining, and integrating AI-generated knowledge artifacts". It synthesizes four higher-level capacities: prompt competence (formulating and revising queries), evaluative judgment (assessing accuracy, coherence, relevance, and contextual appropriateness), epistemic vigilance (maintaining critical scrutiny even when output appears fluent or plausible), and integrative synthesis (combining AI content with prior knowledge to produce meaning exceeding the AI output). The article treats it as a condition for meaningful learning, not merely a technical skill.
requirements: Learners need these capacities to transform AI output into understanding rather than consuming it as a replacement for their own thinking; the article states learners cannot make sound delegation decisions without them.
constraints: The article notes existing AI literacy frameworks do not adequately address the unique challenges posed by generative systems, positioning this construct as an extension of prior frameworks such as ED-AI Lit and Long and Magerko's competencies.
target_learners: learners working with generative AI systems in educational settings
target_learning_goals: evaluating, refining, and integrating AI-generated outputs in support of genuine understanding

article_title: Measuring How Students Rely on Generative AI in Academic Writing: Development and Multi-Source Validation of the Generative AI Reliance Types Scale (GenAI-RTS)
citation: Hossain, S., & Nawmi, T. A. (2026). Measuring How Students Rely on Generative AI in Academic Writing: Development and Multi-Source Validation of the Generative AI Reliance Types Scale (GenAI-RTS). https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14301
title: A theory-derived four-type typology of GenAI reliance organized by cognitive governance retained and scope of delegation
description: The typology conceptualizes reliance on generative AI not as a quantity to be calibrated but as "a repertoire of qualitatively distinct behavioral patterns whose consequences for learning differ." It derives from metacognition, critical AI literacy, and approaches-to-learning theory, organized along two dimensions: "the degree of cognitive governance the writer retains" and "the scope of delegation." Strategic reliance denotes metacognitively governed, critically evaluated engagement; Instrumental reliance denotes efficiency-targeted surface-level delegation; Dependent reliance denotes wholesale outsourcing with uncritical acceptance; and Dialogic reliance denotes iterative co-construction with the tool as interlocutor.
requirements: The typology was specified deductively from named theoretical frameworks before item writing, with each facet grounded in a source framework such as metacognitive regulation, critical AI literacy competencies, surface approaches to learning, cognitive offloading, or sociocultural co-construction.
constraints: The typology was developed for extended academic writing contexts, and the article notes each instrument's coverage reflects its task ecology, with Instrumental reliance having no counterpart in problem-solving-domain structures.
target_learners: undergraduate students using generative AI in academic writing
target_learning_goals: identifying qualitatively distinct patterns of reliance on generative AI during academic writing
supporting AI literacy intervention and responsible GenAI use
examples: The GenAI-RTS operationalizes the typology with 20 items: four Deliberate Use items, four Critical Evaluation items, and four items each for Instrumental, Dependent, and Dialogic reliance, rated on 7-point Likert scales.
key_sources: Hossain, S., & Nawmi, T. A. (2026). Measuring How Students Rely on Generative AI in Academic Writing: Development and Multi-Source Validation of the Generative AI Reliance Types Scale (GenAI-RTS). https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14301

article_title: Measuring How Students Rely on Generative AI in Academic Writing: Development and Multi-Source Validation of the Generative AI Reliance Types Scale (GenAI-RTS)
citation: Hossain, S., & Nawmi, T. A. (2026). Measuring How Students Rely on Generative AI in Academic Writing: Development and Multi-Source Validation of the Generative AI Reliance Types Scale (GenAI-RTS). https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14301
title: GenAI Reliance Types Scale (GenAI-RTS), a 20-item instrument measuring four reliance types across five facets
description: The GenAI-RTS is a 20-item self-report instrument measuring reliance on generative AI in academic writing, with all items rated on 7-point Likert scales (1 = Strongly Disagree, 7 = Strongly Agree). It operationalizes four theoretically derived types across five measurement facets: "four Deliberate Use items informed by metacognitive awareness theory" and four Critical Evaluation items adapted from critical AI literacy competencies, plus four items each for Instrumental, Dependent, and Dialogic reliance. Subscale scores are item means (range 1–7), and the Strategic composite weights its two facets equally.
requirements: Administration as a self-report survey; the article recommends revising the response format from seven to five points based on Rasch category-functioning results.
constraints: Scores describe reliance profiles rather than assign students to types; no diagnostic cut scores are proposed, and the highest-subscale classification serves research description only.
target_learners: undergraduate students at higher education institutions
target_learning_goals: measuring how students rely on generative AI during academic writing
identifying reliance profiles for research, assessment, and AI literacy intervention
examples: Sample items include "I set clear objectives for using generative AI tools before each writing session" (Deliberate Use) and "I verify facts in text produced by generative AI tools against authoritative sources" (Critical Evaluation).

article_title: Beyond Generation and Accuracy: Diagnosing and Enhancing Visual Chain-of-Thought for Geometry Problem Solving
citation: Zhitong Dong, Jicai Pan, Yingguo Gao, Jingting Ding, Hao Chen, Jinjie Gu. (2026). Beyond Generation and Accuracy: Diagnosing and Enhancing Visual Chain-of-Thought for Geometry Problem Solving. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.12606
title: GeoVAD-Bench: a trajectory-level diagnostic benchmark for visual chain-of-thought geometry solving
description: GeoVAD-Bench is a diagnostic benchmark of "600 geometry problems requiring auxiliary-line constructions", each recast into a trajectory-level evaluation spanning five dimensions: original-diagram perception, auxiliary-diagram quality, auxiliary-diagram utilization, reasoning-process correctness, and final-answer accuracy. It pairs these metrics with three controlled auxiliary conditions (No-Aux, Auto-Aux, GT-Aux) that isolate intermediate error modes, the causal gains of visual aids, and the autonomy gap. Problems are stratified by difficulty, language (Chinese and English), and answer format (multiple-choice and open-ended). The article positions it as the only listed benchmark evaluating all five dimensions with explicit, separately reported metrics.
requirements: Problems must strictly necessitate auxiliary-line constructions, and each instance requires a verifiable answer plus a validated reference construction and corresponding auxiliary diagram.
constraints: Evaluation of the four process metrics relies on Gemini-3.1-Pro as the judge, and non-interleaved models are approximated with an external image-editing pipeline.
target_learners: multimodal reasoning models evaluated on geometry problem solving
target_learning_goals: diagnosing where visual chain-of-thought reasoning fails across perception, construction, utilization, and deduction
examples: The article uses the benchmark to compare closed- and open-source models and to attribute error categories among incorrect solutions for MathCanvas-7B and CodePlot-CoT-32B.
key_sources: Zhitong Dong, Jicai Pan, Yingguo Gao, Jingting Ding, Hao Chen, Jinjie Gu. (2026). Beyond Generation and Accuracy: Diagnosing and Enhancing Visual Chain-of-Thought for Geometry Problem Solving. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.12606

article_title: Beyond Generation and Accuracy: Diagnosing and Enhancing Visual Chain-of-Thought for Geometry Problem Solving
citation: Zhitong Dong, Jicai Pan, Yingguo Gao, Jingting Ding, Hao Chen, Jinjie Gu. (2026). Beyond Generation and Accuracy: Diagnosing and Enhancing Visual Chain-of-Thought for Geometry Problem Solving. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.12606
title: GeoWeave: a progressive evaluation-to-optimization framework pairing capability-ordered SFT with interleaved RL and step-level credit assignment
description: GeoWeave is a post-training framework that converts diagnostic findings into targeted training. It combines a modular data construction pipeline covering "fine-grained geometric perception, faithful diagram editing, and coherent interleaved reasoning" with a progressive training framework: three SFT stages (perception warmup, auxiliary-diagram editing, unified interleaved solving) that first train separate model branches and then all parameters, followed by Interleave-RL. The RL stage organizes text and image actions in a single rollout, applies group-relative policy optimization to text, retains a velocity-MSE constraint for image generation, and uses step-level credit assignment that localizes erroneous perception and deduction steps and upweights their low-entropy tokens.
requirements: Requires a base multimodal model supporting native interleaved generation, curated perception, editing, and interleaved-reasoning datasets, and verifiable outcome and process rewards.
constraints: The image-generation branch receives no independent policy-gradient update; its effect is reflected indirectly through the updated visual state and final answer.
target_learners: multimodal reasoning models (8B-scale unified multimodal models)
target_learning_goals: planning auxiliary constructions, generating faithful edited diagrams, grounding deduction in updated visual states, and producing correct answers
examples: Applied to SenseNova-U1-8B, the framework produced GeoWeave-8B, trained with three SFT stages (4,000, 10,000, and 6,000 steps) and Interleave-RL on 9K samples.

article_title: Generative AI and Extended Reality in Collaborative Architectural Design Education: An Exploratory Studio Study
citation: Xiao, Y., Chen, M., Li, Y., Powers, N., Wiesenfeld, M., Smith, G., Farzin, S., Liu, S. (2026). Generative AI and Extended Reality in Collaborative Architectural Design Education: An Exploratory Studio Study. arXiv preprint arXiv:2609.13494. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13494
title: GenARch: a GenAI-assisted multi-user XR pipeline for collaborative architectural conceptual design
description: GenARch is a pipeline integrating GenAI-based visual generation with collaborative XR environments, deployed as a technology probe embedded in an existing studio workflow. Its "in-house web and XR clients support structured or free-text/speech prompting, 2D image generation, 2D-to-3D conversion, and sharedreview." Generated assets are stored in a common gallery so students need not remain in-headset during processing, and selected assets are exported to Arkio for tabletop and full-scale inspection, collaborative manipulation, site/context viewing, and lighting-based shadow analysis. Technically it uses synchronized Meta Quest 3 and web clients, a Python/FastAPI backend, DALL·E 3 for text-to-image, Shap-E/TripoSR/Tripo3D for 2D-to-3D reconstruction, and Photon networking with Meta spatial anchors.
requirements: Used primarily during conceptual ideation and collaborative visualization, with students continuing their usual design tools for subsequent development
constraints: The study evaluates the addition of the structured GenARch workflow rather than isolating the effects of GenAI or XR from all other tools
Technical limitations in 2D-to-3D generation, scale fidelity, latency, contextual data, and control were inseparable from the educational experience
target_learners: undergraduate architectural engineering students in a design studio course
target_learning_goals: collaborative architectural conceptual design
visual ideation and representation
spatial evaluation and shared design review
examples: Four teams (N=16) incorporated GenARch into their usual course workflow across a tutorial, a 35-minute ideation session, and an 80-minute immersive collaborative visualization activity, while three teams (N=11) continued the usual workflow
key_sources: Xiao, Y., Chen, M., Li, Y., Powers, N., Wiesenfeld, M., Smith, G., Farzin, S., Liu, S. (2026). Generative AI and Extended Reality in Collaborative Architectural Design Education: An Exploratory Studio Study. arXiv preprint arXiv:2609.13494. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13494

article_title: From Prompts to Physical Laws: A Generative AI Workflow for Engineering Physics Education
citation: Laura B. Alvarado-Cruz, Josep Ll. Suñer, Pedro Yuste, Juan C. Castro-Palacio, Juan A. Monsoriu, and Francisco M. Muñoz-Pérez. (2026). From Prompts to Physical Laws: A Generative AI Workflow for Engineering Physics Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19400
title: Four-phase generative-AI physics workflow: video generation, Tracker tracking, Excel Solver curve fitting, parameter validation
description: A replicable instructional workflow combining generative-AI video platforms (PixVerse.ai, Grok Imagine, Pippit), the open-source Tracker video analysis tool, and the Microsoft Excel Solver GRG Nonlinear algorithm. As the article states, "The proposed workflow is organized into four sequential phases: (i) generation of synthetic videos using generative AI, (ii) extraction of kinematic data throug video analysis with software Tracker, (iii) estimation of model parameters by means of non-linear curve fitting, and (iv) identification and validation of the recovered physical parameters." It functions as a virtual laboratory mirroring experimental practice from model construction to quantitative validation.
requirements: Access to generative-AI video platforms, the Tracker open-source video analysis tool, and the Excel Solver add-in with the GRG Nonlinear algorithm
constraints: The agreement achieved is approximate rather than exact, since videos are generated from natural-language descriptions rather than explicit physical equations
target_learning_goals: experimental design
data acquisition
parameter estimation
model evaluation
modelling of physical systems
examples: Three scenarios were generated: a wooden block sliding with constant friction, a silicone rubber sphere falling in glycerin, and a skydiver with deployed parachute, each tracked and fitted to its analytical model
key_sources: Laura B. Alvarado-Cruz, Josep Ll. Suñer, Pedro Yuste, Juan C. Castro-Palacio, Juan A. Monsoriu, and Francisco M. Muñoz-Pérez. (2026). From Prompts to Physical Laws: A Generative AI Workflow for Engineering Physics Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19400

citation: Laura B. Alvarado-Cruz, Josep Ll. Suñer, Pedro Yuste, Juan C. Castro-Palacio, Juan A. Monsoriu, and Francisco M. Muñoz-Pérez. (2026). From Prompts to Physical Laws: A Generative AI Workflow for Engineering Physics Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19400

citation: Reza Farzi. (2026). Human–AI Collaboration in Academic Writing Instruction: Calibrated Feedback Model for EAP. OLBI Journal. https://doi.org/10.18192/olbij.v15i1.7773
title: Use generative AI to supplement, not replace, instructor feedback in academic writing instruction
description: The article recommends that language instructors leverage generative AI to support formative assessment while maintaining pedagogical oversight, because the study found GenAI "can supplement human feedback effectively but will not replace it." The principle preserves instructional quality and student agency by keeping the instructor responsible for depth and pedagogical framing while AI provides immediacy.

constraints: GenAI alone is less effective on rhetorical structure and contextual nuance

article_title: Layer-Sensitive Cognitive Offloading in Generative AI-Assisted Writing: Supported Performance and Independent No-AI Outcomes
citation: Chen X (2026) Layer-sensitive cognitive offloading in generative AI-assisted writing: supported performance and independent no-AI outcomes. Front. Psychol. 17:1906199. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1906199
title: Keep GenAI assistance away from the claim, evidence, and revision operations through which writing competence develops
description: The article's instructional implications recommend designing GenAI-supported writing so that the tool assists without assuming responsibility for core reasoning operations. Recommended practices include that "Students can complete an independent claim–evidence plan before consulting AI", that AI access initially be limited to diagnostic questions, alternatives, reader feedback, and local language clarification, and that students classify each AI-influenced change as accepted, modified, or rejected with a rationale. Rubrics can credit reasoning provenance and revision ownership, and support can then be faded with periodic independent tasks.
requirements: Logging or documentation of adoption decisions so students justify how AI suggestions were accepted, changed, or rejected
constraints: The bounded condition combined delegation restrictions with compulsory reflection, so the design cannot isolate the effect of either component; results are classroom-level associations from six intact classes, not definitive causal effects
target_learning_goals: Independent writing competence after AI support is removed
Higher-order thinking and revision ownership
examples: In the study, bounded-support students could request brainstorming questions, alternative outline options, reader-response feedback, and language clarification, while requests for complete paragraphs, final thesis statements, or full-text rewriting were prohibited

citation: Albert Munoz, Mercedez Hinchcliff, Cameron Langfield and Ann Rogerson. (2026). How strong is the evidence in generative AI-related academic misconduct allegations? A mixed-methods analysis. International Journal for Educational Integrity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00235-9
title: 15-code evidence taxonomy for GenAI misconduct proceedings organised into eight substantive categories
description: An empirically derived classification of evidence items in GenAI-related misconduct cases, developed through hybrid deductive-inductive framework analysis of 1,162 institutional case records. The finalised taxonomy "contained 15 codes organised into eight substantive categories", spanning non-probative assertions, student work and textual evidence, detection tool outputs, reference and source evidence, documentary admissions, interview evidence, examination and proctoring evidence, collusion evidence, and system records. Each code carries an operational definition, example indicator language, and probative-quality rating profiles across relevance, credibility and inferential force.

target_learning_goals: Fair and evidence-based adjudication of GenAI-related academic misconduct allegations
examples: Fabricated references (414 items, 22.3%) rated High relevance and credibility but predominantly Moderate inferential force; Interview Admissions (410 items, 22.1%) rated 97.2% Strong inferential force
