article_title: Experiential Versus Instructional Approaches for Eliciting Metacognitive Awareness in AI-Assisted Learning
citation: Pau Benazet i Montobbio, Janne Rotter, Davinia Hernández-Leo. (2026). Experiential Versus Instructional Approaches for Eliciting Metacognitive Awareness in AI-Assisted Learning: A Short-Term Longitudinal Study. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20047
title: Structured experiential exercise cycle: GenAI-assisted task, distraction, then unaided transfer task
description: Each experiential exercise in the intervention followed a three-step cycle: "(1) participants perform a task with the help of a GenAI system (approx. 5-10 min), (2) afterwards, participants performs a distraction task, on an unrelated topic (approx. 5 min), (3) finally participant perform a similar task related to the initial one, this time without the help of any GenAI systems (approx. 10 min)." The intervention paired two productive exercises (generation effect, Socratic questioning) with two unproductive ones (solution bypass, passive summary) so students directly experienced consequences of productive and unproductive GenAI use. Each exercise specified the task, the form of GenAI interaction, and a built-in reflection step.
requirements: Students receive condensed direct instruction before each exercise; the exercise specifies the task, the form of GenAI interaction, and a built-in reflection step.
constraints: The article describes this as structured and scaffolded practice providing the guidance novice learners require, not minimally guided discovery.
target_learning_goals: metacognitive awareness of productive and unproductive GenAI collaboration patterns
examples: Productive Exercise 1, 'The Generation Effect Activator', had students write a summary unaided, revise it from GenAI feedback, then apply concepts to novel scenarios after a distraction task.

article_title: The role of generative AI in facilitating children’s creative thinking and cognitive development: a systematic scoping review
citation: Niu T, Liu H, Pang P, Luo YT and Liu T (2026) The role of generative AI in facilitating children's creative thinking and cognitive development: a systematic scoping review. Front. Psychol. 17:1880052. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1880052
title: Four-modality taxonomy of GenAI used with children: text-based, multi-modal, image-based, and audio/music-based
description: The review organizes the GenAI technologies used across the included studies into four modalities: text-based GenAI (12 studies, mainly LLMs such as ChatGPT 3.5/4, Gemini and Claude), multi-modal text-and-image GenAI (seven studies), image-based text-to-image tools such as Midjourney and DALL-E 2 (four studies), and audio/music-based GenAI (one study). The review states that "Text-based and multi-modal GenAI are the dominant modalities used in the included studies, with image-based GenAI as a secondary focus, and audio/music-based GenAI minimally represented", attributing the distribution to the maturity and accessibility of each modality for K-12 creative learning.
requirements: Studies must apply GenAI (LLMs, image synthesis, or multi-modal tools) to children's creative-thinking outcomes to be classified within this taxonomy
constraints: Audio/music-based GenAI is minimally represented, with only one study, reflecting the relative immaturity of child-appropriate audio tools as the review states
target_learners: school-aged children and young adolescents (core target ages 6–15)
target_learning_goals: creative thinking dimensions including originality, fluency, flexibility, and elaboration
examples: Image-based GenAI is described as decoupling creative intent from technical artistic execution, enabling children with limited fine motor skills to visualize their creative ideas

title: Three intervention forms for GenAI in children's creative learning: workshop-based, classroom-integrated, and comparative interaction designs
description: The review classifies GenAI interventions into recurring forms: workshop-based interventions (nine studies), typically 90-min sessions with 4–10 total sessions over 1–4 months and participatory co-creation of prompts; classroom-based integrated interventions (seven studies) embedded in formal curricula from single 60-min sessions to 10-week programs; and comparative interaction interventions (five studies) completing identical creative tasks with GenAI versus human scaffolding or different modalities. The review reports that "Workshop-based interventions (nine studies) are the most common form across both formal and informal settings, typically consisting of 90-min sessions with 4–10 total sessions delivered over 1–4 months."

target_learning_goals: creative ideation, storytelling, visual expression, and creative problem-solving

description: This taxonomy organises student-identified priorities for GenAI curriculum development into three areas: understanding and optimising GenAI functionality, exploring GenAI applications across contexts, and navigating ethical and legal dimensions of GenAI. article_title: Helpful or harmful? Generative AI dependence, self-reported critical thinking disposition, and self-perceived employability among business students
citation: Shojaei SA, Armosh F, Lihe R, Hamacha R and Labib J (2026) Helpful or harmful? generative AI dependence, self-reported critical thinking disposition, and self-perceived employability among business students. Front. Educ. 11:1885990. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1885990
title: Augmentation–automation distinction with cognitive offloading and habit formation as a boundary-condition account of GenAI's educational effects
description: The article integrates four complementary perspectives to explain why GenAI use can help or harm learning. It states that "Cognitive load theory explains why bounded GenAI use may free cognitive resources for higher-order activities; cognitive offloading explains why excessive reliance may reduce opportunities for independent cognitive practice" and that habit-formation theory explains increasingly automatic reliance. The augmentation–automation distinction supplies the boundary-condition logic: at lower dependence, use functions as augmentation (comparing, verifying, evaluating), while at higher dependence it becomes substitutive, bypassing independent attempts and accepting outputs with limited scrutiny.
requirements: GenAI dependence must be modelled both as an endogenous construct and as a moderator, with direct paths from dependence to the outcomes retained as constituent main effects of a properly specified interaction model.
constraints: The article states the cross-sectional evidence should not be interpreted as demonstrating a temporal transition from augmentation to dependence; longitudinal or repeated-measures research is needed.

GenAI dependence encompasses several related experiences (habitual reliance, limited verification, access-related discomfort, reduced confidence), so results should not be interpreted as proving one single psychological mechanism causes the outcomes.
target_learning_goals: critical-thinking disposition
self-perceived employability
responsible and reflective GenAI use
examples: The study operationalised dependence as a moderator of the GenAI use–outcome associations in a PLS-SEM model of 412 Omani business students, with simple-slopes analysis showing attenuation at high dependence.

article_title: Is Solving Better Than Evaluating GenAI Solutions?
citation: Ethan Dickey, Marios Mertzanidis, Alexandros Psomas. (2026). Is Solving Better Than Evaluating GenAI Solutions? https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27586v1
title: GenAI-evaluation homework exercise: grading a flawed ChatGPT-generated solution to a challenging algorithm problem
description: An instructional element in which students prompt ChatGPT-4o with a standardized problem statement, then evaluate the generated solution: "evaluating the generated solution, including identifying and explaining any errors or omissions". Students distinguish minor issues (arithmetic, presentation) from major issues (incorrect algorithm, invalid recurrence, missing invariant, flawed proof step) and submit a share link and screenshot for verification. Problems were pre-tested so GenAI "could not reliably produce correct solutions"; generated solutions fell into recurring error patterns, e.g., failing to sort input or using a one-dimensional instead of two-dimensional DP table.
requirements: Standardized prompts without modification, share links and screenshots for verification, and instruction to evaluate the initial generated solution rather than iterating with the model
constraints: LLM output variability means students may receive meaningfully different artifacts to evaluate; grading rubrics differed from the solving condition
target_learners: undergraduate computing students in upper-division algorithms courses
target_learning_goals: solution verification, error diagnosis, proof evaluation, and justified confidence in algorithmic reasoning

article_title: Trust calibration and perceived developmental gains in university students' collaboration with generative AI: an exploratory sequential mixed methods study
citation: Fan Bu and Wei Li (2026). Trust calibration and perceived developmental gains in university students' collaboration with generative AI: an exploratory sequential mixed methods study. Front. Psychol. 17:1861072. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1861072
title: A four-construct process model of GenAI-supported learning: contextual support, trust calibration, collaborative regulation, and perceived transfer gains
description: The article proposes a layered process model in which contextual support (teacher guidance, assessment design, peer norms, institutional policy) is a context-level antecedent; trust calibration is a judgment-level hinge; collaborative regulation is a process-level mechanism of prompting, checking, comparing, rewriting, and integrating; and perceived transfer gains is an outcome-level, author-developed construct. Trust calibration is defined as the degree to which trust is "appropriately matched to task demands, output quality, and system limitations rather than being indiscriminately high or low". The model is grounded in social cognitive theory, self-regulated learning theory, cognitive load theory, and human-automation trust research.
requirements: Constructs are differentiated by analytic level (context, judgment, process, outcome) to reduce overlap among psychologically adjacent variables
constraints: The outcome is perceived transfer gains, not objective competence improvement; the model tests a focal analytic direction and does not claim a permanently one-way sequence, and cognitive load is not measured
target_learners: university undergraduates using GenAI for academic tasks
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
appropriate reliance on AI output
evaluative judgment and cross-task strategy transfer
examples: Study 1 interviews elicited task-sensitive reliance, e.g. a student who would use AI for ideas or wording but would not trust a citation or technical claim until verifying it

article_title: Generative artificial intelligence in university chemistry education: a critical review using Johnstone’s chemistry triplet and Biggs’ 3P model

title: Use GenAI for comparison and critique rather than as an authority
description: The review recommends positioning GenAI as a fallible object of disciplinary inquiry rather than an autonomous source of chemical truth. As it states, "GenAI should be used for comparison and critique rather than as an authority", with students asking for alternatives and counterexamples and comparing outputs with textbooks, primary literature, and experimental data. Classroom implementations cited used generated responses as objects of critique rather than final answers, turning model failures into assessable evidence of chemical reasoning.
requirements: Tasks must make uncertainty and error visible, for example by asking students to formulate questions that expose model limitations
constraints: The review notes that a design rewarding only the final product makes outsourcing rational
target_learning_goals: Critical evaluation of AI-generated chemical explanations
Metacognition and critical thinking
examples: Exintaris et al. (2023) and Guo and Lee (2023) used generated responses as objects of critique; Lopez-Perez et al. (2026) asked students to formulate questions exposing ChatGPT's limitations

citation: Wang Guanhua, Wang Wenna, Yang Daozhou, Ren Jifan. (2026). Generative AI, Cognitive Offloading, and Learner Agency in Higher Education: A Scoping Review. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071150
title: Dual-pattern framework: GenAI use in higher education splits into agency-supportive and agency-eroding patterns
description: The review's organizing framework interprets GenAI's educational significance through two recurring patterns rather than a single effect. Agency-supportive patterns involve self-regulated learning, self-efficacy, feedback literacy, and reflective engagement, while agency-eroding patterns involve cognitive offloading, overreliance, dependence, and uncritical uptake. The review states these are "best interpreted through an interpretive dual-pattern account" and stresses they are a configurative synthesis of heterogeneous evidence, not causal effect estimates.
requirements: Evidence must be charted as substantively addressing agency or offloading mechanisms, not merely keyword presence
constraints: The framework is an interpretive synthesis of heterogeneous, mostly non-causal evidence, not a causal model or ranking of mechanisms

citation: Yueqiao Jin, Roberto Martinez-Maldonado, Dragan Gašević and Lixiang Yan. (2024). GLAT: The Generative AI Literacy Assessment Test. https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.00283

description: The GLAT blueprint operationalises GenAI literacy using the four AI literacy dimensions proposed by Ng et al. description: The article proposes a conceptual framework with two dimensions: student–GenAI interaction and students' perceptions of GenAI use. citation: Ó Ceallaigh, T. J. & Murphy, S. (2026). Teaching the teachers: A systematic review of genAI-specific technological pedagogical knowledge (TPK) in teacher education. Computers and Education Open, 10, 100367. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeo.2026.100367

The review uses this construct as its organizing axis, treating ethical reasoning as embedded within pedagogical judgment rather than a separate domain.

citation: Bradley Irwin and Theron Muller. (2026). Positioning Generative AI in EFL Peer Feedback: Training Feedback Literacy and Enabling Uptake in Speaking Classes. Educ. Sci. 2026, 16, 544. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci16040544
title: GenAI as Trainer and Synthesizer: two complementary roles in EFL speaking peer feedback
description: The article proposes a theory-informed design framework positioning generative AI in two constrained roles within L2 speaking peer feedback. The Trainer supports feedback givers through "calibration with exemplars, rubric-guided practice, and feedback-on-feedback", while the Synthesizer supports recipients by aggregating peer input into concise, actionable guidance linked to criteria and learning goals. citation: Marcin Jukiewicz and Michał Wyrwa. (2026). Can ChatGPT Replace the Teacher in Assessment? A Review of Research on the Use of Large Language Models in Grading and Providing Feedback. Appl. Sci. 2026, 16, 680. https://doi.org/10.3390/app16020680
title: Three-role taxonomy of GenAI operationalization in grading workflows: automatic grader, grader-plus-feedback-generator, and co-grader
description: The review organizes how GenAI is operationalized in assessment workflows by the role the model plays. In most studies AI acted as "an automatic grader, independently assigning points or grades to student responses with minimal human involvement"; in others it both assigned a score and generated feedback on strengths and weaknesses; and in co-grading it suggested a grade the educator could verify. The taxonomy is paired with a task-type distribution (essays in 16 studies, short written answers in 11) and a prompting characterization: GenAI was typically guided using rubric- or exemplar-based prompts, with 32 studies including a scoring rubric or sample correct answer.
requirements: Deployment requires deciding the model's role (automatic grader, grader plus feedback generator, or co-grader) and supplying rubric- or exemplar-based prompts.
constraints: The taxonomy derives from the 42 studies reviewed, published 2023–2025, most in higher education.
target_learners: students across educational levels, from primary school through higher education
target_learning_goals: accurate grading and feedback on student written work, short answers, code, and calculation tasks
examples: The review counts 20 studies using API integration and 16 entering data manually into the ChatGPT interface.

article_title: Eight Ways to Promote Generative Learning
citation: Fiorella, L., & Mayer, R. E. (2016). Eight Ways to Promote Generative Learning. Educational Psychology Review, 28, 717–741. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9348-9
title: Generative learning theory grounded in Wittrock's generative model of comprehension and reflected in Mayer's select-organize-integrate (SOI) framework
description: The article organizes its review around generative learning theory, which it describes as "grounded in Wittrock's (1974) generative model of comprehension and reflected in more recent frameworks of active learning, such as Mayer's (2014) select-organize-integrate (SOI) framework." The theory holds that learning occurs when learners actively make sense of material by reorganizing and integrating it with prior knowledge, rather than passively receiving it. The eight strategies the review covers are presented as instructional implementations of this generative account of comprehension and active learning.
requirements: Learners must actively engage in sense-making processes that connect new information to prior knowledge for the theory's predicted benefits to occur
target_learners: Learners across educational settings studying to-be-learned informational material
target_learning_goals: Meaningful comprehension and transfer of learned material to new situations
examples: The review uses the theory to structure its treatment of eight strategies, providing for each "a description, review exemplary research studies, discuss potential boundary conditions, and provide practical recommendations for implementation."

article_title: Generative AI enhances individual creativity but reduces the collective diversity of novel content
citation: Anil R. Doshi and Oliver P. Hauser. (2023). Generative artificial intelligence enhances creativity but reduces the diversity of novel content. https://aspredicted.org/136723
title: Dual-pathway account: GenAI ideas as springboard versus anchor for human creativity
description: The article proposes two non-exclusive causal pathways by which access to GenAI ideas can affect human creative output. In the enhancing pathway, generated ideas serve as a "springboard" for the human mind, offering starting points that branch into a "tree structure" of storylines and helping writers overcome "writer's block" and the fear of a blank page. In the hampering pathway, GenAI anchors the writer to a specific starting idea, restricting the variability of the writer's own ideas and yielding derivative output. The study's findings — creativity gains alongside increased story similarity — are interpreted through both pathways operating at once.
requirements: Access to GenAI-generated starting ideas during a creative production task, with the writer free to use or ignore them
constraints: The two pathways "may not be mutually exclusive": enhancement on some dimensions (e.g. novelty) need not accompany enhancement on others (e.g. usefulness)
target_learners: adult writers on open-ended creative production tasks
target_learning_goals: produce creative written content (novel and useful stories)
examples: The experiment operationalized the pathways by offering writers one or up to five three-sentence GPT-4 story ideas versus no access, then measuring both evaluated creativity and embedding-based story similarity.
key_sources: Anil R. Doshi and Oliver P. Hauser. (2023). Generative artificial intelligence enhances creativity but reduces the diversity of novel content. https://aspredicted.org/136723

article_title: Investigating the higher education institutions’ guidelines and policies regarding the use of generative AI in teaching, learning, research, and administration
citation: Yunjo An, Ji Hyun Yu and Shadarra James. (2025). Investigating the higher education institutions' guidelines and policies regarding the use of generative AI in teaching, learning, research, and administration. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-025-00507-3
title: Faculty GenAI guidance pattern: syllabus statements, course policy communication, and redesigned authentic/process-oriented assessments
description: The article identifies a recurring pattern in faculty-targeted GenAI guidelines: providing template syllabus statements (e.g., Stanford's three categories from "AI tools permitted freely" to "AI tools not permitted"), advising faculty to set and communicate course policies (54%), and redesigning assignments and assessments (48%). Specifically, "authentic assessments (e.g., real-world tasks, projects), process-oriented assessments (e.g., low-stakes writing, drafts, presentations, oral exams, portfolios), and assignments requiring higher-order thinking were commonly recommended". This pattern operationalizes institutional guidance for teaching in the GenAI era.
requirements: Faculty must establish and communicate course-specific GenAI policies to students through syllabi and assignment prompts
constraints: The article notes guidance for faculty can become burdensome since continuous revisions are recommended in the policies (citing McDonald et al., 2024)
target_learning_goals: academic integrity
assessment design in the era of GenAI
AI literacy
examples: Stanford University provided template syllabus statements in three categories; the University of Chicago provided examples in four categories; 48% of universities advised redesigning assignments and assessments

article_title: Using generative ai as a simulation to support higher-order thinking
citation: Borge, M., Smith, B.K. & Aldemir, T. (2024). Using generative ai as a simulation to support higher-order thinking. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn 19, 479–532. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09437-0
title: GenAI as a social interaction and cultural simulation tool for practicing collective sensemaking skills
description: The article frames chat-based generative AI as a learning environment in which learners can engage in collaborative sense-making with an AI partner. Its initial findings "indicate the promise of GenAI as a valuable social interaction and cultural simulation tool for learners to practice collective sensemaking skills". The framework positions GenAI technology as capable of creating "stimulating new learning environments that support complex sense-making activities", with the AI serving as a partner rather than an answer source.

constraints: Chat-based GenAI technologies have "a tendency to provide definitive answers unsupported by evidence"

Metacognition and sociometacognition

article_title: Students’ voices on generative AI: perceptions, benefits, and challenges in higher education
citation: Chan, C. K. Y., & Hu, W. (2023). Students’ voices on generative AI: perceptions, benefits, and challenges in higher education. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education, 20:43. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-023-00411-8
title: Five perceived benefit categories of GenAI in student learning: personalized support, writing and brainstorming, research and analysis, multimedia, and administrative support
description: Thematic analysis of open-ended survey responses (n = 387 coded by two coders with a consensus codebook) yielded five benefit categories students gave for willingness to use GenAI: "1. Personalized and immediate learning support", "2. Writing and brainstorming support", "3. Research and analysis support", "4. Visual and audio multi-media support", and "5. Administrative support" (Table 5). Students described GenAI as a virtual tutor giving immediate answers, a writing assistant for idea generation and polishing, a research aid for literature searching and hypothesis generation, and a handler of repetitive tasks.
requirements: Applies where students have access to GenAI tools and tasks suited to learning support, writing, research, multimedia creation, or administrative work
constraints: Perceptions from a convenience sample of Hong Kong university students; GenAI was not yet fully used in formal academic settings at the time of the study
target_learning_goals: learning support, writing skills, research and analysis skills, multimedia creation
examples: A student described ChatGPT as "a top student" offering help when no one else could; an English major proposed generating short texts to memorize vocabulary; science and engineering students used DALL-E and Stable Diffusion to create artwork.

citation: Chan, C. K. Y., & Hu, W. (2023). Students’ voices on generative AI: perceptions, benefits, and challenges in higher education. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education, 20:43. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-023-00411-8
title: Six perceived challenge categories of GenAI: accuracy and transparency, privacy and ethics, holistic competencies, career prospects, human values, and uncertain policies
description: Thematic analysis of open-ended responses yielded six challenge categories: "1. Accuracy and transparency", "2. Privacy and ethical issues", "3. Holistic competencies", "4. Career prospects", "5. Human values", and "6. Uncertain policies" (Table 5). Students worried they "cannot predict or accurately verify the accuracy or validity of AI generated information", about data privacy, plagiarism detection, over-reliance harming critical thinking and creativity, job replacement, value misalignment and inequality, and the absence of institutional guidance.

constraints: Perceptions from a convenience sample of Hong Kong university students; more than half of participants expressed concerns while some were optimistic

description: The article introduces a two-stage semi-supervised framework: a high-capacity language model is first trained on a large unlabeled corpus with a language modeling objective, then adapted to supervised target tasks. As the article states, "Our training procedure consists of two stages. The ﬁrst stage is learning a high-capacity language model on a large corpus of text." The goal is a universal representation that transfers with little adaptation across diverse tasks.

article_title: Cognitive Load Theory: How Many Types of Load Does It Really Need?
citation: Kalyuga, S. (2011). Cognitive Load Theory: How Many Types of Load Does It Really Need?. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9150-7
title: Redefined germane load as actual working memory resources devoted to dealing with intrinsic rather than extraneous load
description: The article proposes a possible redefinition under which germane load could keep an independent role within the cognitive load framework. Following a recent suggestion the article attributes to John Sweller, germane load would refer to "the actual working memory resources devoted to dealing with intrinsic rather than extraneous load". This reframing ties germane load to the processing of intrinsic load rather than treating it as a separate additive load type. It is offered as a conditional alternative to dropping the concept entirely.
requirements: The redefinition presupposes retaining the intrinsic/extraneous distinction within the cognitive load framework
constraints: The article presents this redefinition as conditional: germane load might have an independent role only if redefined in this way
target_learners: All learners addressed by cognitive load theory
target_learning_goals: Managing working memory load during learning and instruction
examples: The article cites John Sweller's recent suggestion as the source of this redefinition of germane load

article_title: A generative theory of textbook design: Using annotated illustrations to foster meaningful learning of science text
citation: Mayer, R.E., Steinhoff, K., Bower, G., & Mars, R. (1995). A generative theory of textbook design: Using annotated illustrations to foster meaningful learning of science text. ETR&D, 43, 31-41. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02300480
title: Generative theory of multimedia learning
description: The article interprets its results in light of a generative theory of multimedia learning, which "posits that meaningful learning requires constructing connections between visual and verbal representations of a system." The theory explains why annotated illustrations integrated with text fostered transfer: they support building cross-representational links during learning. It draws on generative views of learning as an active constructive process.
requirements: Learning materials must present visual and verbal representations that learners can connect during learning
constraints: The theory is applied here to learning of explanatory science text with illustrations by college students
target_learning_goals: meaningful learning of explanatory science text and problem-solving transfer
examples: In three experiments, annotated lightning-formation illustrations placed adjacent to corresponding text paragraphs produced more creative transfer solutions than the same illustrations shown separately without annotations.

article_title: The Self-Regulation-View in Writing-to-Learn: Using Journal Writing to Optimize Cognitive Load in Self-Regulated Learning
citation: Nückles, M., Roelle, J., Glogger-Frey, I., Waldeyer, J., & Renkl, A. (2020). The Self-Regulation-View in Writing-to-Learn: Using Journal Writing to Optimize Cognitive Load in Self-Regulated Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09541-1
title: The genre-free principle: journal writing without prescribed rhetorical structure as a variant of the goal-free effect in cognitive load theory
description: The genre-free principle holds that learning journals, unlike genres such as argumentative essays or scientific reports, have no conventionalized rhetorical structure, so a high-quality learning journal entry is not expected to be a rhetorically well-shaped text. The authors suggest this principle can be considered, at least on a more general level, as a particular variant of the goal-free effect in cognitive load theory: taking away the goal to stick to a rhetorical format allows learners to devote more cognitive capacity to germane processing of subject matter rather than to extraneous genre-conforming strategies.
requirements: The writing task must genuinely lack a prescribed rhetorical format so writers are offloaded from instantiating rhetorical schemata
constraints: Stated as a theoretical assumption grounded in cognitive load theory rather than as a separately tested manipulation in the studies summarized
target_learners: novice writers in secondary and higher education
target_learning_goals: germane processing of subject matter
deep comprehension

description: The principle holds that generative AI technologies like ChatGPT should be integrated into VR learning environments to provide "targeted, real-time feedback, thus addressing limitations of traditional VR feedback mechanisms." The article argues this integration supports deeper engagement and more effective learning outcomes, particularly in problem-solving and critical thinking, and offers it as guidance for future educational technology implementations.

article_title: Learning against the machine: the double edged sword of (Gen)AI in STEM education
citation: Peter Wulff and Marcus Kubsch. (2025). Learning against the machine: the double edged sword of (Gen)AI in STEM education. International Journal of STEM Education 12:66. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-025-00588-6
title: Treat GenAI adoption in STEM education with a default assumption that it might hamper active learning, placing the burden of proof on adopters
description: The article recommends that responsible actors adopt GenAI only with substantive pedagogical, ethical, and economic rationales, stating "The default assumption should be that GenAI might hamper active learning in STEM disciplines". It argues the onus lies on institutions and providers to prove their systems worthy of adoption for learning, "just as new drugs have to be rigorously approved in the medical sector", and that performing well on exams does not count as evidence of usefulness for STEM learning.
requirements: A robust, empirically grounded argument for why to use GenAI instead of other tools or reforms, supported by replicable discipline-based research
constraints: The article acknowledges adoption is arguably not a question of if but of when, and that no conclusive evidence on when, how, and why has yet been gathered
target_learners: STEM learners at all educational levels
target_learning_goals: Active, critical, and in-depth engagement with STEM subject matter
examples: The authors report that ChatGPT's study mode did not convince them in multiple trials given lack of pedagogically grounded guidance and repeated factual errors, and that they would not recommend a GenAI-generated textbook's basketball example for Newton's third law.

article_title: Calculating and reporting effect sizes to facilitate cumulative science: a practical primer for t-tests and ANOVAs
citation: Lakens, D. (2013). Calculating and reporting effect sizes to facilitate cumulative science: a practical primer for t-tests and ANOVAs. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2013.00863
title: Two viewpoints on effect sizes: the generalizable effect size estimate viewpoint versus the statistical significance viewpoint
description: The article distinguishes two perspectives on which effect size is the "true" effect size for the same data. The generalizable effect size estimate viewpoint seeks metrics that can be interpreted across studies regardless of design, regarding within-subjects effect sizes like η²p as overestimations. The statistical significance viewpoint treats individual differences as irrelevant to the tested hypothesis and prefers effect sizes and confidence intervals that reflect the statistical test, so design-dependent values are a benefit of a more powerful design. The article notes the viewpoints are not mutually exclusive but determine practical reporting choices.
requirements: Researchers must decide which viewpoint their reported effect size serves, since the choice determines the practical reporting decisions they make
constraints: The article applies the distinction to standardized mean differences in between- and within-subjects designs for t-tests and ANOVAs
target_learners: experimental researchers in psychology and education
target_learning_goals: calculating and reporting effect sizes for t-tests and ANOVAs
planning sample sizes via a-priori power analysis
examples: The article illustrates the divergence with the same two observations yielding η²p of 0.26 or 0.71 depending on design

citation: Tessa H. S. Eysink & Ton de Jong (2012). Does Instructional Approach Matter? How Elaboration Plays a Crucial Role in Multimedia Learning. Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2011.611776
title: Generic learning processes coding scheme for think-aloud protocols
description: A coding scheme used to classify think-aloud utterances into mutually exclusive categories of superficial processes (e.g., reading/watching and filtering, checking solution steps), elaborative processes (developing and testing hypotheses, relating and integrating, giving (self-)explanations), and regulative processes (orienting, planning, monitoring, reflecting). It was piloted and adjusted, and "was constructed to have a generic character allowing the representation of all instructional approaches and applicability to problem-solving domains other than probability theory". Interrater reliability reached .85 (Cohen's kappa) for the three main categories and .74 for subcategories.
requirements: Protocols segmented into utterances, each defined as a statement expressing one distinct learner activity, coded by trained coders
constraints: Reflection was restricted to purely regulative activities, with deeper reflective processes placed in the elaborative category
target_learning_goals: characterizing the learning processes elicited by different instructional approaches
examples: Applied to think-aloud protocols of 40 students working through one of the four probability-theory learning environments

article_title: Enhancing Student Competency Models for Game-Based Learning with a Hybrid Stealth Assessment Framework
citation: Henderson, N., Kumaran, V., Min, W., Mott, B., Wu, Z., Boulden, D., Lord, T., Reichsman, F., Dorsey, C., Wiebe, E., & Lester, J. (2020). Enhancing Student Competency Models for Game-Based Learning with a Hybrid Stealth Assessment Framework. Proceedings of The 13th International Conference on Educational Data Mining (EDM 2020), 92-103. https://educationaldatamining.org/EDM2020/proceedings/
title: Geniventure: a game-based learning environment for introductory genetics
description: Geniventure is a game-based learning environment for introductory genetics targeting middle and high school students ages 11-18. Students breed and study drakes, "a model species for dragons," to explore heredity, dominant and recessive traits, and the protein-to-trait relationship. The game consists of "60 increasingly difficult puzzle-like challenges across 6 levels," with scaffolded hints and progressive complexity covering concepts aligned with the Next Generation Science Standards. Students can validate their work at any time and receive system-generated hints based on their perceived understanding. The game records fine-grained trace data including navigated challenges, allele changes, submitted answers, and received hints.

Pre- and post-test assessments aligned to the game's ECD competency model

target_learning_goals: introductory genetics including heredity, dominance and recessive traits, protein-to-trait relationship, breeding and inheritance, test cross, X-linked and polyallelic traits
examples: Students played Geniventure during teacher-led classroom implementations over several days, attempting between 5 and 248 challenges, with gameplay recorded as JSON-format trace data logs

article_title: The Effects of Generative Learning Strategy Prompts and Metacognitive Feedback on Learners' Self-Regulation, Generation Process, and Achievement
citation: Lee, Hyeon Woo. (2008). The effects of generative learning strategy prompts and metacognitive feedback on learners' self-regulation, generation process, and achievement. Dissertation in Instructional Systems, The Pennsylvania State University. https://etda.libraries.psu.edu
title: Generative learning theory: meaningful learning arises from learners actively generating relations between new information and prior knowledge
description: Generative learning theory, attributed to Wittrock, holds that comprehension results from learners' active generation of meaning rather than transfer of presented information into memory. At its essence are processes people use "actively and dynamically to (a) selectively attend to events and (b) generate meaning for events by constructing relations between new or incoming information and previously acquired information, conceptions, and background knowledge". The dissertation uses this theory as the framework for its path model, in which self-regulation controls generative activities and generative strategy use produces knowledge generation. Strategies range from simple coding (underlining, note taking, adjunct questions) to complex coding (summarizing, concept mapping) and elaborative integration (imaging, analogies).
requirements: Learners must be mentally active in creating relationships between new content and what they already know, with motivation and metacognitive control supporting the meaning-making process
constraints: The article notes the effects of generative learning strategies are not always consistent in every learning environment
target_learners: undergraduate students in computer-based learning environments
target_learning_goals: recall and comprehension of complex instructional material through meaningful knowledge generation
examples: The study operationalized generative strategies as highlighting important sentences, note taking, and interacting with adjunct questions within static visualized instruction
key_sources: Lee, Hyeon Woo. (2008). The effects of generative learning strategy prompts and metacognitive feedback on learners' self-regulation, generation process, and achievement. Dissertation in Instructional Systems, The Pennsylvania State University. https://etda.libraries.psu.edu

description: The chapter identifies Gee's monograph's chief contribution as a set of learning principles extracted from commercial video games. As the chapter states, "Gee offers up the chief contribution of his text, thirty-six principles of learning which he identifies in quality video games." These principles undergird later games-and-learning scholarship, with subsets later drawn on to inform serious game design and integrated with home-discipline work.

article_title: Instrumental learning and cognitive flexibility processes are impaired in children exposed to early life stress
citation: Harms Madeline B., Shannon-Bowen Katherine E., Hanson Jamie L., Pollak Seth D. (2018). Instrumental Learning and Cognitive Flexibility Processes are Impaired in Children Exposed to Early Life Stress. Developmental Science. https://doi.org/10.1111/desc.12596
title: General learning mechanism account of early-stress social problems
description: The article proposes that broad social and cognitive deficits in stress-exposed children arise not from domain-specific socio-emotional impairments but from disrupted "general learning mechanisms". Chronic caregiver inconsistency, poor emotional signaling, and reduced exploration create a challenging learning environment that impairs associative learning and flexible updating, which in turn undermines social adaptation. The fMRI task results are presented as converging behavioral and neural support.
requirements: Exposure to severe early life stress such as documented physical abuse
constraints: The account is tested in adolescents with documented childhood physical abuse; SES and abuse co-occur, though findings held when controlling for SES
target_learners: adolescents exposed to early life stress
target_learning_goals: associative learning of stimulus-response contingencies
cognitive flexibility in updating learned associations
examples: The instrumental learning task required responding to images for reward or avoiding response for punishment, then reversing half the associations
