article_title: Examining the Differential Role of General and Specific Processing Speed in Predicting Mathematical Achievement in Junior High School
citation: Cheng Dazhi, Shi Kaihui, Wang Naiyi, Miao Xinyang, Zhou Xinlin. (2022). Examining the Differential Role of General and Specific Processing Speed in Predicting Mathematical Achievement in Junior High School. Journal of Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.3390/jintelligence10010001
title: CHC-based division of processing speed into general (perceptual and decision speed) and specific (reading and arithmetic fluency) components
description: Following the Cattell–Horn–Carroll theory of cognitive abilities as presented by Schneider and McGrew (2012), the article organizes processing speed into two components: general processing speed, comprising perceptual speed and decision speed, and specific processing speed, comprising reading fluency and arithmetic fluency, which the authors treat as representing academic fluency. The article states that "Processing speed is divided into general processing speed (perceptual and decision speed) and specific processing speed (number facility/arithmetic and reading fluency [representing the academic fluency])". The study operationalizes general speed with choice reaction time and figure matching, and specific speed with word semantics and three arithmetic tasks, then tests their differential prediction of achievement.
requirements: Tasks must separately measure perceptual/decision speed and domain-specific symbolic fluency (reading and arithmetic)
constraints: The distinction is tested in junior high school students in a Chinese school context using timed computerized tasks
target_learning_goals: mathematical achievement and academic achievement in major subjects (mathematics, Chinese, English)
examples: The study administered choice reaction time and figure matching as general speed tasks, and word semantic, simple subtraction, complex subtraction, and complex multiplication as specific speed tasks
key_sources: Cheng Dazhi, Shi Kaihui, Wang Naiyi, Miao Xinyang, Zhou Xinlin. (2022). Examining the Differential Role of General and Specific Processing Speed in Predicting Mathematical Achievement in Junior High School. Journal of Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.3390/jintelligence10010001

article_title: Transfer from spatial education to verbal reasoning and prediction of transfer from learning-related neural change
citation: Cortes, R. A., Peterson, E. G., Kraemer, D. J. M., Kolvoord, R. A., Uttal, D. H., Dinh, N., Weinberger, A. B., Daker, R. J., Lyons, I. M., Goldman, D., & Green, A. E. (2022). Transfer from spatial education to verbal reasoning and prediction of transfer from learning-related neural change. Science Advances. https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.abo3555
title: Geospatial Semester: a GIS-based in-school spatial curriculum for high school STEM
description: The Geospatial Semester is a real-world high school course, first adopted by Virginia high schools in 2005 and now implemented over two semesters, in which students construct and evaluate spatial representations (maps) of real-world geographical datasets using GIS technology. A central component is to develop students' ability to scan maps to identify key spatial features and determine how these features are related across maps, and to foster more frequent use of spatial thinking strategies. Students take the course for either 45 min daily or 90 min every other day and receive college credit from James Madison University, whose faculty mentor the high school teachers. In this study it was the intervention, offered by the schools and completely unaltered by the researchers to ensure ecological validity.
requirements: GIS technology such as ArcGIS
partnership between schools and a university providing technical support and teacher mentoring
constraints: The study reflects an ecologically valid classroom implementation; the curriculum's content focuses on two-dimensional spatial representations
target_learning_goals: spatial scanning
spatial habits of mind
spatial thinking with geospatial technology
examples: Student projects included GIS-based visualizations of spatial data relationships, such as mapping the distribution of high-speed internet resources within a geographic region
key_sources: Cortes, R. A., Peterson, E. G., Kraemer, D. J. M., Kolvoord, R. A., Uttal, D. H., Dinh, N., Weinberger, A. B., Daker, R. J., Lyons, I. M., Goldman, D., & Green, A. E. (2022). Transfer from spatial education to verbal reasoning and prediction of transfer from learning-related neural change. Science Advances. https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.abo3555

article_title: Early life stress and development: potential mechanisms for adverse outcomes
citation: Karen E. Smith and Seth D. Pollak. (2020). Early life stress and development: potential mechanisms for adverse outcomes. Journal of Neurodevelopmental Disorders. https://doi.org/10.1186/s11689-020-09337-y
title: General (lumping) models treat early life stress as a heterogeneous cumulative category of adverse events
description: The review describes general or lumping models as one of two predominant approaches to conceptualizing early life stress. In this approach, various types of stressors are treated as a heterogeneous, broad category, and individuals are queried about whether they experienced a pre-defined set of potential adverse events in childhood, with total exposure summed. Examples include Life Stressors Checklists and the Adverse Child Experiences Scale. The approach rests on animal literature suggesting repeated exposure to stress, regardless of type, chronically activates stress response systems and alters neural synaptic plasticity.
requirements: Assessment instruments that query a pre-defined set of potential adverse events in childhood and sum total exposure, such as Life Stressors Checklists and the Adverse Child Experiences Scale
constraints: The review states cumulative models have lacked consistent insight into the neurobiological mechanisms underlying individual differences in children's responses to stress
target_learners: children exposed to chronic or extreme stress in early life
target_learning_goals: understanding how cumulative adversity shapes neurobiological development and long-term cognitive, emotional, and behavioral outcomes
examples: A recent longitudinal study from 18 months to mid-adulthood found that cumulative stress rather than physical abuse alone was predictive of adult depressive symptoms
key_sources: Karen E. Smith and Seth D. Pollak. (2020). Early life stress and development: potential mechanisms for adverse outcomes. Journal of Neurodevelopmental Disorders. https://doi.org/10.1186/s11689-020-09337-y

article_title: Cognitive Load Theory: New Conceptualizations, Specifications, and Integrated Research Perspectives
citation: Fred Paas, Tamara van Gog, John Sweller. (2010). Cognitive Load Theory: New Conceptualizations, Specifications, and Integrated Research Perspectives. Educational Psychology Review, 22, 115-121. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9133-8
title: Generalized knowledge structures at a medium level of generality as a means to facilitate flexible problem-solving skills
description: The special issue's fourth article (Kalyuga, Renkl & Paas) suggests CLT could be improved by increased emphasis on generalized knowledge structures rather than its current emphasis on domain-specific knowledge. The focus is not on generic universal problem-solving heuristics but on domain-specific knowledge at "a medium level of generality between generic knowledge and the routine low-level knowledge structures". Based on a review of theoretical and empirical evidence, the authors conclude such structures could be important for developing flexible expertise.
requirements: The proposed emphasis concerns domain-specific knowledge of medium generality, not generic universal problem-solving heuristics
constraints: CLT's success derives largely from its emphasis on domain-specific knowledge, and it was devised partly as a reaction to failed theories advocating general knowledge structures
target_learning_goals: flexible problem-solving skills
adaptive instruction
examples: The conclusion rests on a review of theoretical foundations and empirical evidence on CLT, problem solving, and adaptive instruction
key_sources: Fred Paas, Tamara van Gog, John Sweller. (2010). Cognitive Load Theory: New Conceptualizations, Specifications, and Integrated Research Perspectives. Educational Psychology Review, 22, 115-121. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9133-8

article_title: Rendering controversial socioscientific issues legible through digital mapping tools
citation: Solli, A., Mäkitalo, Å., & Hillman, T. (2018). Rendering controversial socioscientific issues legible through digital mapping tools. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9286-x
title: Gephi network visualization tool for controversy mapping in classrooms
description: Gephi is "an interactive visualization and exploration tool for all kinds of networks" used by students to render hyperlinked website corpora as network maps. It displays nodes as websites and edges as hyperlinks, showing "the relative centrality of a website in relation to a particular issue" through size (inbound links), position (edge quantity), and color attributes that update in real time as students rank, filter, and colorize nodes.
requirements: A corpus of hyperlink data exported as a network file, generated by collecting web browsing data with a tool such as Navicrawler
constraints: Operates only on relationships between nodes, not website content; multi-purpose functions irrelevant to students' categorizing task; not developed for pedagogical use or for judging trustworthiness of claims
target_learning_goals: evaluating information sources and distinguishing scientific from non-scientific claims about socio-scientific controversies
examples: Students working on the HPV vaccine controversy produced maps typically based on visits to approximately 400 websites, coloring nodes by category (public, media, against the vaccine)
key_sources: Solli, A., Mäkitalo, Å., & Hillman, T. (2018). Rendering controversial socioscientific issues legible through digital mapping tools. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9286-x

article_title: Coordinating modalities of mathematical collaboration in shared VR environments
citation: Wen Huang, Candace Walkington, Mitchell J. Nathan. (2023). Coordinating modalities of mathematical collaboration in shared VR environments. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09397-x
title: Geometry Simulation Environment (GSE)
description: The GSE is a shared VR simulation installed on Oculus Quest goggles, designed by the research team as part of a design-based research program on mixed reality for geometry learning. Learners log into a single virtual classroom from their homes, see each other's avatars, and collaboratively manipulate shared geometric shapes with real-time measurement displays. Its design supports gestural congruency: virtual objects are manipulated intuitively through hand gestures.
requirements: Oculus Quest VR goggles with hand-tracking capability and a virtual classroom dashboard for joining a shared session
target_learning_goals: geometric conjecture evaluation
3D perspective-taking
volume and scaling reasoning
justification and proof
examples: Participants manipulated cylinders, triangles, cubes, and other solids; critical measurements such as height, volume, and radius were displayed and updated in real time
key_sources: Wen Huang, Candace Walkington, Mitchell J. Nathan. (2023). Coordinating modalities of mathematical collaboration in shared VR environments. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09397-x

article_title: Is drawing after learning effective for metacognitive monitoring only when supported by spatial scaffolds?
citation: Julia Kollmer, Katrin Schleinschok, Katharina Scheiter, Alexander Eitel. (2020). Is drawing after learning effective for metacognitive monitoring only when supported by spatial scaffolds? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09521-6
title: Generative tasks foster metacognitive monitoring by prompting situation-model reasoning that yields more diagnostic JOL cues
description: The article's explanatory framework holds that inaccurate monitoring stems from learners basing JOLs on superficial cues such as the ease-of-processing heuristic. Generative tasks like drawing "require situation-model reasoning, because they require constructing a 'new' representation in a different code", transforming verbal relations into spatial ones and giving implicit feedback about knowledge gaps. JOLs grounded in situation-model comprehension are less inflated because less forgetting occurs at that level, improving calibration. The study tests this account by comparing drawing conditions against mental reactivation.
requirements: Learners must perform the generative task after reading and directly before providing JOLs, without access to the text (closed-book conditions).
constraints: The account was tested with high visuo-spatial content; the authors state it remains open whether drawing supports monitoring for contents lower in visuo-spatial reasoning demands.
target_learners: university students learning expository text independently
target_learning_goals: accurate metacognitive monitoring (calibration and resolution) of expository text comprehension
examples: Students drew the crucial concepts from each aurora-text paragraph and labeled the diagram before giving a JOL on an 11-point 0-100 scale.
key_sources: Julia Kollmer, Katrin Schleinschok, Katharina Scheiter, Alexander Eitel. (2020). Is drawing after learning effective for metacognitive monitoring only when supported by spatial scaffolds? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09521-6

article_title: Example-based learning: should learners receive closed-book or open-book self-explanation prompts?
citation: Sara Hiller · Stefan Rumann · Kirsten Berthold · Julian Roelle. (2020). Example-based learning: should learners receive closed-book or open-book self-explanation prompts? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09523-4
title: Dual theoretical lenses: generative learning theory and retrieval-based learning theory applied to self-explanation prompt format
description: The article analyzes self-explanation prompts through two theoretical frameworks. Generative learning theory predicts open-book prompts are more effective because "a closed-book format likely reduces the amount of generated self-explanations", since the number of generated self-explanations is considered crucial while retrieval amount is not. Retrieval-based learning theory instead predicts closed-book benefits, because closed-book prompts require retrieval practice, which fosters long-term retention via memory-trace consolidation. The article argues that combining both lenses, plus the imperfection of retrieval, yields time-dependent predictions.
requirements: The dual-lens account applies to generative learning tasks that can be implemented with or without access to source material during generation
constraints: The article notes the simple retrieval-practice rationale "might be too simple" because learners seldomly retrieve information perfectly
Conclusions limited to retention intervals not exceeding 1 week
target_learners: secondary school students learning from worked examples
target_learning_goals: conceptual knowledge of science principles and examples
examples: The experiments manipulated prompt format (closed- vs. open-book) and active processing of instructional explanation prompts in a 2 × 2 factorial between-subjects design
key_sources: Sara Hiller · Stefan Rumann · Kirsten Berthold · Julian Roelle. (2020). Example-based learning: should learners receive closed-book or open-book self-explanation prompts? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09523-4

article_title: Teacher versus student perspectives on instructional quality in mathematics education across countries
citation: Xin Liu, Kajsa Yang Hansen, Jan De Neve, Martin Valcke. (2023). Teacher versus student perspectives on instructional quality in mathematics education across countries. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09652-6
title: Continuum for classifying instructional quality frameworks: generic, subject-specific, and hybrid
description: The article organizes frameworks for conceptualizing instructional quality along a continuum adapted from Charalambous and Praetorius (2018), in which "Senden et al. (2022) adjusted this continuum by building on three categories: generic frameworks, subject-specific frameworks, and hybrid frameworks." Generic frameworks emphasize general-level aspects without subject-specific teaching demands (e.g., the Three Basic Dimensional framework of classroom management, cognitive activation, and supportive climate); subject-specific frameworks focus on content-related interactions (e.g., MQI, M-Scan, IQA); hybrid frameworks combine both, exemplified by the Dynamic Model of Educational Effectiveness with eight key decisions. The study uses this continuum to interpret whether its identified dimensions reflect generic or mathematics-specific features.
requirements: The article applies mathematics as the specific domain to describe the primary frameworks and dimensions on the continuum (Fig. 1).
constraints: The article notes researchers consider the DMEE a generic framework without subject-specific instruction, though its own findings suggest DMEE can be seen as hybrid.
target_learners: mathematics students in primary and secondary education
target_learning_goals: conceptualizing and evaluating the quality of mathematics instruction
examples: The article situates the Three Basic Dimensional framework (classroom management, cognitive activation, supportive climate) as generic and the DMEE's eight dimensions (management of time, classroom climate, orientation, questioning, structuring, teaching-modeling, application, assessment) as hybrid.
key_sources: Xin Liu, Kajsa Yang Hansen, Jan De Neve, Martin Valcke. (2023). Teacher versus student perspectives on instructional quality in mathematics education across countries. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09652-6

article_title: Instruction in creative and argumentative writing: transfer and crossover effects on writing process and text quality
citation: Anouk ten Peze, Tanja Janssen, Gert Rijlaarsdam, Daphne van Weijen. (2024). Instruction in creative and argumentative writing: transfer and crossover effects on writing process and text quality. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09647-3
title: Dual-process (Geneplore) creative writing instruction design framework with Schacter's five creative teaching areas
description: The article grounds its creative writing unit in Finke et al.'s dual-process Geneplore model, in which "Generative and exploratory processes alternate continuously", mapped onto writing as alternation between the fictionworld (generative) and the writingrealm (explorative), following Csikszentmihalyi and Doyle. For instructional conditions it uses Schacter et al.'s Creative Teaching Framework: "Schacter et al. identified five areas that increase the likelihood of creative outcomes" — explicit teaching of creative thinking strategies, choice and discovery, intrinsic motivation, a creativity-conducive environment, and imagination and fantasy. These are restructured into a nested design of learning content embedded in learning mode and conditions.
requirements: Creative thinking strategies must be taught explicitly and be domain-specific, aligned to the task at hand, since divergent-thinking training alone did not transfer to unaligned genres in prior work the article cites (Baer)
constraints: The framework is applied to little-c creativity in fictional short-story writing in upper secondary education; Press (environmental contribution) was excluded
target_learning_goals: Creative (fictional story) writing quality
Divergent thinking
Writing flow/speed
examples: The six-lesson Writing Lab operationalized the alternation: e.g., lesson 2 'Mix your story' has students generate three story ideas (divergent) then select (convergent) before drafting and peer-evaluating
key_sources: Anouk ten Peze, Tanja Janssen, Gert Rijlaarsdam, Daphne van Weijen. (2024). Instruction in creative and argumentative writing: transfer and crossover effects on writing process and text quality. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09647-3

article_title: Germane processes moderate the effectiveness of complex desirable difficulty tasks
citation: Ines Zeitlhofer, Joerg Zumbach. (2026). Germane processes moderate the effectiveness of complex desirable difficulty tasks. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09807-1
title: Germane processes as a moderating account of complex desirable difficulty tasks
description: The article adopts Sweller's (2010) view of germane load as working memory resources allocated to managing intrinsic load, using the term "germane processes" to emphasize its functional, learner-driven nature. It proposes two sources of germane processes in complex desirable difficulty tasks — desirable difficulties and constantly high task complexity — which trigger metacognitive regulation and control strategies. The account holds that "germane resources are only invested if the learning task would not be solved without them", modifying CLT's stable-motivation assumption.
requirements: Learners must have sufficient prior knowledge for challenging tasks to be effective, per the article's practical implications
constraints: Findings stem from only one experiment in one domain (Italian verb conjugation), limiting generalizability as the authors state
target_learners: university students without prior Italian knowledge
target_learning_goals: grammar skill acquisition (verb conjugation) and long-term retention
examples: The 2×2 experiment crossed constantly high vs. gradually increasing complexity with interleaved vs. blocked practice schedules
key_sources: Ines Zeitlhofer, Joerg Zumbach. (2026). Germane processes moderate the effectiveness of complex desirable difficulty tasks. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09807-1

article_title: Towards a Comprehensive View of Object-Oriented Play
citation: Wynberg, E. R., Boland, A., Raijmakers, M. E. J., & van der Veen, C. (2021). Towards a Comprehensive View of Object-Oriented Play. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09608-7
title: Genetic epistemological account of object-oriented play as practice/functional play serving scheme construction
description: Within genetic epistemology, children's exploration and/or manipulation of objects is labeled practice play (Piaget) or functional play (Smilansky), defined as "the repetition of already acquired behavior, detached from its function, purely for the joy of practicing and mastering it". Casby subdivides this play into exploratory sensorimotor, relational-nonfunctional, and functional-conventional levels, with constructive play as a separate later term. The perspective holds that cognitive development is rooted in sensorimotor interactions with objects, with schemes built through assimilation and accommodation, and play progressing through Piaget's six sensorimotor substages toward early symbolic thought.
requirements: Progression through the play levels relies on imitation and repetition as the main features of practice and functional play
constraints: The authors note Piaget's stages of cognitive development and accompanying stages of play received some criticism early on, though the theory is still used, for example in prescriptive play therapy
target_learners: children from infancy through early childhood (sensorimotor stage, around 0 to 2 years)
target_learning_goals: cognitive development
sensorimotor development
scheme formation
examples: The introductory example of Bobby twisting a bottle top is classified as practice play, with his spoon-in-bottle behavior as constructive play and his functional use of the bottle as functional-conventional play.
key_sources: Wynberg, E. R., Boland, A., Raijmakers, M. E. J., & van der Veen, C. (2021). Towards a Comprehensive View of Object-Oriented Play. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09608-7

article_title: Beyond the “Wow” Factor: Using Generative AI for Increasing Generative Sense-Making
citation: Guido Makransky, Ban M. Shiwalia, Tue Herlau, Steven Blurton. (2025). Beyond the "Wow" Factor: Using Generative AI for Increasing Generative Sense-Making. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10039-x
title: Use theoretically informed GenAI chatbots to scale personalized scaffolding of generative learning activities where instructor formative assessment is not feasible
description: The principle is that GenAI chatbots should be designed to prompt and guide generative learning activities with personalized, formative feedback, because assessing knowledge gaps and giving targeted feedback is time-consuming for instructors. The authors propose that "GenAI can be used to scale this process when resources to formatively assess students and provide personalized support are not possible." Support should progress through explicit instruction, scaffolded practice, and independent practice, with specific rather than generic prompts, since specific prompting and scaffolding have been shown to be more effective in explaining, visualizing, or enacting concepts.
requirements: Guided rather than discovery-only use, since complete discovery without guidance is ineffective for novices; the chatbot needs targeted prompts and a knowledge bank aligned with the curriculum
constraints: The authors state they are not proposing GenAI is necessary or currently optimal for progressing from explicit instruction to independent practice, and independent practice was not investigated in this study
target_learners: novice learners who do not spontaneously engage in sense-making
target_learning_goals: generative sense-making through teaching and self-explanation
durable conceptual knowledge
examples: ChatTutor prompts students to explain specific content, provides scaffolded feedback correcting misconceptions, and was tested against generic ChatGPT and control conditions in two between-subjects experiments
key_sources: Guido Makransky, Ban M. Shiwalia, Tue Herlau, Steven Blurton. (2025). Beyond the "Wow" Factor: Using Generative AI for Increasing Generative Sense-Making. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10039-x

article_title: The Social Construction of Data: Methodological Problems of Investigating Learning in the Zone of Proximal Development
citation: Peter Smagorinsky. (1995). The Social Construction of Data: Methodological Problems of Investigating Learning in the Zone of Proximal Development. Review of Educational Research, 65(3), 191-212. http://rer.aera.net
title: Vygotsky's genetic method: development as tool- and sign-mediated social process
description: The article describes Vygotsky's genetic method, 'a term translated from the Russian word geneticheskii and referring to development rather than genes or genetic codes'. It rests on three themes the article attributes to Wertsch: a developmental method, the social origins of consciousness, and mediation of mental processes by tools and signs. Signs such as speech genres, art, dance, and physical space structure the developmental environment and mediate internalization of cultural values. The article uses this framework to argue that data are social constructs.
requirements: Analysis of development must use goal-directed, tool-mediated activity as the unit of analysis, per Wertsch's position the article endorses
constraints: The article notes Vygotsky's work has been translated three times under two titles and interpreted in incompatible ways, so any neo-Vygotskian claim is itself a social practice of knowledge construction
target_learners: learners across cultures participating in tool-mediated activity
target_learning_goals: internalization of culturally valued ways of thinking through mediational tools
examples: The article cites Tulviste's heterogeneity principle: overlapping social networks present learners with varied problems, allowing several frameworks for thinking to develop simultaneously
key_sources: Peter Smagorinsky. (1995). The Social Construction of Data: Methodological Problems of Investigating Learning in the Zone of Proximal Development. Review of Educational Research, 65(3), 191-212. https://doi.org/10.2307/1170682

article_title: The Development of Cognitive Load Theory: Replication Crises and Incorporation of Other Theories Can Lead to Theory Expansion
citation: John Sweller. (2023). The Development of Cognitive Load Theory: Replication Crises and Incorporation of Other Theories Can Lead to Theory Expansion. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09817-2
title: Incorporation of Geary's biologically primary versus secondary knowledge distinction into cognitive load theory
description: The article incorporates Geary's categorisation of knowledge into biologically primary knowledge, which humans have evolved to acquire easily and unconsciously through immersion, and biologically secondary knowledge, which culture deems important and which requires conscious effort and explicit teaching. The author states that 'The incorporation of Geary's distinction between biologically primary and secondary knowledge has considerably strengthened the cognitive architecture that underlies cognitive load theory.' This distinction explains why minimal-guidance discovery approaches, which assume school learning proceeds like primary acquisition, conflict with randomised controlled trial results favouring explicit instruction for school-based material.
requirements: Educational institutions and explicit instruction are needed for biologically secondary knowledge because it is not acquired automatically
constraints: The theory's instructional procedures apply to biologically secondary knowledge, not to biologically primary knowledge acquired through species-typical childhood behaviours
target_learners: students in formal educational institutions acquiring biologically secondary knowledge
target_learning_goals: explicit instruction of biologically secondary knowledge such as reading, writing, and mathematics
examples: The article notes that randomised controlled trials on the worked example effect showed novice learners studying worked examples frequently proved superior to solving the equivalent problems, the reverse of what discovery learning advocates expected
key_sources: John Sweller. (2023). The Development of Cognitive Load Theory: Replication Crises and Incorporation of Other Theories Can Lead to Theory Expansion. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09817-2

article_title: Ten Years of Dimensional Comparison Theory: On the Development of a Theory from Educational Psychology
citation: Jens Möller. (2024). Ten Years of Dimensional Comparison Theory: On the Development of a Theory from Educational Psychology. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09918-6
title: The Generalized I/E (GI/E) model: dimensional comparisons between any life domains, with multiple criteria and possible assimilation effects
description: The generalized I/E model (Möller et al., 2016) is the main extension of the classic I/E model within DCT. It removes three restrictions of the original model: it covers comparisons between more subjects than math and first language, criteria beyond self-concept, and effect directions beyond negative contrast. The review states that "the GI/E model postulates that dimensional comparisons occur between achievements in more subjects than just math and the first language, also between perceptions of teacher characteristics (such as agency or communion, self-concepts, interests) and even indeed beyond academic domains." It further holds that "dimensional comparisons need not lead to negative contrast effects but rather may lead to near-zero or even positive assimilation effects."
requirements: Dimensional comparisons are defined as comparisons between a person's ability in one domain against those in one or more other domains
constraints: The direction and strength of effects depend on the perceived similarity of the compared domains, with near comparisons yielding weaker contrast or assimilation effects
target_learning_goals: academic self-concept formation
subject-specific task values and motivation
examples: Studies extending comparisons to physics, second language, history, physical education, earth science, social studies, and music, and to perceived teacher characteristics as predictors
key_sources: Jens Möller. (2024). Ten Years of Dimensional Comparison Theory: On the Development of a Theory from Educational Psychology. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09918-6

article_title: How Learners’ Visuospatial Ability and Different Ways of Changing the Perspective Influence Learning About Movements in Desktop and Immersive Virtual Reality Environments
citation: Birgit Brucker, Georg Pardi, Fabienne Uehlin, Laura Moosmann, Martin Lachmair, Marc Halfmann, Peter Gerjets. (2024). How Learners' Visuospatial Ability and Different Ways of Changing the Perspective Influence Learning About Movements in Desktop and Immersive Virtual Reality Environments. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09895-w
title: GES framework: grounding, embodiment, and situatedness as a cognitive framework for VR interaction design
description: The GES framework, introduced by Fischer and Brugger (2011) and cited by the article, is a model of cognition emphasizing the role of the body, and has been used to inform interaction guidelines for VR user interface design. It comprises three components: "Grounding refers to universal principles applicable to all individuals, such as physical laws"; embodiment captures individual-specific bodily traits such as handedness and sensory-motor proficiency; and situatedness encompasses context-specific experiences arising from interaction within a particular environment. The article uses it to reason about how VR interactions should follow real-world principles.
requirements: The framework treats grounding principles as a foundational element of cognitive architecture that is resistant to change, so designs should align with physical laws
constraints: The article presents it as a framework for informing interaction guidelines, not as a tested intervention in this study
target_learners: adults learning about movements in VR environments
target_learning_goals: understanding dynamic 3D content from multiple perspectives
examples: The article uses the GES framework, via Lachmair et al. (2022), to argue that whole-body immersive VR interactions might overwhelm users
key_sources: Birgit Brucker, Georg Pardi, Fabienne Uehlin, Laura Moosmann, Martin Lachmair, Marc Halfmann, Peter Gerjets. (2024). How Learners' Visuospatial Ability and Different Ways of Changing the Perspective Influence Learning About Movements in Desktop and Immersive Virtual Reality Environments. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09895-w

article_title: Happy Together? On the Relationship Between Research on Retrieval Practice and Generative Learning Using the Case of Follow-Up Learning Tasks
citation: Julian Roelle, Tino Endres, Roman Abel, Niklas Obergassel, Matthias Nückles, Alexander Renkl. (2023). Happy Together? On the Relationship Between Research on Retrieval Practice and Generative Learning Using the Case of Follow-Up Learning Tasks. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09810-9
title: Generative learning activities as construction of coherent mental representations
description: The review characterizes generative learning tasks as tasks requiring sense-making through organization, elaboration, and inference generation. It states that according to various generative learning theories, such activities foster the coherence of learners' mental representations of the to-be-learned content and the integration of these mental representations with prior knowledge. This constructing function is presented as complementary to the consolidating function of retrieval practice when designing follow-up learning tasks.
requirements: Task instructions must require generative activities such as organization, elaboration, or inference generation
constraints: The review distinguishes this concept from the classical generation effect, noting the activities restructure information rather than generate parts of it
target_learners: learners studying expository texts or multimedia material
target_learning_goals: conceptual knowledge and transfer
key_sources: Julian Roelle, Tino Endres, Roman Abel, Niklas Obergassel, Matthias Nückles, Alexander Renkl. (2023). Happy Together? On the Relationship Between Research on Retrieval Practice and Generative Learning Using the Case of Follow-Up Learning Tasks. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09810-9

article_title: Making Sense of Generative Learning
citation: Fiorella, L. (2023). Making Sense of Generative Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09769-7
title: Generative sense-making framework: explaining, visualizing, and enacting modes with grounded sense-making
description: The article proposes a framework in which sense-making involves three qualitatively distinct modes: explaining (coherent verbal representations), visualizing (coherent visual representations), and enacting (coherent motor representations). Its core assumption is that 'the visualizing and enacting modes function to facilitate the explaining mode', so learners mentally organize and simulate material to support generalizing it through explanation. The framework maintains SOI/ICAP assumptions (limited working memory, role of prior knowledge, GLA advantage over non-generative activities) while specifying how instructor-provided and learner-generated representations interact to support internal sense-making.
requirements: Learners must have sufficient background knowledge and GLA guidance for GLAs to be effective, as the framework assumes
constraints: The framework targets conceptual learning materials, such as scientific phenomena and mathematics principles
target_learners: Learners of conceptual science and mathematics material
target_learning_goals: Constructing coherent mental representations that support comprehension and transfer
examples: Fig. 1 depicts how instruction, learner characteristics, and GLAs interact with internal sense-making processes to support comprehension and transfer

article_title: Twelve- and Fourteen-Year-Old School Children Differentially Benefit from Sensorimotor- and Multisensory-Enriched Vocabulary Training
citation: Brian Mathias, Christian Andrä, Anika Schwager, Manuela Macedonia, Katharina von Kriegstein. (2022). Twelve- and Fourteen-Year-Old School Children Differentially Benefit from Sensorimotor- and Multisensory-Enriched Vocabulary Training. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09648-z
title: Integrate gestures rather than pictures into L2 vocabulary pedagogy starting at 14 years of age
description: Because gesture-enriched learning was more beneficial than picture-enriched learning for 14-year-olds but not for 12-year-olds, the authors conclude these "findings provide evidence for opting to integrate gestures rather than pictures into L2 pedagogy starting at 14 years of age". Both enrichment forms still beat auditory-only learning at every age tested, so pictures remain valuable for younger learners. The recommendation follows from a classroom intervention in which children performed gestures with their teacher while reciting translations.

Words not yet encountered in lessons and excluded from the curriculum during the study period

article_title: A critical review of the refutation text literature: Methodological confounds, theoretical problems, and possible solutions
citation: Allison Zengilowski, Brendan Schuetze, Brady Nash, Diane Schallert. (2020). Coding Notes for “A Critical Review of the Refutation Text Literature: Methodological Confounds, Theoretical Problems, and Possible Solutions”. Version 2. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=%22A+Critical+Review+of+the+Refutation+Text+Literature%22
title: Taxonomy of general-knowledge misconception topics (sets A–D) used across refutation-text studies
description: The notes organise the general-knowledge misconceptions used as refutation-text topics in the reviewed studies into four labelled sets. Set A collects ten common folk beliefs such as "Chameleons change color to match their surroundings" and "People only use ten percent of their brains"; set B collects psychology-related myths such as learning-styles matching; set C collects everyday factual misconceptions; and set D combines a personality-development misconception with topics drawn from sets A and B, with each set tied to the studies that featured it.
requirements: Each topic entry is tied to the specific reviewed studies (e.g., Kendeou et al. 2014, 2019; van Loon et al. 2015; Beker et al. 2019) in which the misconception appeared as stimulus material.
constraints: The taxonomy covers only topics the authors label "General Knowledge"; scientific and socio-political topics were coded in separate, non-exclusive categories.

target_learning_goals: Conceptual change and correction of persistent misconceptions through refutation texts
examples: Set A's ten topics include "Seasons are caused by the Earth being closer to the Sun in the summer than in the winter" and "Lightning never strikes the same place twice"; set B includes "Students learn best when teaching styles are matched to their learning styles".

article_title: Two hands and a tale: When gestures benefit adult narrative comprehension
citation: Dargue, N; Sweller, N. (2020). Two hands and a tale: When gestures benefit adult narrative comprehension. Learning and Instruction, 68. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2020.101331
title: Adult narrative comprehension gesture observation-and-production experiment
description: An experimental study with adult learners that manipulated gesture observation (typical versus atypical gestures) and gesture production to test their roles in narrative comprehension. The article describes it as a study that "examined the role of gesture observation and production in adult narrative comprehension, through investigating whether gesture production moderates the effect of gesture observation." It provides evidence that iconic gestures can benefit adult narrative comprehension and highlights conditions of benefit.
requirements: Adult learners comprehending narrative (verbal message) material
Gesture stimuli distinguishable as typical versus atypical

comprehension of verbal messages

article_title: The point of view of genetic psychology.
citation: E. A. Kirkpatrick. (1910). The Point of View of Genetic Psychology. The Journal of Educational Psychology.
title: Genetic psychology is a point of view and method that traces mental activities back to their origins and development, not a separate body of knowledge
description: The article defines genetic psychology as psychology that inquires how present mental states originated and traces them back to their beginnings. It argues the term indicates 'a point of view and a method of studying the phenomena in question' rather than a separate body of knowledge, analogous to evolutionary botany or zoology. In its special sense it denotes the evolutionary study of mind in the race.
requirements: The search for origins must be 'made prominent and carried back farther and farther toward ultimate beginnings' for a psychology to count as genetic
constraints: In its special sense the term designates only the evolutionary study of the beginnings of mind in lower organisms and the development of consciousness in the race
target_learners: learners across species and developmental stages
target_learning_goals: understanding how mental activities and learning processes develop from their beginnings
examples: The author classifies introspective, experimental, physiological, comparative and social psychology as genetic only insofar as each investigates processes of development rather than present states

article_title: Intelligence and its measurement: A symposium--VII.
citation: Pressey, S. L. (1920). Intelligence and Its Measurement. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Intelligence+and+Its+Measurement+Pressey
title: General intelligence as a working hypothesis for prognosis, to be kept only while it works better than alternatives
description: Pressey's account treats the concept of general intelligence not as a discovered entity but as a pragmatic tool that arose from an educational situation. He states that "the concept of general intelligence is for the writer, primarily, simply a working hypothesis which has been very helpful in the first attack upon problems of prognosis," and that it "should continue as a working hypothesis until other hypotheses are found to work better." The hypothesis earns its keep by suggesting general lines of approach and giving investigators courage to attack the otherwise impossibly complex prognosis problem, but it must not prevent analysis of that problem.
requirements: The hypothetical nature of the concept, and the educational situation which first gave rise to such tests, must be kept in mind
constraints: Pressey warns against being dominated by the concept or hypnotized by statistics, and against the notion that intelligence testing is a short-cut that will put everything in the schools to rights
target_learners: school children whose educational prognosis is being assessed
target_learning_goals: prognosis of capacity for school work
key_sources: Pressey, S. L. (1920). Intelligence and Its Measurement. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Intelligence+and+Its+Measurement+Pressey

article_title: Chance or Purpose in the Origin and Evolution of Adaptation.
citation: Paul Knuth and W. C. B., abstractors. (1910). Journal of Educational Psychology abstracts page: theory of sleep; T. H. Morgan, Chance or Purpose in the Origin and Evolution of Adaptation. Science, 33: 789.
title: Morgan's account of adaptation: an initial accidental adaptation loads the dice for further variation in the same direction
description: The abstract reports T. H. Morgan's argument against explaining adaptation purely by chance fit between variations and environments. Morgan posits "some closer bond that 'insures the continuance in a given direction of variations once begun'": once germinal material shows itself susceptible of change in an environment, it tends to vary further in the same direction in that environment. The abstract quotes Morgan's summary that "Each step that the organism has taken guarantees further responses in the same direction," so that the mechanism of survival insures success where it is most called for.
requirements: The account presupposes germinal material that, once susceptible of change in an environment, tends to vary further in the same direction in that environment.
constraints: The theory concerns the origin and evolution of biological adaptation, not human learning or instruction.
target_learners: readers of evolutionary theory in educational psychology, as addressed by the abstract
target_learning_goals: understanding directedness of variation in the evolution of adaptation
examples: The abstract presents Morgan's dissatisfaction with the chance-explanation of adaptation and his proposed germinal-tendency alternative as printed in Science, 33: 789.

article_title: Practice and transference in normal and feeble-minded children.
citation: Woodrow, H. (1915). Practice and transference in normal and feeble-minded children. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=%22Practice+and+Transference+in+Normal+and+Feeble-Minded+Children%22
title: Geometrical form sorting practice test using gun wads with printed form labels
description: A speeded sorting task in which children sort gun wads bearing printed outlines of five geometrical forms (star, circle, square, cross, triangle, from the Woodworth-Wells substitution test) into correspondingly labeled small boxes. Each trial involves sorting 250 wads within 4 minutes, using one hand, picking up one wad at a time. The box order is changed every second day to prevent the task from becoming too automatic. Scoring is the total number correctly sorted.
requirements: Requires 250 gun wads with pasted form labels, five labeled small boxes, a large pasteboard box, and instructions emphasizing speed with no mention of accuracy
constraints: Only one set of tests was used due to the labor of preparation, requiring wads to be dumped and resorted within each session
target_learners: feeble-minded children of about nine years mental age
normal children of about nine years chronological age
target_learning_goals: speeded perceptual classification and sorting
examples: Thirteen consecutive days of practice (excluding Saturdays and Sundays) were given to practice groups, with end tests administered before and after

It functions as a taxonomy for quantitative textbook analysis in this domain.

article_title: Cognitive predictors of calculations and number line estimation with whole numbers and fractions among at-risk students.
citation: Namkung, J. M., & Fuchs, L. S. (2016). Cognitive Predictors of Calculations and Number Line Estimation with Whole Numbers and Fractions among At-Risk Students. Journal of Educational Psychology, 108(2), 214-228. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000055
title: Geary's (2004) model of mathematics learning distinguishing concepts, procedures, and supporting cognitive systems
description: The study's conceptual framework is Geary's (2004) model of mathematics learning, which the authors extend with additional cognitive variables. The model "distinguishes between mathematics concepts and mathematics procedures," treats conceptual and procedural knowledge as mutually supportive, and holds that "general cognitive processes, such as working memory and attention, support learning of both math concepts and procedures." It further identifies symbolic and nonverbal systems: language for number names and counting, and nonverbal reasoning for representing and comparing numerical magnitudes. The authors state this model "guided the processes that were assessed in the present study."
requirements: Assessment of both conceptual (number line estimation) and procedural (calculations) outcomes to capture the model's distinction
constraints: The study extends the model by adding attentive behavior, processing speed, and concept formation, which were not part of the original formulation
target_learners: at-risk fourth-grade students performing below the 35th percentile in calculations
target_learning_goals: whole-number and fraction calculation skill
whole-number and fraction number line estimation (numerical magnitude representation)
examples: The study operationalized the model's constructs as seven cognitive predictors (numerical working memory, working memory-sentences, language, attentive behavior, processing speed, nonverbal reasoning, concept formation) plus incoming calculation skill, tested against whole-number and fraction outcomes in one structural model.
key_sources: Namkung, J. M., & Fuchs, L. S. (2016). Cognitive Predictors of Calculations and Number Line Estimation with Whole Numbers and Fractions among At-Risk Students. Journal of Educational Psychology, 108(2), 214-228. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000055

article_title: Parental education and children’s depression, anxiety, and ADHD traits, a within-family study in MoBa
citation: Hughes, A. M., Torvik, F. A., van Bergen, E., Hannigan, L. J., Corfield, E. C., Andreassen, O. A., Ystrom, E., Ask, H., Davey Smith, G., Davies, N. M. & Havdahl, A. (2024). Parental education and children’s depression, anxiety, and ADHD traits, a within-family study in MoBa. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00260-8
title: Genetic nurture (dynastic effects) versus direct genetic transmission as competing accounts of intergenerational associations
description: The article's organizing framework distinguishes genetic nurture — indirect effects of parents' genotypes on children via environmental pathways — from direct genetic transmission of variants from parents to children. It operationalizes this with within-family Mendelian randomization, which instruments parental education with polygenic indexes and adjusts for the child's own genotype to block bias from inherited variants. The article states: "their impact on children’s outcomes can be considered a case of genetic nurture, or dynastic effects: an indirect effect of parents’or other relatives’genotype on children’s traits via environmental pathways".
requirements: Requires genetic data on large numbers of mothers, fathers, and children to separate maternal from paternal effects, which few studies have
constraints: Within-family MR estimates were imprecise in this sample; PGI-based approaches capture only genetic liability associated with specific SNPs, unlike variance-decomposition designs
target_learning_goals: understanding environmental versus genetic origins of social gradients in children's emotional and behavioural outcomes
examples: Applied to 40,879 MoBa trios to estimate conditional effects of maternal and paternal educational attainment on children's age-8 traits

Parental education and children’s depression, anxiety, and ADHD traits, a within-family study in MoBa. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00260-8

article_title: Identification of loci involved in childhood visual acuity and associations with cognitive skills and educational attainment
citation: Schmitz, J., Abbondanza, F., Marianski, K., Luciano, M. & Paracchini, S. (2023). Identification of loci involved in childhood visual acuity and associations with cognitive skills and educational attainment. npj Science of Learning, 8:25. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00175-w
title: Gene-environment correlation model linking EA polygenic propensities to childhood visual acuity and adult myopia risk
description: The article proposes a gene-environment correlation model in which genetic factors associated with higher educational attainment (EA PGS) are also associated with better childhood visual acuity, given visual acuity's positive links to cognitive skills and school grades. Because EA PGS are known to be associated with myopia in adults, the model holds that "environmental exposures linked to higher EA might have detrimental effects on vision offsetting the initial positive effect", e.g. more reading and near work increasing myopia risk once educational trajectories diverge. The study tested the model's predictions: EA PGS positively associated with childhood visual acuity while myopia PGS showed a negative association.
requirements: Testing the model requires polygenic scores for EA and myopia and measures of childhood visual acuity before educational trajectories diverge, as in the ALSPAC analyses at age ~11.8
constraints: The authors state they cannot rule out residual confounding by unmeasured variables, and vision and education were assessed at only a single time point
target_learners: children in the ALSPAC longitudinal cohort (mean age 11.8 years)
target_learning_goals: understanding how genetic propensity toward educational attainment relates to sensory function and academic outcomes during childhood
examples: The study found EA PGS positively related to childhood visual acuity in ALSPAC children before the end of compulsory education, while a prior study found EA PGS was not predictive of visual function in ALSPAC mothers
key_sources: Schmitz, J., Abbondanza, F., Marianski, K., Luciano, M. & Paracchini, S. (2023). Identification of loci involved in childhood visual acuity and associations with cognitive skills and educational attainment. npj Science of Learning, 8:25. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00175-w

article_title: Socioeconomic and genomic roots of verbal ability from current evidence
citation: Guang Guo, Meng-Jung Lin and Kathleen Mullan Harris. (2022). Socioeconomic and genomic roots of verbal ability from current evidence. npj Science of Learning 7:22. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00137-8
title: Conceptual model of the genomic component within parental SES shaping verbal ability
description: The article proposes that parental SES, traditionally viewed as environmental, "could be decomposed into an environmental component and a genomic component," the latter originating from parental genomes that shape family education, occupation, income, neighborhood, and schools. Because 50% of each parent's alleles transmit to offspring while 100% act on parental SES, offspring genome and parental SES are correlated (path C), so regression estimates of both are upwardly biased when estimated separately. The model (Fig. 1) motivates correcting the offspring-genome effect by including parental SES and estimating the genomic component as about twice the reduction in the SES effect.
requirements: Data with both offspring genome and parental SES measures at the individual level
constraints: Without parental genomic data the non-transmitted allele effect cannot be estimated directly; the analysis capitalizes on offspring genome and parental SES
The two genomic subcomponents being about the same is a hypothesis, since each is acted upon by about 50% of total parental alleles
target_learners: Youth aged 12–18 in the United States
target_learning_goals: Verbal ability (Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test score)
examples: The article regresses verbal ability on parental SES and offspring genome in an Add Health sample of 7194 to estimate the model's paths
key_sources: Guang Guo, Meng-Jung Lin and Kathleen Mullan Harris. (2022). Socioeconomic and genomic roots of verbal ability from current evidence. npj Science of Learning 7:22. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00137-8

article_title: Genetics of cognitive performance, education and learning: from research to policy?
citation: Peter M. Visscher. (2022). Genetics of cognitive performance, education and learning: from research to policy? npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00124-z
title: Human genomics and polygenic scores should be fully embedded in social-science and neuroscience research designs
description: The article proposes that "human genomics, in particular the use of polygenic scores, should become fully embedded into social sciences research, including economics, sociology and psychology". The rationale is that because a substantial proportion of differences in life outcomes is due to DNA, genomic information can strengthen research: it allows more powerful experimental designs by accounting for a proportion of variation among samples, detecting biases and confounders such as genetic ancestry differences between treatment and control groups, and moving from associations to causation. The same principles are said to apply to human-subjects neuroscience, since variation in any measured trait, including brain imaging data, is partly genetic.
requirements: Availability of polygenic score data on research samples, which the article says is increasing in power over time and requires large experimental sample sizes
constraints: The article's examples rest on studies it itself qualifies as indirect (twin tracking study) or underpowered (the 131-adult learning study)
target_learning_goals: understanding the role of genetic variation in cognitive performance and educational outcomes
improving experimental design in education and learning research
examples: The commentary points to the Knigge twin study of delayed tracking and the Youn et al. 100-day learning study as snapshots of how genetics can address questions about cognitive performance, learning and social outcomes
key_sources: Peter M. Visscher. (2022). Genetics of cognitive performance, education and learning: from research to policy? npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00124-z

article_title: Gender similarities in the brain during mathematics development
citation: Kersey, A. J., Csumitta, K. D., & Cantlon, J. F. (2019). Gender similarities in the brain during mathematics development. npj Science of Learning 4:19. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0057-x
title: Gender Similarities Hypothesis as applied to early childhood mathematical cognition
description: The Gender Similarities Hypothesis argues that boys and girls function similarly in most areas of cognition. This study tests it neurally in early childhood mathematics and reports that the data are consistent with it: "gender similarities in early childhood mathematics show, as proposed in the domain of spatial cognition, that gender differences in STEM fields in adults are not derived from intrinsic differences in children's brains but likely from a complex environmental origin." The theory treats male and female brains as one heterogeneous population rather than two categorical groups, supported here by equivalence testing, Bayes factors, and null variance and interaction tests.
requirements: Testing similarities, not just differences, requires statistical equivalence tests and Bayesian analyses rather than reliance on null t tests
constraints: The article notes gender differences in STEM may emerge later in development or from interactions with puberty-related hormone changes, which these childhood data do not address
target_learners: children aged 3–10 in early mathematics development
target_learning_goals: early mathematics and numerical cognition development
examples: The study measured 104 children's neural maturity during mathematics education videos and found equivalence rather than difference across all five whole-brain analyses
key_sources: Kersey, A. J., Csumitta, K. D., & Cantlon, J. F. (2019). Gender similarities in the brain during mathematics development. npj Science of Learning 4:19. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0057-x

article_title: The practical utility of genetic screening in school settings
citation: Shero, J., van Dijk, W., Edwards, A., Schatschneider, C., Solari, E. J., & Hart, S. A. (2021). The practical utility of genetic screening in school settings. npj Science of Learning, 6:12. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00090-y
title: Genetically informed personalized education framework (precision medicine analogy)
description: The article describes a framework, imported from precision medicine, in which educators would use various tools and screeners — potentially including a polygenic score — to understand individual students and tailor instruction. The authors "define personalized education as differentiated and targeted instruction at the individual level." Under this framework PGS results are treated as probabilistic, non-deterministic information to be combined with other data to predict general trends in achievement. The paper's simulations were designed to quantify whether this framework's genetic component adds incremental value over existing screening in schools.
requirements: Educators would need to use PGS alongside other tools and screeners, and communicate that results are risk probabilities rather than diagnoses.
constraints: The framework faces ethical concerns (genetic essentialism, scientific racism risks), inequitable effectiveness across ancestry groups, and the article concludes the evidence does not support individual-level genetic personalization at current technology levels.
target_learners: School-age students, particularly those at academic risk
target_learning_goals: Personalizing instruction and identifying academic risk at the individual (or group) level
examples: The authors conclude the best path to using PGS may be as a learning-disability screener rather than individual-level personalization, though group-level (quartile-level) differentiation could have some utility.
key_sources: Shero, J., van Dijk, W., Edwards, A., Schatschneider, C., Solari, E. J., & Hart, S. A. (2021). The practical utility of genetic screening in school settings. npj Science of Learning, 6:12. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00090-y

article_title: Understanding the effects of education through the lens of biology
citation: H. Moriah Sokolowski and Daniel Ansari. (2018). Understanding the effects of education through the lens of biology. npj Science of Learning 3:17. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0032-y
title: Gene–environment interplay framework explaining persistent individual differences in educational outcomes
description: The review organizes biological mechanisms underlying individual differences under the umbrella of "gene– environment interplay", which "incorporates the effect of genetics, gene – environment correlations, and gene – environment interactions". It argues that additive G + E models are insufficient because genes and experiences modify each other's effects. Scarr and McCartney's account that genotypes direct experience grounds the framework, and it is used to explain why rank orders of ability persist after intervention and why intervention gains fade.
requirements: Genes and environment must be treated as dynamically interdependent rather than as a nature-versus-nurture dichotomy
constraints: The gene–environment interaction field is criticized for sample sizes, varying assessments, and inconsistent statistical methods
Scarr and McCartney's theory is noted as not without criticism and counterarguments
target_learners: children in educational systems across development
target_learning_goals: explaining individual differences in educational attainment and response to intervention
key_sources: H. Moriah Sokolowski and Daniel Ansari. (2018). Understanding the effects of education through the lens of biology. npj Science of Learning 3:17. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0032-y

article_title: Nurture might be nature: cautionary tales and proposed solutions
citation: Hart, S. A., Little, C. & van Bergen, E. (2021). Nurture might be nature: cautionary tales and proposed solutions. npj Science of Learning 6:2. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00079-z
title: Gene–environment correlation framework: passive, evocative, and active types produce genetic confounds in environment–outcome research
description: Gene–environment correlation describes "the process by which a person's genotype inﬂuences their exposure to the environment". The article distinguishes "three types of gene–environment correlations that can result in genetic confounds": passive (association between inherited genotype and the rearing environment), evocative (a genetically influenced trait elicits responses from others), and active (genetically influenced traits shape which environments people select). Genes act indirectly through personality, behaviors and cognitions, not directly. The article focuses on passive gene–environment correlation because it is theorized to have greater effect in childhood.
requirements: Interpreting environment–outcome associations requires considering that genotypes shape exposure to environments via personality, behaviors, and cognitions
constraints: The article focuses on passive gene–environment correlation as the confound of interest for rearing-environment studies, theorized to be stronger in childhood
target_learners: children in family-based developmental and educational research
target_learning_goals: interpreting causal claims about home environments and children's academic and behavioral outcomes
examples: Examples given: home environments less chaotic for children with high effortful control (passive); genes associated with being rated as "more likeable" (evocative); childhood socialization associated with adolescent exposure to risky environments (active)
key_sources: Hart, S. A., Little, C. & van Bergen, E. (2021). Nurture might be nature: cautionary tales and proposed solutions. npj Science of Learning 6:2. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00079-z

article_title: Literature Review on the Integration of Generative AI in Programming Education
citation: Jemimah Nathaniel, Solomon Sunday Oyelere, Jarkko Suhonen, Matti Tedre. (2025). Literature Review on the Integration of Generative AI in Programming Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00524-3
title: GenAI-Ped framework for integrating GenAI in programming education
description: The GenAI-Ped framework is a structured four-phase approach to guide GenAI integration in programming education while preserving foundational programming principles and higher-order thinking skills. The article states it is designed "to guide GenAI integration in programming education and ensure that foundational programming principles and higher-order thinking skills are preserved and enhanced." It adapts a self-regulated learning framework, Bloom's taxonomy, needs analysis, an AI-Lab prompt-engineering framework, and Universal Design for Learning principles across four phases: learner needs analysis and objective development, GenAI tool analysis, teaching/assessment/prompt engineering methods, and lesson-level GenAI integration.
requirements: Requires learner needs analysis, SMART objectives grounded in Bloom's taxonomy, evaluated and configured GenAI tools, and formative plus summative assessment aligned with learning objectives
constraints: Adapted from prior frameworks (Prasad et al. SRL, Roth et al. UDL, Dickey et al. AI-Lab); presented as a proposal built from review findings, not empirically validated in this article
target_learning_goals: foundational programming logic
higher-order thinking skills
prompt engineering competence
examples: Phase 3 describes hybrid pedagogical models such as live code-along demonstrations where instructor and class co-develop a function using ChatGPT's suggestions while critiquing output and refining prompts
key_sources: Jemimah Nathaniel, Solomon Sunday Oyelere, Jarkko Suhonen, Matti Tedre. (2025). Literature Review on the Integration of Generative AI in Programming Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00524-3

article_title: Reasoning Mind Genie 2: An Intelligent Tutoring System as a Vehicle for International Transfer of Instructional Methods in Mathematics
citation: Khachatryan, G. A., Romashov, A. V., Khachatryan, A. R., Gaudino, S. J., Khachatryan, J. M., Guarian, K. R., & Yufa, N. V. (2014). Reasoning Mind Genie 2: An Intelligent Tutoring System as a Vehicle for International Transfer of Instructional Methods in Mathematics. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0019-7
title: Genie 2: a knowledge-engineered intelligent tutoring system delivering an entire national curriculum tradition
description: Genie 2 is an intelligent tutoring system for grades 2–6 mathematics that "represents and delivers an existing curriculum in its entirety — i.e., as a system of interconnected pedagogical practices". Its behavior was created by interviewing a panel of expert Russian mathematics teachers and codifying their practices into a decision system plus student model, instructional data structures, and detailed scripts. Unlike Cognitive Tutor's paper-and-pencil curriculum companion, in Genie 2 the intelligent tutoring system is "the primary vehicle for the introduction and discussion of new material".
requirements: A panel of expert teachers from the source tradition must be interviewed and must also participate in software design decisions and content authoring
Iterative design-research cycles of development, piloting, and analysis in destination-country schools
constraints: Core 5th and 6th grade curricula take about 120 h each; grades 2–4 curricula take 70 h each
Online Tutoring mode saw limited use since few schools are willing to pay for online tutoring
target_learners: United States students in grades 2–6 mathematics
target_learning_goals: School mathematics curriculum content and procedures aligned with the Russian mathematics tradition
examples: Students work at their own computers at their own pace while the teacher monitors and works with individuals or small groups; the system's modes include Guided Study, Homework, Review Mode, and Wall of Mastery
key_sources: Khachatryan, G. A., Romashov, A. V., Khachatryan, A. R., Gaudino, S. J., Khachatryan, J. M., Guarian, K. R., & Yufa, N. V. (2014). Reasoning Mind Genie 2: An Intelligent Tutoring System as a Vehicle for International Transfer of Instructional Methods in Mathematics. citation: Khachatryan, G. A., Romashov, A. V., Khachatryan, A. R., Gaudino, S. J., Khachatryan, J. M., Guarian, K. R., & Yufa, N. V. (2014). title: Detailed lesson scripts capturing expert teachers' instructional decision-making
description: For each objective, an expert Russian teacher writes a detailed script describing how they would present it, including material presented to students plus bracketed instructions for which questions to ask and how to respond to different answers. An early failure led to redesign: initial textbook-style Theory content involved little student activity, so the system was changed to ask students questions on every screen, or roughly every half minute. Curriculum developers then revise scripts for cultural fit while a lead teacher reviews to ensure the mathematical and pedagogical structure is preserved.
requirements: Expert teacher authors, translation to English, curriculum developer revision, and lead-teacher review
Scripts must preserve the mathematical and pedagogical structure through revision
constraints: The level of detail of the scripts varies considerably from teacher to teacher, especially in the degree of interactivity
target_learners: Grades 2–6 students studying mathematics through Genie 2
target_learning_goals: Delivery of content-specific expert teaching practices, including questioning, explanations, and misconception handling
examples: A script excerpt shows solving 12 + _ = 83, with branching on whether the student identifies it as an equation with an unknown summand
