article_title: Automated Test Assembly for Handling Learner Cold-Start in Large-Scale Assessments
citation: Jill-Jêenn Vie, Fabrice Popineau, Éric Bruillard, Yolaine Bourda. (2018). Automated Test Assembly for Handling Learner Cold-Start in Large-Scale Assessments. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0163-y
title: General Diagnostic Model for learner ability estimation over knowledge components
description: The General Diagnostic Model (GDM) is a cognitive-diagnosis student model in which learners carry ability vectors with one component per knowledge component and questions carry discrimination vectors and an easiness parameter, combined through a logistic probability of a correct answer. The article states it "choose[s] to calibrate a General Diagnostic Model, because it predicts student performance better than other cognitive diagnosis models", citing its prior work, and assumes the learner's level does not change during the initial question bundle. Estimated ability components can be interpreted as degrees of mastery per knowledge component.
requirements: An expert-specified q-matrix mapping each question to the knowledge components involved in its resolution
A history of dichotomous learner responses over the item bank for calibration
constraints: Assumes the learner's level does not change across the initial bundle of questions
Discrimination components are fixed at zero for knowledge components a question does not involve
target_learning_goals: diagnosing mastery of knowledge components in mathematics assessment
examples: The model was calibrated with the mirt R package using a Metropolis-Hastings Robbins-Monro algorithm, and its ability estimates fed the prediction of remaining question outcomes in the cold-start experiments
key_sources: Jill-Jêenn Vie, Fabrice Popineau, Éric Bruillard, Yolaine Bourda. (2018). Automated Test Assembly for Handling Learner Cold-Start in Large-Scale Assessments. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0163-y

article_title: Perceived Task-Difficulty Recognition from Log-file Information for the Use in Adaptive Intelligent Tutoring Systems
citation: Ruth Janning, Carlotta Schatten, Lars Schmidt-Thieme. (2016). Perceived Task-Difficulty Recognition from Log-file Information for the Use in Adaptive Intelligent Tutoring Systems. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0097-9
title: Generalised classification plait: a layered stacking ensemble that feeds previous classifiers' decisions back as additional inputs to improve multi-class recognition with small noisy datasets
description: The generalised classification plait is an ensemble structure in which classifiers such as SVM, DCT or KNN "are i enough.nterweaved within a plait structure by combining the classification decisions of classifiers in previous plait layers with the feature vectors and feeding these combined new feature vectors into further classifiers". It generalises the earlier SVM plait to other classification models and multi-class problems, and "Different from plain stacking, the presented plait consists of several layered stackings with different additional inputs". It has three hyper-parameters: the number of plait layers, the number of classifiers per layer, and the number of features per classifier.
requirements: The original feature vector must be splittable into s input vectors of n features each; if l is too small, input vectors may overlap to ensure enough feature values per classifier.
constraints: Experiments used 3 classifiers per layer, 4 features per classifier and 20 layers, with error converging after at most 7 layers; the article states additional tests and experiments with larger data should be conducted for generalisability.
target_learners: students practicing mathematics in intelligent tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: recognition of students' perceived task-difficulty to support adaptivity and task sequencing
examples: The experiments split the 11 per-task log-file features into 3 input vectors of 4 features and retrained classifiers over 7 layers, then fed the seventh-layer outputs to a second stage classifier for the final decision.
key_sources: Ruth Janning, Carlotta Schatten, Lars Schmidt-Thieme. (2016). Perceived Task-Difficulty Recognition from Log-file Information for the Use in Adaptive Intelligent Tutoring Systems. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0097-9

article_title: Exploring Gender Differences in Computational Thinking Learning in a VR Classroom: Developing Machine Learning Models Using Eye-Tracking Data and Explaining the Models
citation: Gao, H., Hasenbein, L., Bozkir, E., Göllner, R., & Kasneci, E. (2023). Exploring Gender Differences in Computational Thinking Learning in a VR Classroom: Developing Machine Learning Models Using Eye-Tracking Data and Explaining the Models. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 33, 929-954. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00316-z
title: Design VR learning environments with awareness that boys and girls may distribute visual attention differently across instructional and social content.
description: The article's findings on differential attention patterns suggest that "intelligent tutoring support by virtual peer learners might vary in its positive impact as it is likely to receive different levels of attention depending on the gender of the learners." Instructional scaffolds and guidance may also be attended to differently, "necessitating differentiated implementation." Designers should consider that girls may benefit from more teacher-guided instruction while boys may engage more with peer-mediated exploration.
requirements: Understanding of which VR elements attract attention from different learner groups
constraints: Findings reflect aggregated attention patterns, not responses to specific lesson content
Results are specific to a CT lesson context in VR
target_learners: Girls and boys in K-12 STEM education
target_learning_goals: Computational thinking skill development
examples: The study found that girls focused more on the virtual teacher and screen while boys attended more to virtual peer learners, suggesting different scaffolding approaches may be needed.

article_title: From the Automated Assessment of Student Essay Content to Highly Informative Feedback: a Case Study
citation: Gombert, S., Fink, A., Giorgashvili, T., Jivet, I., Di Mitri, D., Yau, J., Frey, A., & Drachsler, H. (2024). From the Automated Assessment of Student Essay Content to Highly Informative Feedback: a Case Study. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00387-6
title: Novel German dataset for analytic essay scoring with segmentation and topic-code labels
description: A novel dataset collected from two cohorts of teacher students solving the essay task as a compulsory lecture assignment. The article states "It consists of N = 698 essays written in German", submitted as PDFs on Moodle, with text extracted via PyPDF and segmented with the SoMaJo tokeniser. Table 2 reports distributional properties including an average of 36.68 sentences and 855.21 tokens per essay and an average type-token ratio of 0.41. The corpus carries two label sets: sentence-to-learning-tip codes and learning-tip-to-lecture-topic codes for multilabel classification.
requirements: Annotation in INCEpTION with pre-tokenisation via SoMaJo, and heuristic removal of title pages and reference lists
constraints: Essays come from one lecture's assignment at one university, in German, on a single video-based task
target_learners: University teacher students writing German-language argumentative essays
target_learning_goals: Analytic scoring of essay content: which learning tips are addressed and which lecture concepts are connected to them
examples: The coded essays were exported from INCEpTION as UIMA XMI files and transformed into a tabular data format with DKPro-Cassis and Pandas

article_title: Towards Automatically Detecting Whether Student Learning is Shallow
citation: Gowda, S. M., Baker, R. S., Corbett, A. T., & Rossi, L. M. (2013). Towards Automatically Detecting Whether Student Learning is Shallow. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0006-4
title: Genetics Cognitive Tutor three-factor cross dataset with transfer, PFL and problem-solving post-tests
description: A dataset from 71 Carnegie Mellon undergraduates using the Genetics Cognitive Tutor's three-factor cross module, first published in Baker et al. (2011a, b). Students completed "a total of 22,885 problem-solving actions across 10,966 problem steps in the tutor" during two 1-h laboratory sessions, followed by a problem-solving post-test, a transfer test, and a PFL test. Average post-test performance was 0.81 (SD=0.18), transfer 0.85 (SD=0.18), and PFL 0.89 (SD=0.15). The dataset supports training and cross-validating shallowness detectors.
requirements: Paper-and-pencil post-tests measuring problem-solving, transfer, and PFL to generate ground-truth shallowness labels
constraints: Data come from a single tutor module (three-factor cross) at one university; the retention test administered 7 weeks later was not analyzed in detail
target_learners: college undergraduates in genetics or introductory biology
target_learning_goals: three-factor cross gene mapping problem solving, transfer of genetics reasoning, preparation for future learning
examples: Students averaged pre-test performance of 0.31 (SD=0.19) and post-test performance of 0.81 (SD=0.18); 18 students achieved a perfect post-test score

article_title: An Educational System for Learning Search Algorithms and Automatically Assessing Student Performance
citation: Grivokostopoulou, F., Perikos, I., & Hatzilygeroudis, I. (2016). An Educational System for Learning Search Algorithms and Automatically Assessing Student Performance. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0116-x
title: General Assessment Framework for Automated Marking Across Domains
description: The authors specify a general framework for the assessment process consisting of four stages: (1) specify similarity between student answer and correct answer, (2) categorize student answer according to the answer categorization scheme, (3) check for important errors, and (4) calculate the mark via the automated marker. The framework can be used in different domains by proper instantiations of three elements: similarity metric, answer categorization scheme, and automated marking algorithm. As implemented in AITS, it could easily be used for domains where answers are strings or could be transformed into strings.
requirements: Domain-appropriate similarity metric
Domain-appropriate answer categorization scheme
Domain-appropriate automated marking algorithm
constraints: Applicable to domains where answers are strings or transformable into strings
target_learners: Students in any domain with string-representable answers
target_learning_goals: Domain-specific exercise completion skills
examples: Instantiated in AITS for search algorithm exercises using edit distance as similarity metric

article_title: A review of ICT-enabled learning for schoolgirls in Asia and its impacts on education equity
citation: Liang, M., Lim, C. P., Park, J., & Mendoza, N. B. (2023). A review of ICT-enabled learning for schoolgirls in Asia and its impacts on education equity. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10178-w
title: Gender Analysis Framework (GAF) as a lens for reviewing ICT-enabled learning for schoolgirls
description: The review adopts the Gender Analysis Framework (GAF; Jhpiego, 2020) as its organizing lens, a "multidimensional framework that systematically examines how ICT-enabled learning influences schoolgirls". GAF comprises four interrelated dimensions: access to assets, practice and participation, belief and perception, and institutions, laws and policies. The review narrows GAF to primary and secondary education and uses it to code and synthesize the 30 included studies.
requirements: The framework requires organizing data on gender differences across social contexts, as the article states GAF "offers a mechanism to organize data on gender differences in a variety of social contexts".
constraints: The review narrows GAF to primary and secondary education, and the article notes the review "only focuses on evidences from empirical research without further analyzing context-related elements" such as GDP, religion, and geographical location.
target_learners: primary and secondary schoolgirls in Asia
target_learning_goals: education inclusiveness and equity
expanding education pathways and opportunities

citation: Stella Y. Kim, Ji Yae Bong, Daniel Maxwell, Beth Oyarzun. (2026). Development and validation of Generative Artificial Intelligence Readiness and Perception (GenAI-RP) Scale for faculty and students in higher education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10713-z
title: GenAI-RP Scale: a validated survey instrument measuring GenAI readiness, benefits, and challenges for both faculty and students in higher education
description: The GenAI-RP Scale is a survey instrument comprising three subscales: Readiness, Benefit, and Challenge, with parallel but role-tailored items for students and instructors. The article states the scale 'comprises three distinct subscales: a) Readiness scale, b) Benefit scale, and c) Challenge scale,' with items adapted from prior instruments and reviewed by three content experts. It was validated via EFA and CFA on data from 460 students and 132 faculty collected in spring 2024.
requirements: Items are tailored to the distinct roles of students and instructors, so the two versions are not identical
constraints: Validation focused on content-related and construct-related validity via CFA; criterion-related validity was not assessed
The faculty challenge scale was not fully validated due to a limited sample size
target_learning_goals: readiness to use generative AI for teaching and learning
perceptions of GenAI benefits and challenges in education
examples: Data collected in spring 2024 via an electronic survey with invitations sent to listservs such as the AERA Online Teaching and Learning SIG and AECT

citation: Stella Y. Kim, Ji Yae Bong, Daniel Maxwell, Beth Oyarzun. (2026). Development and validation of Generative Artificial Intelligence Readiness and Perception (GenAI-RP) Scale for faculty and students in higher education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10713-z
title: GenAI readiness conceptualized as three components: comprehension, ethical awareness, and utilization/proficiency
description: The article defines readiness to use GenAI for education as 'the perceived state of preparedness of an individual (student or instructor) in terms of cognitive understanding, ethical consideration, and practical skills regarding the use of generative artificial intelligence for teaching or learning.' Unlike Wang et al.'s four-factor AI readiness framework (Cognition, Ability, Vision, Ethics), this study conceptualized readiness with three components — GenAI Comprehension, Ethical Awareness of GenAI, and GenAI Utilization and Proficiency — merging Cognition and Vision, with factor definitions differentiated for learners and instructors.
requirements: Factor definitions were revised after content and factor-structure validation to ensure accuracy
constraints: The conceptualization was developed for GenAI specifically rather than general AI technologies, targeting both students and instructors across diverse disciplines in higher education
target_learning_goals: understanding of GenAI technologies
ethical awareness of GenAI
proficiency in using GenAI for learning or teaching
examples: The final readiness scale comprises Factor 1 GenAI Comprehension (six items), Factor 2 Ethical Awareness of GenAI (three items), and Factor 3 GenAI Utilization and Proficiency (three student items, seven faculty items)

article_title: Towards reliable generative AI-driven scaffolding: Reducing hallucinations and enhancing quality in self-regulated learning support
citation: Qian, K., Liu, S., Li, T., Raković, M., Li, X., Guan, R., Molenaar, I., Nawaz, S., Swiecki, Z., Yan, L., & Gašević, D. (2025). Towards Reliable Generative AI-Driven Scaffolding: Reducing Hallucinations and Enhancing Quality in Self-Regulated Learning Support. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.05929
title: GenAI-enabled SRL scaffolding system with pre-delivery reliability and quality evaluation
description: A system that uses LLMs to generate personalised SRL scaffolds from student trace data, then evaluates them through a multi-agent reliability evaluation (checking whether scaffolds target the correct SRL processes) and an LLM-as-a-Judge quality evaluation (selecting the most helpful scaffold from pairs) before delivery to students. The system aims to automatically screen out low-quality and hallucinated scaffolds, trigger LLM regeneration, and select high-quality scaffolds from multiple candidates.
requirements: Access to student trace data from a learning task
A process library mapping SRL processes to trace action patterns
At least one LLM for scaffold generation and one for evaluation
constraints: Even GPT-4-Turbo as a Judge achieved only moderate alignment with human expert labels, suggesting room for improvement in eliminating hallucinations entirely
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning during reading-writing tasks
examples: The system was tested on a dataset of 594 scaffolds generated by three LLMs (GPT-4-Turbo, GPT-3.5-Turbo, and Gemini-Pro) for 66 secondary school students at three time points during a reading-writing task.

article_title: Efficacy of Hand Gestures and the Hand as Foot Teaching Method Compared to Traditional Methods in Medical and Dental Education: A Scoping Review.
citation: Vats Shivangi, Thomas Manuel S., Jathanna Vinod. (2026). Efficacy of Hand Gestures and the Hand as Foot Teaching Method Compared to Traditional Methods in Medical and Dental Education: A Scoping Review. Journal of Dental Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/jdd.70190
title: Shared pedagogical framework of gestural teaching methods: gestural simulation, analogical induction, and active engagement making the invisible visible
description: The review proposes that Air Anatomy, the Hand as Foot method, and non-verbal communication techniques rest on one pedagogical philosophy: "using the body as a dynamic, interactive tool to make the invisible visible." Its core principle is "turning abstract information into concrete, physical experiences." The framework identifies shared mechanisms — gestural simulation of anatomical structures, analogical induction by comparing familiar with complex systems, and enhanced engagement that transforms passive learning into an active, participatory process.
requirements: An educator who can shape and manipulate the hand to model the target anatomical structures or concepts during instruction
constraints: Hand as Foot is described as focusing on a specific analogy, upper limb for lower limb, while Air Anatomy is a broader application of gestural simulation
target_learners: medical and dental undergraduate and postgraduate students
target_learning_goals: spatial understanding of anatomy and complex physiological concepts
comprehension and retention of difficult knowledge points
examples: The review notes Hand as Foot might use "a clenched fist to represent the femoral head," while Air Anatomy might use cupped hands to "grip" the thalamus
key_sources: Vats Shivangi, Thomas Manuel S., Jathanna Vinod. (2026). Efficacy of Hand Gestures and the Hand as Foot Teaching Method Compared to Traditional Methods in Medical and Dental Education: A Scoping Review. Journal of Dental Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/jdd.70190

article_title: Efficacy of Hand Gestures and the Hand as Foot Teaching Method Compared to Traditional Methods in Medical and Dental Education: A Scoping Review.
citation: Vats Shivangi, Thomas Manuel S., Jathanna Vinod. (2026). Efficacy of Hand Gestures and the Hand as Foot Teaching Method Compared to Traditional Methods in Medical and Dental Education: A Scoping Review. Journal of Dental Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/jdd.70190
title: Use low-cost, equipment-free gestural teaching methods in educational settings with limited resources
description: The review presents Air Anatomy, the Hand as Foot method, and the pen and palm model as accessible, "no‐cost" or low-cost alternatives to expensive high-tech teaching aids like virtual reality or 3D models. Because "they can be implemented without special equipment," these techniques are "particularly valuable in educational settings with limited resources." In regions with limited medical education resources, an image-based teaching method can address the scarcity and simplicity of traditional teaching aids while also reducing teaching expenses.
requirements: An educator able to perform the gestural demonstrations; no special equipment
constraints: Evidence base is small: the review notes a scarcity of studies directly comparing the Hand as Foot method with conventional teaching, making relative effectiveness difficult to conclude
target_learners: medical and dental undergraduate and postgraduate students in resource-limited settings
target_learning_goals: understanding of anatomy and complex physiological concepts
examples: The review describes Hand as Foot in dentistry as a cost-effective, low-tech complement to extracted teeth, wax carving, and digital models

article_title: Systematic Review of Assessment in General Chemistry: Trends, Digital Innovations, and Integration of Theory-Laboratory Course.
citation: Oktariani O, Nahadi N, Munawaroh HSH, Rusyati L, Baruri A, Mellyzar M, Nabuasa DA, Almubarak A. (2026). Systematic Review of Assessment in General Chemistry: Trends, Digital Innovations, and Integration of Theory-Laboratory Course. F1000Research 15:1338. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.182947.1
title: Classification matrix of assessment components, instruments, and methods in general chemistry theory and laboratory (Table 3)
description: The review organizes the assessment practices of its 30 included articles into a classification matrix mapping nine assessment components — e.g. "understanding and connecting concepts", "scientific argumentation", "design and conduct experiments", and "affective experience in the laboratory" — to the instruments and methods used to measure them. It reports that "assessment is mostly dominated by the use of instruments such as multiple choice questions and description questions and assessment methods in the form of tests or written or electronic-based tasks," with rubrics, inventories, concept maps, questionnaires, checklists, interviews, and peer/self-assessment also represented. Each matrix cell cites the specific included articles (A1–A30) using that combination.
requirements: Used to map assessment components, instruments and methods across the 30 included studies for cross-study comparison
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding
laboratory skills
scientific argumentation
metacognition
affective engagement
examples: Table 3 maps, for example, the component 'design and conduct experiments' to instruments such as the EDAT skills test, IDEAA-GC1 rubric and observation checklists across articles A7, A8, A15, A19, A20, A23, A30

article_title: GenAI-Supported Virtual Patients in Health Care Education: Systematic Review.
citation: Jiang Juming, Ye Megan Zichen, Kwok Tyrone Tai-On, Wong Janet Yuen Ha. (2026). GenAI-Supported Virtual Patients in Health Care Education: Systematic Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/82756
title: Three-category design taxonomy for GenAI-supported virtual patients: input, output, and avatar
description: The review organizes the design choices of GenAI-supported virtual patients into three categories: "The designs of GenAI-supported virtual patients can be classified into three distinct categories: (1) input, (2) output, and (3) avatar." Input modalities were text (11 of 15 studies), voice (5), or hybrid (1); output corresponded closely to input mechanisms; and avatar design distinguished 6 studies using 3D-embodied virtual patients from 9 using nonembodied interfaces. The review uses this taxonomy in Table 2 to characterize the field and support its design-implementation research question.
requirements: Studies must specify input modality, output modality, and avatar embodiment for comparison across implementations

article_title: Team based learning pedagogy enhances the education quality: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

TBL not only enhances theoretical scores of medical students but also enables them to benefit from and enjoy the classes. The authors note TBL is suitable for medical students at any stage, particularly in group teaching involving a large number of students, and call for more global, high-quality studies and more standardized evaluation methods.

satisfaction

It argues TBL "provides the advantage that ensuring the effectiveness of small-group learning with high student faculty ratios", fitting understaffed pharmacy education, and states it "should be generalized in more Chinese classrooms" based on the meta-analytic evidence of higher test scores and improved student-reported abilities.

article_title: From Pilots to Practices: A Scoping Review of GenAI-Enabled Personalization in Computer Science Education
citation: Reihanian, I.; Hou, Y.; Sun, Q. (2026). From Pilots to Practices: A Scoping Review of GenAI-Enabled Personalization in Computer Science Education. AI. https://doi.org/10.3390/ai7010006
title: Theoretical grounding: GenAI personalization as a mechanism for implementing evidence-based learning-science practices at scale
description: The review connects its design-pattern findings to four established learning-science constructs. Solution-withholding designs connect to desirable difficulties theory, where introducing challenges that require effort during learning can improve long-term retention and transfer; graduated hint ladders operationalize the distinction between productive and unproductive struggle. Course-aligned worked examples and Parsons problems reflect worked-example research and the key insight of fading, progressively reducing support as competence grows, with LLMs enabling dynamic, individualized fading at finer granularity than cohort-level progressions. Test-driven tutoring and rubric-guided feedback exemplify assessment for learning, making success criteria explicit and creating revision opportunities. Artifact-grounded assistance aligns with cognitive load theory, where context-aware hints reduce the load of translating generic advice to specific code. The review concludes that GenAI personalization is not pedagogically novel so much as a mechanism for implementing evidence-based practices at scale.
requirements: Designs must preserve theoretically grounded features (desirable difficulty, graduated scaffolding, and criterion transparency) rather than optimizing for superficial metrics
constraints: The review presents these as interpretive connections to explain why certain design patterns succeed, not as empirically tested mediations
target_learning_goals: Long-term retention and transfer
Schema construction and self-regulated improvement
examples: The review states that GenAI personalization appears most promising when it maintains challenge within the zone of proximal development while reducing unproductive struggle such as environment setup, obscure syntax errors, and tooling friction
key_sources: Reihanian, I.; Hou, Y.; Sun, Q. (2026). From Pilots to Practices: A Scoping Review of GenAI-Enabled Personalization in Computer Science Education. AI. https://doi.org/10.3390/ai7010006

title: The genre-based approach derived from systemic functional linguistics, operationalized as the teaching-learning cycle of modeling, joint negotiation of text, and independent construction
description: The article presents the genre-based approach as derived from systemic functional linguistics, "concerned with the relationship between language and its functions in social settings" (Hyon, 1996, p. 696, as cited). Learning different genres is the means of language acquisition for understanding communicative purposes and linguistic features. Callaghen and Rothery (1988) developed the teaching and learning cycle with three phases: modeling (explicit teaching of lexico-grammatical and rhetorical patterns), joint negotiation of text (combining background knowledge with genre structure to compose new text with teacher guidance), and independent construction (learners draw on learnt structures to write their own text, encouraging self-learning and collaborative skills).
requirements: Instruction proceeds through the three phases of modeling, joint negotiation of text, and independent construction as described in the teaching and learning cycle.

target_learning_goals: English reading comprehension
understanding of genre structures and linguistic features
examples: The study's experimental treatment extended this cycle into a five-step applied instruction over 18 teaching hours across three units.

article_title: Teaching Mathematical Functions Using Geometric Functions Approach and Its Effect on Ninth Grade Students' Motivation
citation: Akçakın, V. (2018). Teaching Mathematical Functions Using Geometric Functions Approach and Its Effect on Ninth Grade Students’ Motivation. International Journal of Instruction, 11(1), 17-32. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.1112a
title: Geometric functions approach
description: The geometric functions approach treats functions as "geometric transformations of a point in the plane — functions that have geometric points as their input and output" (Steketee, 2012, as cited in the article). Steketee gives four reasons to prioritise it when teaching functions: cognitive (independent variable, dependent variable, and the rule connecting them), kinaesthetic (students create and change the independent variable with a simple drag motion), visual (function behaviour is observed as a visual, dynamic change), and structural (comprehension of domain, range, symbolic display, and set matching in composite functions). The article applies it with GeoGebra dynamic mathematics software on interactive whiteboards in a functions unit.
requirements: Use of advanced technologies such as dynamic mathematics software for application of the approach
constraints: Studied here only for effects on motivation, not other affective domains or achievement
target_learning_goals: understanding the function concept, including domain, range, and the vertical line test
examples: GeoGebra activities in which a slider-driven vertical line test was demonstrated on the interactive whiteboard in Experimental groups I and II

title: Genre-based instruction as an explicit, systematic, needs-based pedagogy grounded in genre analysis
description: Genre-based instruction (GBI) teaches language skills by making the structures and communicative purposes of genres explicit. The article defines genre via Swales as "a class of communicative events, the members of which share some set of communicative purposes" and lists Hyland's features of GBI: explicit, systematic, needs-based, supportive, empowering, critical, and consciousness-raising. In this study GBI was operationalized as directing students' attention to collocations, genre types, lexical and grammatical features, and similarities and differences among texts.
requirements: Overt teaching of the language patterns and social conventions of genres students commonly need, so students become aware of genre structures
constraints: The article notes critics' concerns that the genre approach neglects skills required to produce content and ignores learners' self-sufficiency, and that at its worst it interferes with learners' creativity

Genre awareness
examples: In the experimental group, teachers activated background knowledge, clarified each passage's main idea, identified its sections, and discussed genre aspects including collocations, genre types, and lexical and grammatical features

title: Generalisation Assessment Game (GAG)
description: GAG is a critical-thinking card game for English Language classes. description: The article grounds multimedia vocabulary annotation in a generative theory of multimedia learning concerned with learners' cognitive load. title: GenAI's two defining capacities in co-created item-writing: responsiveness to prompts and responsiveness to feedback
description: Within the CCSD framework, GenAI functions as the technological collaborator defined by two capacities: "responsiveness to prompts and responsiveness to feedback." Responsiveness to structured prompts preserves validity and reliability through consistent interpretation, while iterative human feedback acts as a calibration mechanism that refines difficulty, distractor plausibility, and content coherence over time. The article also identifies chain-of-thought reasoning as a key characteristic, externalising rationale so educators and learners can critically appraise items — supporting educational impact, metacognition, and acceptability.
requirements: Iterative human review; educator verification, since GenAI models have not yet reached the accuracy required for reliable high-stakes items without human refinement
constraints: Repeated generation from similar prompt structures may reduce content diversity (over-homogeneity), paradoxically undermining educational impact while appearing to enhance reliability; models may reproduce dataset biases
target_learners: Medical educators and assessment developers using GenAI
target_learning_goals: Producing and refining high-quality SBA items collaboratively with GenAI
examples: The article gives an example of reviewing a model's rationale revealing an incorrect claim in an atrial fibrillation item that rhythm control is never indicated, illustrating transparency's value for critical evaluation

title: Generational status moderates stereotype threat susceptibility: second-generation students' longer exposure to deficit-oriented narratives heightens vulnerability
description: The article advances an explanatory account in which first- and second-generation students of migrant descent differ in stereotype threat susceptibility because of socialization: second-generation students, "socialized in the relevant country from birth," experience continuous exposure to subtle deficit-oriented messages and may be more sensitive to societal stereotypes, while first-generation students' stronger immigrant identity and family "immigrant optimism" may act as a psychological buffer. title: GETAMEL — the General Extended Technology Acceptance Model for E-Learning
description: GETAMEL, proposed by Abdullah and Ward, extends the Technology Acceptance Model for e-learning contexts by adding five external variables — self-efficacy, computer anxiety, subjective norm, enjoyment, and experience — to the core TAM variables of perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, and behavioral intention. The article describes that GETAMEL "postulates a positive correlation between self‐efficacy, enjoyment, subjective norm, and experience and each perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness, as well as a negative correlation between computer anxiety and perceived ease of use". examples: The study measured all GETAMEL variables with 22 Likert items and tested the model's hypothesized paths via correlation and regression in a VR anatomy learning context

title: Gender-intensification and physiological accounts of gender-specific mental health–achievement links
description: The article offers an explanatory framework for why mental health relates to academic performance differently by gender, drawing on the "gender-intensification hypothesis" and biological accounts. It proposes that "sex hormones play a crucial role in emotional regulation and cognitive functioning throughout development", that girls' earlier pubertal maturation may increase vulnerability to academic and social pressures, and that gender stereotypes impose pressure on female students while males may benefit from positive stereotypes. Female students' stronger commitment to long-term academic goals may intensify the impact of mental health challenges on performance.

constraints: The authors present these as possible explanations, noting differences "likely reflect complex interactions between biological, psychological, and sociocultural factors"
target_learning_goals: understanding gender-specific pathways from mental health to academic outcomes
examples: The article cites Okano et al. on girls' goal commitment intensifying mental health impacts, and notes female students achieve higher grades while experiencing greater internal distress

description: Based on the bifactor results, the authors propose that the common component underlying the AGS's determination, resilience, and focus items is a single capacity they label self-regulatory resources. They suggest "general academic grit may refer to the ability to self-regulate within the academic context": coordinating determination, resilience, and focus to change thoughts, feelings, and actions so as to keep striving toward academic goals even under stressful or unfavorable conditions. citation: Ng Melvin M. R., Bowers Peter N., Bowers Jeffrey S. (2022). A promising new tool for literacy instruction: The morphological matrix. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0262260
title: Organized, generative encoding account of why morphological matrices improve memory
description: The article explains its findings via the principle that "learning and memory is best when information can be encoded in a meaningful and organized manner", drawing on Bower et al.'s hierarchical retrieval work and Fiorella and Mayer's generative learning strategies. Organized retrieval plans may improve both retrieval and encoding through generative learning, and a matrix organizer was the most effective generative strategy with "a median effect of d = 1.07 across eight studies". The base rather than affix constitutes a word's core meaning, allowing deeper semantic links when words are organized by base.
requirements: Learners who already know the meanings of the base words and affixes being organized, as in the experiments described
constraints: The article notes a large gulf between the memory experiments with undergraduates and classroom teaching of children, and that which literacy skills the matrices best suit (word naming, spelling, vocabulary) remains unclear

spelling, vocabulary, and word naming

article_title: Using DNA From Mothers and Children to Study Parental Investment in Children's Educational Attainment.
citation: Wertz J., Moffitt T. E., Agnew-Blais J., Arseneault L., Belsky D. W., Corcoran D. L., Houts R., Matthews T., Prinz J. A., Richmond-Rakerd L. S., Sugden K., Williams B., Caspi A. (2020). Using DNA from mothers and children to study parental investment in children's educational attainment. Child Development, 91(5), 1745-1761. https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.13329
title: Genetic nurture and the social genome: genetics and parenting effects are not a dichotomy, environments lie on the pathway from genotype to phenotype
description: This framework holds that parents' education-associated genetics shape the family environments they create, which in turn influence children's outcomes over and above direct genetic transmission. The article shows that "genetic influences on children's educational attainment partly manifested through parenting; an environmentally mediated genetic effect." It argues genetics should not be treated only as a confound of parenting effects, and that "environments are part of the pathway from genotype to phenotype", implying a 'social genome' encompassing the genomes of others in a person's social context. It cautions that genetic associations with outcomes may partly reflect environments created by other people's genes, so environmental confounding must be considered when estimating genetic effects.
requirements: Genotype data from both generations (parents and children) plus longitudinal measures of the environments parents create, to separate transmitted from non-transmitted genetic effects.
constraints: Estimates of genetic nurture rely on the assumption that mothers' and children's polygenic scores are measured with identical error; the education polygenic score captures only a portion of genetic influences, so effects may be underestimated.
target_learning_goals: educational attainment

article_title: Intergenerational Transmission of Education and ADHD: Effects of Parental Genotypes.
citation: de Zeeuw Eveline L., Hottenga Jouke-Jan, Ouwens Klaasjan G., Dolan Conor V., Ehli Erik A., Davies Gareth E., Boomsma Dorret I., van Bergen Elsje. (2020). Intergenerational Transmission of Education and ADHD: Effects of Parental Genotypes. Behavior Genetics, Volume 50, Issue 4. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10519-020-09992-w
title: Genetic nurturing design exploiting transmitted versus non-transmitted parental alleles
description: The genetic nurturing design separates, within genotyped parent–offspring trios, polygenic scores based on alleles parents transmitted to their offspring from scores based on non-transmitted alleles. Because non-transmitted alleles cannot affect the child directly, "The effect of the non-transmitted PGS is necessarily mediated by parental phenotypes, insofar as they contribute to the rearing environment of the offspring (genetic nurturing)". Transmitted alleles carry both direct genetic effects and indirect effects mediated by the environment parents create. The article applies this design to educational attainment and ADHD polygenic scores to test environmental transmission of parental characteristics to offspring outcomes.
requirements: Requires measured genotypes and phenotypes in offspring and measured genotypes in both parents, so transmission at each locus can be determined
constraints: GWAS limitations carry over, including residual population stratification, variation in phenotype definitions in discovery samples, and population differences; the EA sample had twice as many females as males, which could have overestimated the genetic nurturing effect
target_learners: children and adult offspring in general-population family samples
target_learning_goals: educational attainment
academic achievement
ADHD symptoms
examples: Polygenic scores for educational attainment and ADHD were computed with LDpred on transmitted and non-transmitted allele datasets from 2649 Dutch trio families and regressed on offspring outcomes

description: The article invokes a theoretical framework proposed by Gee, Griffin, and McCardle to explain how human–animal interaction influences learning. citation: Phillips SC, Hawley CE, Triantafylidis LK, Schwartz AW. (2019). Geriatrics 5Ms for Primary Care Workshop. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.10814
title: Geriatrics 5Ms framework: Mobility, Medications, Mind, Multicomplexity, and Matters Most as an organizing framework for geriatric care and education
description: The Geriatrics 5Ms is a framework for caring for older adults comprising "Mobility, Medications, Mind, Multicomplexity, and Matters Most," debuted by Tinetti, Huang, and Molnar in 2017. The article uses it as a "unifying framework" to structure a half-day workshop, mapping each M to ACGME core geriatrics competency domains for internal and family medicine residents (e.g., Mobility to Ambulatory Care; Matters Most to Palliative and End-of-Life Care). The framework aligns with the age-friendly health system imperative and concisely communicates core competencies related to issues of aging.
requirements: Facilitators with experience in primary care of older adults, geriatric medicine fellows, and/or clinical pharmacists; implementable by one to four facilitators
constraints: The article states the workshop is not meant to be a comprehensive review of all topics included in the Geriatrics 5Ms; its main goal is providing evidence-based tools tied to the framework
target_learners: Internal and family medicine residents in primary care settings
Medical students, nurse practitioner or physician assistant trainees, and practicing clinicians (stated as adaptable audiences)
target_learning_goals: Applying the Geriatrics 5Ms framework to care for older adults
Meeting ACGME core geriatrics competencies for residency education
examples: The workshop structured five interactive modules (Mobility, Medications, Mind, Multicomplexity and Matters Most) around a longitudinal primary care patient case, each building on prior module content
key_sources: Phillips SC, Hawley CE, Triantafylidis LK, Schwartz AW. (2019). Geriatrics 5Ms for Primary Care Workshop. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.10814

article_title: Geriatrics 5Ms for Primary Care Workshop.
citation: Phillips SC, Hawley CE, Triantafylidis LK, Schwartz AW. (2019). Geriatrics 5Ms for Primary Care Workshop. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.10814
title: Geriatrics 5Ms half-day primary care workshop with longitudinal patient case and point-of-care tools
description: A half-day (2.5-hour time block, 2 hours 45 minutes class time) workshop piloted with 33 internal medicine residents, built through Kern's six-step curriculum development approach. It comprises five interactive modules—Mobility (falls risk factors), Medications (polypharmacy and deprescribing), Mind (cognitive impairment evaluation), and Multicomplexity and Matters Most (prognostication and cancer screening)—centered on "a longitudinal patient case with unfolding information." Learners receive point-of-care tools including a Geriatrics 5Ms summary and EMR template, a deprescribing algorithm, and access to ePrognosis and the Mini-Cog. Peer-reviewed appendices include slide decks, handouts, a facilitator checklist, and evaluation instruments.
requirements: Computer and projector, PowerPoint slides (Appendices A–E), whiteboard or poster board with sticky notes and markers, learner handouts, and a lead facilitator checklist; clinics closed to permit attendance
constraints: Scheduling challenges and time constraints for implementation; blocking clinic patient care sessions "is not feasible at all institutions"; sustainability depends on institutional support and dedicated teaching time
target_learners: Clinical-year resident physicians in primary care settings
target_learning_goals: Applying the Geriatrics 5Ms framework to older adult care
Applying a five-step deprescribing plan
Listing dementia warning signs and diagnostic workup components
Making patient-centered cancer screening recommendations aligned with goals and prognosis
examples: Three pilot sessions over 4 weeks with six to 14 learners each, facilitated by three geriatricians, one geriatric fellow, one PGY 3 resident, and two pharmacists
key_sources: Phillips SC, Hawley CE, Triantafylidis LK, Schwartz AW. (2019). Geriatrics 5Ms for Primary Care Workshop. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.10814

article_title: Skills for generalist and specialist nurses working in the prevention and control of infections in Brazil.
citation: Massaroli Aline, Martini Jussara Gue, Moya José Luis Medina, Pereira Milca Severino, Tipple Anaclara Ferreira Veiga, Maestri Eleine. (2019). Skills for generalist and specialist nurses working in the prevention and control of infections in Brazil. Revista Latino-Americana de Enfermagem. https://doi.org/10.1590/1518-8345.2620.3134
title: Initial nurse training should develop generic HCRI competencies because infection issues are present in all health services
description: The article argues that the generic infection prevention and control competencies belong in undergraduate nursing curricula. It states that "the generic competences for the prevention and control of HCRI are crucial in the training of the generalist nurse, since the issue of HCRI is present in all services", because the generalist nurse works at any point in the health care network. Defining the competencies is presented as "the first step to begin the rethinking of the teaching and learning process in the initial training of nurses".
requirements: Undergraduate courses must establish the moments in which each competency is developed throughout the course
constraints: The differentiation of generic and specific competences is not intended to fragment or isolate them
target_learning_goals: prevention and control of healthcare-related infections
comprehensive care across different health services
examples: The panel listed 14 generic competencies, from hand hygiene to collaboration with epidemiological surveillance, that the generalist nurse must have upon graduation
key_sources: Massaroli Aline, Martini Jussara Gue, Moya José Luis Medina, Pereira Milca Severino, Tipple Anaclara Ferreira Veiga, Maestri Eleine. (2019). Skills for generalist and specialist nurses working in the prevention and control of infections in Brazil. Revista Latino-Americana de Enfermagem. https://doi.org/10.1590/1518-8345.2620.3134

article_title: Using social network analysis to understand online Problem-Based Learning and predict performance.
citation: Saqr M, Fors U, Nouri J. (2018). Using social network analysis to understand online Problem-Based Learning and predict performance. PLoS ONE 13(9): e0203590. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0203590
title: SNA sociogram visualization of online PBL interactions using Gephi
description: The article describes rendering interaction networks ("sociograms") of blended PBL courses in the open-source SNA software Gephi (version 9.1), using the Fruchterman Reingold force-directed layout. Nodes represent students and tutors, edges represent interactions, and node size denotes degree centrality, so "active and inactive groups can be quickly identified" and influential or isolated learners spotted. The authors present this visualization as a practical, cost-effective alternative to effortful manual content analysis, deliverable automatically via learning-management-system plugins.
requirements: Interaction data extracted from the learning management system (Moodle), processed into network files with each group or course analysed as a separate network
constraints: The article notes its results may have contextual constraints limiting generalizability to other interactive course environments
target_learners: undergraduate dental students in blended problem-based learning courses
target_learning_goals: monitoring collaborative engagement and identifying influential and isolated learners in online PBL
examples: Fig 2 summarizes interactions across the four courses; Fig 3 shows Principles of Dental Sciences (QDENT 214), where groups D and E showed marked interactivity and group C was less interactive
key_sources: Saqr M, Fors U, Nouri J. (2018). Using social network analysis to understand online Problem-Based Learning and predict performance. PLoS ONE 13(9): e0203590. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0203590

article_title: Cognitive Style and Mobile E-Learning in Emergent Otorhinolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery Disorders for Millennial Undergraduate Medical Students: Randomized Controlled Trial.
citation: Lee Li-Ang, Chao Yi-Ping, Huang Chung-Guei, Fang Ji-Tseng, Wang Shu-Ling, Chuang Cheng-Keng, Kang Chung-Jan, Hsin Li-Jen, Lin Wan-Ni, Fang Tuan-Jen, Li Hsueh-Yu. (2018). Cognitive Style and Mobile E-Learning in Emergent Otorhinolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery Disorders for Millennial Undergraduate Medical Students: Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.8987
title: Cognitive style classification of field-dependent, field-intermediate, and field-independent learners via the Group Embedded Figures Test
description: The article uses the 25-item Group Embedded Figures Test (Spearman-Brown reliability 0.82) to assess cognitive style, where "the GEFT scores ranged from 0 (the most FD) to 18 (the most FI)". The classical dichotomy (FD ≤12, FI >12) left most students classified FI, so the authors adopted a modified three-category classification (FD, FINT, FI) based on the mean GEFT score ± 0.25 SD, yielding FD n=15, FINT n=17, FI n=28. This framework organizes the study's analysis of how cognitive style moderates module effects on knowledge gain and satisfaction.
requirements: Preinstructional assessment of cognitive style with the GEFT before assigning or designing instructional materials
constraints: The article notes the classical classification did not seem associated with learning preference or outcomes and that relatively few students were classical FD learners, motivating the modified classification
target_learning_goals: matching instructional modules to learners' cognitive style
designing varied e-learning modules for different cognitive styles
examples: The study stratified students into classical FD (GEFT ≤12) and classical FI (GEFT >12) subgroups, then reclassified them into modified FD, FINT, and FI groups for post hoc analysis

article_title: Teaching clinical reasoning through hypothetico-deduction is (slightly) better than self-explanation in tutorial groups: An experimental study.
citation: Al Rumayyan Ahmed, Ahmed Nasr, Al Subait Reem, Al Ghamdi Ghassan, Mohammed Mahzari Moeber, Awad Mohamed Tarig, Rotgans Jerome I., Donmez Mustafa, Mamede Silvia, Schmidt Henk G. (2018). Teaching clinical reasoning through hypothetico-deduction is (slightly) better than self-explanation in tutorial groups: An experimental study. Perspectives on Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40037-018-0409-x
title: When teaching diagnostic reasoning with sequential cases, have learners generate multiple hypotheses per case
description: The article suggests the advantage of the hypothetico-deductive condition arose because students were "encouraged to explicitly consider more than one hypothesis, while the self-explanation condition did not". Since learning and test cases differed, generating multiple candidate diagnoses gave hypothesizing students a chance that one of their hypotheses would return in the test phase. Teaching with explicit multi-hypothesis generation is therefore the article's tentative explanation-based recommendation.
requirements: Clinical cases whose learning and test exemplars vary; learners must articulate several candidate diagnoses rather than one.
constraints: The authors present this as a tentative explanation, not a tested manipulation: "further research is required to explore which approach works better and under which conditions."
target_learners: Undergraduate medical students learning diagnostic reasoning
target_learning_goals: Building a differential diagnosis; transferring diagnostic skill to new exemplars of a clinical presentation
examples: Hypothetico-deduction students wrote one or more diagnoses after the history, after the physical examination, and after the laboratory data, and discussed hypotheses with peers at each stage.
key_sources: Al Rumayyan Ahmed, Ahmed Nasr, Al Subait Reem, Al Ghamdi Ghassan, Mohammed Mahzari Moeber, Awad Mohamed Tarig, Rotgans Jerome I., Donmez Mustafa, Mamede Silvia, Schmidt Henk G. (2018). Teaching clinical reasoning through hypothetico-deduction is (slightly) better than self-explanation in tutorial groups: An experimental study. article_title: A comparison of medical education in Germany and the United States: from applying to medical school to the beginnings of residency.
citation: Zavlin D, Jubbal KT, Noé JG, Gansbacher B. (2017). A comparison of medical education in Germany and the United States: from applying to medical school to the beginnings of residency. GMS German Medical Science, Vol. 15, Doc15. http://www.egms.de/en/journals/gms/2017-15/000256.shtml
title: Two contrasting medical education pathways: Germany's integrated 6-year post-secondary model versus the US two-stage Bachelor's-plus-4-year M.D. model
description: The review's organizing framework is a chronological comparison of the two national medical education systems from application through the beginnings of residency. Germany employs an integrated curriculum: "Germany currently employs an integrated medical curriculum that typically begins right after high school and consists of a 2-year long pre-clinical segment teaching basic sciences and a 4-year clinical segment". The US instead uses a two-stage process in which a Bachelor's degree precedes a 4-year medical program of 2 basic-science and 2 clinical years. The framework is populated by comparing application, curriculum, examinations, financing, and residency entry in each country.
requirements: Sources include recent publications, legal guidelines of official organizations, media articles, and the authors' personal experiences
constraints: Non-systematic narrative review; private German universities and Caribbean medical schools are explicitly excluded from consideration
target_learners: medical students at any stage of training
graduating high school students considering study abroad
target_learning_goals: understanding the structure of medical education in Germany and the United States
planning international rotations or study abroad
examples: The review stratifies all findings following the typical chronological career path of a medical student, from application through residency entry
key_sources: Zavlin D, Jubbal KT, Noé JG, Gansbacher B. (2017). A comparison of medical education in Germany and the United States: from applying to medical school to the beginnings of residency. GMS German Medical Science, Vol. 15, Doc15. http://www.egms.de/en/journals/gms/2017-15/000256.shtml

article_title: Genetics affects choice of academic subjects as well as achievement.
citation: Rimfeld, K., Ayorech, Z., Dale, P. S., Kovas, Y. & Plomin, R. (2016). Genetics affects choice of academic subjects as well as achievement. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/srep26373
title: Genotype-environment correlation: individuals actively choose and create educational experiences based in part on their genetic propensities
description: The article proposes a genetic way of thinking about education in which "individuals actively choose and create educational experiences on the basis of their genetic propensities, called genotype-environment correlation". This active view ('leading out') contrasts with what the authors call "the traditional passive model of instruction ('shoving in')". The finding that DNA differences affect appetites (choice) as well as aptitudes (achievement) grounds the account: children are "not passive recipients of instruction, but instead are active participants in their path to knowledge".
requirements: Requires that learners face genuine choices among educational options, as at A-level where students are free to choose from over 80 different subjects
constraints: The authors state the findings "may not generalize to other populations" and that heritability "describes what is, not what could be"
target_learners: post-16 students choosing A-level subjects in England and Wales
target_learning_goals: academic subject choice
educational achievement
key_sources: Rimfeld, K., Ayorech, Z., Dale, P. S., Kovas, Y. & Plomin, R. (2016). Genetics affects choice of academic subjects as well as achievement. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/srep26373

article_title: Evaluation of a National Online Educational Program in Geriatric Psychiatry.
citation: Law Marcus, Rapoport Mark J., Seitz Dallas, Davidson Marla, Madan Robert, Wiens Andrew. (2015). Evaluation of a National Online Educational Program in Geriatric Psychiatry. Academic Psychiatry. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40596-015-0377-y
title: Online study group (OSG) for geriatric psychiatry CPD
description: An interactive, expert-facilitated, asynchronous online study group for psychiatrists and residents preparing for the RCPSC geriatric psychiatry certification exam. It comprised 22 fourteen-day modules; each facilitator recommended readings, and participants used four discussion rooms: short-answer questions, reflective discussion, a journal club, and a "Clinical Corner" for cases and questions. The first cohort ran October 2012 to August 2013 with 45 practicing psychiatrists and 5 trainees.
requirements: A facilitator (geriatric psychiatrist) per module who recommends readings and poses questions
A web portal with group discussion rooms and access to parallel didactic lecture recordings
constraints: Participation was not mandatory and the course was self-accredited, which the authors identify as possible barriers to active participation
target_learners: Practicing psychiatrists caring for the elderly
target_learning_goals: Preparation for the RCPSC geriatric psychiatry certification examination
Knowledge of assessment and treatment of geriatric psychiatric disorders
examples: Midway through 2012–2013, five study groups were consolidated into three to generate more discussion within each group
key_sources: Law Marcus, Rapoport Mark J., Seitz Dallas, Davidson Marla, Madan Robert, Wiens Andrew. (2015). Evaluation of a National Online Educational Program in Geriatric Psychiatry. Academic Psychiatry. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40596-015-0377-y

article_title: Effects of geriatric clinical skills training on the attitudes of medical students.
citation: Goeldlin Adrian O, Siegenthaler Andrea, Moser André, Stoeckli Yvette D, Stuck Andreas E, Schoenenberger Andreas W. (2014). Effects of geriatric clinical skills training on the attitudes of medical students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6920-14-233
title: Geriatric clinical skills training: four 2.5-hour bedside sessions with real patients plus a self-preparation textbook
description: The intervention was a geriatric clinical skills training (CST) of "four 2.5-hour teaching sessions" covering central geriatric assessment domains (activities of daily living, cognition, mobility, social situation, nutrition, medication, continence, hearing and vision screening, and a consolidating complete geriatric assessment). Each session began with a 45-minute interactive introduction, then students worked in small groups of four to five with real patients at the bedside, supervised by a clinician experienced in geriatric medicine, using only validated instruments (MMSE, BADL) with a textbook for self-preparation.
requirements: A textbook with detailed instructions on performing and interpreting the validated instruments, distributed before the first session
Supervision by a clinician experienced in geriatric medicine
Small groups of four to five students working with real patients at the bedside
constraints: Students did not do ward work during the intervention period
Evaluated at a single academic institution with several teachers, limiting generalizability
target_learning_goals: Geriatric assessment skills (cognition, mobility, ADL, nutrition, medication, continence, sensory screening)
Attitudes toward elderly patients
Geriatric knowledge
examples: Students were allocated to CST groups in alphabetical order by family name, and completed the questionnaire either at the beginning of the first or the last session
key_sources: Goeldlin Adrian O, Siegenthaler Andrea, Moser André, Stoeckli Yvette D, Stuck Andreas E, Schoenenberger Andreas W. (2014). Effects of geriatric clinical skills training on the attitudes of medical students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6920-14-233

article_title: Sustained effects of online genetics education: a randomized controlled trial on oncogenetics.
citation: Houwink Elisa JF, van Teeffelen Sarah R, Muijtjens Arno MM, Henneman Lidewij, Jacobi Florijn, van Luijk Scheltus J, Jan Dinant Geert, van der Vleuten Cees, Cornel Martina C. (2014). Sustained effects of online genetics education: a randomized controlled trial on oncogenetics. European Journal of Human Genetics. https://doi.org/10.1038/ejhg.2013.163
title: Genetics e-learning CPD module on oncogenetics for general practitioners
description: A 2-hour online continuing professional development module on oncogenetics for primary-care physicians, containing "multimedia presentations, interactive cases with feedback, enabling tools (for referral, family history and online information searches)" and step-by-step clinical practice guides. Its contents were designed to include 10 items prioritized in a multidisciplinary Delphi study on core competencies of health professionals endorsed by the NHG. Participants could freely revisit program sections, and the module was designed to enable completion within 2 hours.
requirements: Designed to enable completion within 2 hours
Content based on a prior multidisciplinary Delphi needs assessment of core competencies endorsed by the NHG
constraints: Developed for the Dutch general-practice context and the NHG's usual online CPD presentation style
target_learning_goals: Identify patients with an inherited predisposition to cancer
Apply oncogenetics guidelines in identifying patients for whom referral is indicated
Explain the possibilities and limitations of oncogenetic testing
examples: Interactive cases on breast cancer due to BRCA mutations and on colon cancer (eg, Lynch syndrome) due to APC/mismatch-repair gene mutations

article_title: Webinar software: a tool for developing more effective lectures (online or in-person).
citation: Mayorga Eduardo P., Bekerman Jesica G., Palis Ana G. (2014). Webinar Software: A Tool for Developing More Effective Lectures (Online or In-Person). Middle East African Journal of Ophthalmology. https://doi.org/10.4103/0974-9233.129756
title: Generational learning: millennial learners' traits and recommended teaching strategies
description: The article presents a generational-cohort framework in which individuals born in the same period share key life experiences, classifying twentieth-century generations from traditionalists to generation Z. It describes generation Y (millennials, born 1980-2000) as having "an orientation to collaborative and team work", comfort with technology, and multitasking preferences, and cites recommendations for teaching them, including clear rules, frequent feedback, clear objectives, and technological resources such as case-based conferences and audience response systems.
requirements: Teaching strategies matched to the described generational traits, such as technological resources and frequent feedback
constraints: The article notes that while there are individual differences, studies describe some characteristics of this generation
target_learning_goals: engagement of new generations of professionals in learning
examples: Moreno-Walton et al.'s consensus recommendations for teaching new generations of residents, including setting clear rules and incorporating peer evaluations
key_sources: Mayorga Eduardo P., Bekerman Jesica G., Palis Ana G. (2014). Webinar Software: A Tool for Developing More Effective Lectures (Online or In-Person). Middle East African Journal of Ophthalmology. https://doi.org/10.4103/0974-9233.129756

article_title: Do different medical curricula influence self-assessed clinical thinking of students?
citation: Gehlhar Kirsten, Klimke-Jung Kathrin, Stosch Christoph, Fischer Martin R. (2014). Do different medical curricula influence self-assessed clinical thinking of students? GMS Zeitschrift für Medizinische Ausbildung 31(2), Doc23. http://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2014-31/zma000915.shtml
title: German-language Diagnostic Thinking Inventory (DTI) for self-assessed clinical reasoning
description: The DTI is a 41-item self-assessment questionnaire measuring "self-evaluated flexibility in thinking and structure of knowledge in memory independently of context". Each item presents a stem with a 6-point scale whose ends hold opposing statements, with the more advanced reasoning response randomly placed at either end. This study administered a German translation (courtesy of Dr. Stieger) in machine-readable form to 247 student volunteers from three medical schools in varying clinical semesters.
requirements: Requires completion of all 41 items; only questionnaires with all questions clearly answered were included in the analysis
constraints: Does not objectively gauge clinical reasoning as such; measures self-assessment only
Subscale internal consistency was meagre in this sample, restricting analyses to total scores
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning
diagnostic thinking
examples: Administered October to December 2010 at three North Rhine-Westphalia medical schools; scores compared with Mann-Whitney tests and Cohen's d, with total scores reaching a maximum of 126 points
key_sources: Gehlhar Kirsten, Klimke-Jung Kathrin, Stosch Christoph, Fischer Martin R. (2014). Do different medical curricula influence self-assessed clinical thinking of students? GMS Zeitschrift für Medizinische Ausbildung 31(2), Doc23. http://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2014-31/zma000915.shtml

article_title: The role of simulation in developing communication and gestural skills in medical students.
citation: Bagnasco Annamaria, Pagnucci Nicola, Tolotti Angela, Rosa Francesca, Torre Giancarlo, Sasso Loredana. (2014). The role of simulation in developing communication and gestural skills in medical students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6920-14-106
title: Clinical skill laboratory programme at the Advanced Simulation Center of the University of Genoa
description: A week of laboratory sessions at the University of Genoa’s Advanced Simulation Center whose seven topics were chosen to “contribute to the development of communication and gestural skills”, from venipuncture and bladder catheterization to physical examination and history taking. Doctor and nurse trainers, simulated patients, interactive multimedia simulators, student-built checklists and a video-recorded role-play session with observation grid supported learning.
requirements: Facilities that allow several laboratories to run at the same time in adjacent rooms with a life-like, realistic quality
An interprofessional team of medical doctor and nurse trainers plus simulated patients
constraints: In this implementation only the teaching staff was interprofessional, and the students were only 3rd Year students of medicine
target_learning_goals: communication and gestural skills
clinical procedural skills such as venipuncture and bladder catheterization
examples: Third-year medical students attended in groups for one week, progressing through observation of simulation, structured brainstorming, production of checklists and reproduction of activities with interactive simulators, fellow students and simulated patients
key_sources: Bagnasco Annamaria, Pagnucci Nicola, Tolotti Angela, Rosa Francesca, Torre Giancarlo, Sasso Loredana. (2014). The role of simulation in developing communication and gestural skills in medical students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6920-14-106
